The epidermis is made up of basal cells and other cells. Basal cell skin cancer occurs when some basal cells become abnormal and grow out of control. Fair skin, red or blond hair, or light eye color – People with lighter-colored skin are at a higher risk of developing skin cancer because melanin (skin pigment) filters out the sun's harmful UV rays. Age – Risk increases with age because sun exposure builds up over time. But skin cancer is becoming more common in younger people. Basal cell skin cancer is highly treatable and curable. Catching it and treating it early is key. Surgery is the most common treatment for basal cell skin cancer. In some cases, radiation therapy or systemic therapy might be used to treat it. Following your treatment, you will have full skin exams with your doctor at least once a year. Between these periods, prevention is important. See Chapter 4: Treatment by risk and recurrence for more information. Recurrence is when basal cell skin cancer returns to the area

results.info_summary: The primary risk factor for basal cell carcinoma is UV light exposure (UV radiation) from the sun or tanning beds, which can damage DNA in basal skin cells. Other risk factors include fair skin, red or blond hair, or light eye color; increasing age (due to cumulative sun exposure); personal or family history of skin cancer; radiation therapy (especially at a young age); and immune suppression (e.g., from organ transplants or autoimmune diseases).

Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) symptoms vary by skin tone:

- **In lighter skin**, lesions may appear as:
  - Flat, pale or yellow areas resembling a scar
  - Red patches that might be itchy
  - Small, pink or red, shiny bumps that may have blue, brown, or black areas
  - Open sores that don't heal and might bleed, or go away and come back

- **In darker (brown and black) skin**, BCC can appear as a brown or glossy black bump with a rolled border, sometimes mistaken for a normal mole.

Also watch for any new, changing, bleeding, or unusual skin growths. BCC most commonly develops in sun-exposed areas (face, head, neck, arms, legs, trunk) but can occur anywhere on the body.

Content: 47: Radiation therapy Radiation therapy (RT) is a type of cancer treatment that uses beams of intense energy – from electrons (beams), photons (high-energy x-rays), or protons (charged particles) -- to kill cancer cells. Radiation therapy usually involves 5 daily brief treatments per week over 3 to 7 weeks. Radiation treatments should be given by a practicing radiation oncologist (a doctor who is an expert in radiation treatment). Types of radiation therapy There are two general types of radiation therapy that can be used to treat CSCC: external beam radiation therapy (EBRT) and brachytherapy. In EBRT, a beam of radiation is directed at the tumor from a machine. The two most common types of external beam radiation for CSCC are electrons and photons. Electrons are used to treat superficial tumors. Photons are used to treat deeper, more invasive tumors. In brachytherapy, a radiation source is placed close to or in direct contact with the tumor for a short period of time. Uses for radiation therapy Radiation therapy is an option for people after resection (surgery) of their cancer, or for those who cannot or choose not to have surgery. However, radiation therapy can be very effective for small tumors, and for tumors in areas such

**Follow-up for basal cell carcinoma (BCC):**

The retrieved information still does **not** provide BCC-specific follow-up recommendations. The available NCCN patient guideline content covers follow-up in detail only for **squamous cell skin cancer (CSCC)**, with general survivorship guidance that may be relevant:

- After treatment, **regular skin exams by a doctor are very important** to monitor for return of skin cancer. These exams should include a **complete check of the skin on the entire body**, plus the **lymph nodes closest to the cancer site**.
- **Frequency depends on risk and extent of cancer:**
  - For **local CSCC**, the first 2 years after treatment are most important: exams at least **every 3–12 months for low-risk patients** or **every 3–6 months for high-risk patients**.
  - If no further skin cancer develops in the first 2 years, exams can be spaced to **every 6–12 months for another 3 years**.
  - After that, NCCN experts recommend **annual exams for life**.
  - For **very high-risk local CSCC**, exams should occur **every 3 months**.

However, radiation therapy can be very effective for small tumors, and for tumors in areas such as the head and neck. Radiation therapy should not be used in people who have certain genetic conditions that put them at higher risk of skin cancer caused by radiation, such as basal cell nevus syndrome or xeroderma pigmentosum. It may also not be appropriate for some people who have connective tissue diseases, such as lupus or scleroderma. The same area generally should not be treated with radiation more than once. When CSCC grows in a radiated area, it usually needs to be removed with surgery. However, the area often doesn’t heal as well because the tissues were weakened by the radiation. This is especially true for CSCC on the scalp. A radiation oncologist should help you determine whether this treatment is appropriate for you. Adjuvant therapy refers to therapy that is given after primary treatment to lower the risk that cancer will come back. Radiation is sometimes used as adjuvant therapy after surgery to kill any remaining cancer cells, or to help prevent recurrence for patients with high-risk tumors. The epidermis is made up of basal cells and other cells. Basal cell skin cancer occurs when some basal cells become abnormal and grow out of control. **Summary:**

Systemic therapy may be considered for BCC (basal cell carcinoma) in the following situations:

- When radiation therapy is not expected to completely eliminate the cancer or may damage critical healthy organs, **systemic therapy alone is recommended**.
- **Immunotherapy with an immune checkpoint inhibitor** is a recommended treatment option if the patient is eligible.
- **Platinum-based chemotherapy** is a recommended option for use alongside radiation when systemic therapy is planned with radiation.
- Enrolling in a **clinical trial** for systemic therapy is also an option; such trials may involve **chemotherapy, targeted therapy, or immunotherapy**.
- If the patient is not eligible for an immune checkpoint inhibitor or a clinical trial, systemic therapy options include **platinum-based chemotherapy and targeted therapy**.

**Note:** The provided information primarily discusses squamous cell skin cancer (CSCC) rather than BCC specifically. However, the systemic therapy options mentioned (immunotherapy/immune checkpoint inhibitors, platinum-based chemotherapy, targeted therapy, and clinical trials) are the relevant details available.

results.info_summary: Yes, BCC (basal cell carcinoma) can potentially spread to lymph nodes, though it is rare. The information provided indicates that cancer cells can travel through blood and lymph fluid to form tumors in other parts of the body, including lymph nodes. Specifically, if lymph nodes feel larger than they should be, cancer may have spread to them (known as "nodal disease"). Diagnosis is confirmed through needle biopsy of the lymph node. Treatment for skin cancer that has spread to nearby lymph nodes typically involves surgery to remove the cancerous lesion and affected lymph nodes, sometimes followed by radiation therapy or systemic therapy.

Basal cell skin cancer, also known as basal cell carcinoma (BCC), is the most common type of skin cancer. About 3 million cases of basal cell skin cancer are diagnosed every year in the United States. The good news is it can be cured in most cases. Treatment usually involves surgery to remove the cancer. Keep reading to find out more. What is basal cell skin cancer? Basal cell skin cancer is the most common of all skin cancer types. If caught early, it is easily treatable and curable. This is because it rarely metastasizes (spreads). Skin cancers often occur in the top layer of the skin (epidermis) and less commonly in the middle layer of the skin (dermis). The epidermis is made up of basal cells and other cells. Basal cell skin cancer occurs when some basal cells become abnormal and grow out of control. This cancer usually develops in areas exposed to the sun, including the face, head, neck, arms, legs, and trunk. But it can occur anywhere on the body. results.info_summary:
Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) symptoms vary by skin tone:

**In lighter skin, lesions can look like:**
- Flat, pale, or yellow areas resembling a scar
- Red patches that may be itchy
- Small, pink or red, shiny bumps that may have blue, brown, or black areas
- Open sores that don't heal and may bleed, or go away and come back

**In darker (brown and black) skin:**
- A brown or glossy black bump with a rolled border, which can be mistaken for a normal mole

**General warning signs:** Any new, changing, bleeding, or unusual skin growths should be checked. BCC most commonly develops in sun-exposed areas (face, head, neck, arms, legs, trunk) but can occur anywhere on the body.

results.info_summary:
Radiation therapy and/or systemic therapy may be used for BCC in the following situations:

- **After surgery when cancer remains:** If surgery (including Mohs or other PDEMA) does not remove all of the cancer and further surgery is not possible, radiation therapy may be used, with or without systemic therapy.
- **When surgery is not an option:** If you are not a candidate for surgery, radiation therapy is typically used instead, and systemic therapy may be given in addition.
- **When radiation is insufficient or risky:** If radiation therapy is not expected to kill the cancer completely or may damage critical healthy organs, systemic therapy alone is recommended.
- **Specific systemic options:** Platinum-based chemotherapy is recommended for use with radiation. Immunotherapy with an immune checkpoint inhibitor is recommended if eligible. Clinical trials for systemic therapy (chemotherapy, targeted therapy, or immunotherapy) are also an option.

Weakened immune system When your immune system is weakened, your body has trouble fighting off viruses, bacteria, and fungi. This can lead to infections and other health risks. Having a weakened immune system can put you at risk of squamous cell skin cancer. An example of when this happens is after organ transplantation. If you received an organ from another person, you likely take drugs to stop your body from attacking the donated organ. These drugs, called immunosuppressants, also reduce the body’s ability to fight infection and disease. The immune system also may not work well if you have other health conditions, such as: Lymphoma (cancer of the lymph nodes) Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (cancer of white blood cells in bone marrow) Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) or AIDS Any of these conditions can weaken the immune system,

**Refined summary:**

In lighter skin, basal cell carcinoma (BCC) lesions can appear as small, pink or red, shiny bumps that may have blue, brown, or black areas. This is one of several possible presentations; BCC in lighter skin can also look like flat, pale or yellow areas (resembling a scar), red patches that may be itchy, or open sores that don't heal and might bleed or go away and come back. In darker (brown and black) skin, BCC can appear as a brown or glossy black bump with a rolled border, which can be mistaken for a normal mole. Any new, changing, bleeding, or unusual skin growth should be evaluated, since skin cancer is easier to cure when caught early. BCC is the most common type of skin cancer (about 3 million U.S. cases diagnosed yearly) and is usually curable, rarely spreading (metastasizing); it most often develops in sun-exposed areas such as the face, head, neck, arms, legs, and trunk. analysis.current_understanding: In the context of basal cell carcinoma (BCC), a shiny bump on the skin is a clinical sign that may suggest BCC. Specifically, in lighter skin, BCC lesions can appear as small, pink or red, shiny bumps that may also have blue, brown, or black areas. In darker skin, BCC can present as a brown or glossy black bump with a rolled border, which can be mistaken for a normal mole. Therefore, a shiny bump is one possible presentation of BCC, and any new, changing, bleeding, or unusual skin growth should be evaluated by a healthcare professional.

Your doctor will choose one based on the size of the affected area, where it is on your body, and other factors. Any biopsy is likely to leave at least a small scar. Different methods can result in different types of scars. Talk to your doctor about the type of biopsy and the risk of scarring before you have the biopsy. No matter which type of biopsy is done, it should remove as much of the suspected area as possible for an accurate diagnosis to be made. Skin biopsies are done using a local anesthetic (numbing medicine), which is injected into the area with a very small needle. You will likely feel a small prick and a little stinging as the medicine is injected, but you should not feel any pain during the biopsy. Skin shave biopsy A skin shave biopsy can be done on the skin surface (superficial) or deeper. Superficial shave biopsies are useful for very flat skin lesions. results.info_summary: For basal cell carcinoma (BCC), surgery is the usual treatment, but alternatives exist when surgery is not possible or not chosen. Radiation therapy is a recommended option for patients who cannot or choose not to have surgery, and it may be used after surgery to kill remaining cancer cells. Systemic therapy (e.g., chemotherapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy) may be an option if surgery and radiation are not possible or were not successful; immunotherapy with an immune checkpoint inhibitor is recommended if eligible. Clinical trials are another treatment option; they are voluntary, and patients can seek treatment outside a trial at any time. Patients should ask their care team whether a clinical trial is available for their situation and whether they meet the requirements, noting that prior standard treatment may affect eligibility. Notably, the source information primarily addresses CSCC (cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma); photodynamic therapy, cryotherapy, and topical therapy are cited as treatments for actinic keratoses (pre-cancerous lesions), not explicitly for BCC.

Title: . Content: 0:About basal cell skin cancer What is basal cell skin cancer? How is basal cell skin cancer treated? What can you do to get the best care? Basal cell skin cancer, also known as basal cell carcinoma (BCC), is the most common type of skin cancer. About 3 million cases of basal cell skin cancer are diagnosed every year in the United States. The good news is it can be cured in most cases. Treatment usually involves surgery to remove the cancer. Keep reading to find out more. What is basal cell skin cancer? Basal cell skin cancer is the most common of all skin cancer types. If caught early, it is easily treatable and curable. This is because it rarely metastasizes (spreads). Skin cancers often occur in the top layer of the skin (epidermis) and less commonly in the middle layer of the skin (dermis). The epidermis is made up of basal cells and other cells. Basal cell skin cancer occurs when some basal cells become abnormal and grow out of control. This cancer usually develops in areas exposed to the sun, including the face, head, neck, arms, legs, and trunk. But it can occur anywhere on the body. results.info_summary: Recurrence of BCC (basal cell skin cancer) occurs when the cancer returns to the original area or metastasizes (spreads) to the lymph nodes or distant body parts. Although BCC rarely metastasizes, recurrence is possible, so management focuses on treatment and ongoing surveillance. Several treatment options exist; details are found in "Chapter 3: Types of treatment" and "Chapter 4: Treatment by risk and recurrence." After treatment, patients should have full skin exams with their doctor at least once a year to monitor for return of the cancer. Between these exams, prevention is emphasized as important. Patients are encouraged to advocate for themselves by asking questions and making shared decisions with their care team, and each chapter includes a "Questions to ask" section to help guide these discussions.

Title: . Content: 560:? Primary central nervous system lymphoma is a rare and aggressive cancer that affects the central nervous system (CNS). Let’s break it down word by word to understand it better: Primary – Primary means first. When talking about cancer, primary refers to the place where cancer first started. Primary CNS lymphoma starts in the central nervous system. Central nervous system – The CNS is made up of the brain and spinal cord. Lymphoma – Lymphoma is cancer that forms from lymphocytes. Lymphocytes are white blood cells that fight infections. Cancer is what happens when cells grow out of control. Primary CNS lymphoma starts in lymphocytes in the immune system. The immune system is your body’s natural defense against infection and disease. results.info_summary:
Primary CNS lymphoma originates from **lymphocytes** — specifically, white blood cells that help fight and prevent infection. Lymphocytes are found in blood, lymph tissue, and every organ of the body, including the brain and spinal cord. There are three main types: **B lymphocytes (B cells)**, which make antibodies; **T lymphocytes (T cells)**, which help fight infections, kill tumor cells, and control immune responses; and **natural killer (NK) cells**, which can kill tumor cells or virus-infected cells.

Primary CNS lymphoma arises when these lymphocytes in the central nervous system grow out of control. It is a form of **non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL)**, which is a cancer of lymphocytes. NHL — and by extension primary CNS lymphoma — most commonly involves **B cells or T cells**. The disease develops when lymphocytes that normally grow in response to infection or inflammation instead grow on their own without proper regulation.

Title: . Content: 564: diagnosed? Primary CNS lymphoma is often found when a person develops symptoms. A symptom is a feeling or problem that may be a sign of disease. Symptoms usually develop over several weeks. Primary CNS lymphoma can cause a variety of symptoms. Symptoms are often related to the lymphoma’s location in the central nervous system. The most common location is in the central part of the brain. A lymphoma located here may cause specific nerve changes such as leg or arm weakness, or problems with coordination or movement. Other such symptoms may include changes in personality or behavior, depression, confusion, memory problems, loss of bladder control (incontinence), or difficulty speaking or swallowing. As the lymphoma tumor grows, it puts pressure on the CNS. This pressure often leads to neurological symptoms and difficulties, including headaches, nausea, vomiting, or seizures. Changes in eyesight, such as blurry vision or double vision, can also occur. You’ll need several tests to confirm whether you have primary CNS lymphoma or a lymphoma that started in another part of your body, or a different disease with similar symptoms. Important tests include a neurological exam, imaging (MRI or CT scan), and biopsies. A biopsy means taking a sample of fluid or tissue from your body to look for cancer

An MRI scan is good at showing the spine and soft tissues, including the brain, as well as other details that are helpful for planning surgery. MRI uses radio waves and powerful magnets to take pictures of the inside of the body. During an MRI, you’ll lie on a table that slides into the scanning machine. (An open MRI scanner may be an option at some health care centers.) It’s important to lie still during the test to get the best pictures. The machine makes loud noises but you can wear earplugs. results.info_summary:
The standard biopsy procedure for diagnosing primary CNS lymphoma is a **stereotactic biopsy**. Key details:

- It is the **main test** and the **only way to be certain** of a cancer diagnosis.
- It is the **recommended procedure** when a brain tumor is in a **hard-to-reach or vital area**.
- Performed by a **neurosurgeon in an operating room**.
- Procedure: a frame or tiny markers are fitted around the head; anesthesia is given; a small area of hair is shaved; a small opening is made in the skull; a **thin, hollow needle** is inserted into the brain to remove a **sliver of the tumor**.
- A **computerized navigation system connected to MRI or CT imaging** guides the surgeon to target and remove the sample with **high precision**.
- The sample is sent to a **pathologist** who examines it under a microscope; testing takes about **one week**.
- If stereotactic biopsy is unavailable, patients should ask to be referred to a **specialized center**.

Note: In some cases, a **vitrectomy** alone can confirm primary CNS lymphoma diagnosis without a brain biopsy.

results.info_summary: A stereotactic biopsy is the main and standard laboratory test used to diagnose primary CNS lymphoma. In this procedure, a thin, hollow needle is inserted into the brain to remove a sliver of tumor tissue, which is sent to a lab and tested for cancer cells. A lumbar puncture (spinal tap), which removes cerebrospinal fluid for testing for cancer cells, can also help confirm a diagnosis. Additionally, a vitrectomy (removing a small amount of vitreous from the eye for testing) can in some cases confirm the diagnosis without the need for brain biopsy. An MRI is the most useful imaging technique for identifying primary CNS lymphoma, but imaging alone is not a laboratory test.

Title: . Content: 564: diagnosed? Primary CNS lymphoma is often found when a person develops symptoms. A symptom is a feeling or problem that may be a sign of disease. Symptoms usually develop over several weeks. Primary CNS lymphoma can cause a variety of symptoms. Symptoms are often related to the lymphoma’s location in the central nervous system. The most common location is in the central part of the brain. A lymphoma located here may cause specific nerve changes such as leg or arm weakness, or problems with coordination or movement. Other such symptoms may include changes in personality or behavior, depression, confusion, memory problems, loss of bladder control (incontinence), or difficulty speaking or swallowing. As the lymphoma tumor grows, it puts pressure on the CNS. This pressure often leads to neurological symptoms and difficulties, including headaches, nausea, vomiting, or seizures. Changes in eyesight, such as blurry vision or double vision, can also occur. You’ll need several tests to confirm whether you have primary CNS lymphoma or a lymphoma that started in another part of your body, or a different disease with similar symptoms. Important tests include a neurological exam, imaging (MRI or CT scan), and biopsies. A biopsy means taking a sample of fluid or tissue from your body to look for cancer

A typical initial clinical assessment for suspected primary CNS lymphoma includes:

1. **Physical examination and general health assessments**, including:
   - **Neurological exam** — simple tests of alertness, balance, coordination, reflexes, hearing, and other senses; may include an eye exam to check the nerves at the back of the eye.
   - **Performance status evaluation** — assessment of how well the patient can perform ordinary day-to-day activities (walking, climbing stairs, cooking, carrying laundry, bathing), used to gauge treatment tolerance and clinical trial eligibility.

2. **Imaging scans** — MRI is the most useful imaging technique for identifying primary CNS lymphoma; CT scan may also be used. Imaging reveals the lymphoma's location, size, and other features.

3. **Biopsy** — the key test to confirm diagnosis. The standard method is a **stereotactic biopsy**, a precise technique using a thin, hollow needle to remove a sliver of tumor tissue (especially for tumors in hard-to-reach or vital areas), which is sent to a lab to test for cancer cells.

Title: . Content: 578: treatment. If cancer cells are found in the spinal fluid, or if you’re having symptoms, another MRI may be needed to find out if there are any lesions in the spine. Lumbar puncture Cancer cells in the spinal fluid may or may not cause symptoms. A lumbar puncture is used to learn whether cancer has spread to the spinal cord. First, the lower back is numbed. Then a long, thin needle is inserted into the lower part of the spinal column to remove cerebrospinal fluid. The fluid is then sent to a lab for testing. More imaging It’s uncommon for primary CNS lymphoma to spread outside of the central nervous system or the eyes. Still, it’s important to have a look at the rest of your body just to be sure. The imaging methods most commonly used for this are positron emission tomography (PET) and/ or computed tomography (CT). PET imaging uses a small amount of a radioactive drug to find cancer cells in the body. After the radioactive drug is injected into a vein, it causes cancer cells to show up as bright spots on PET scans. A CT scan takes many x-rays of the same body part from different angles. A computer combines all the x-ray pictures to make a single detailed image.

Title: . Content: 589: Treatment may include a single chemotherapy drug or a combination of drugs. A combination of drugs is sometimes chosen because the drugs work better when they’re used together. Most chemotherapy drugs for primary CNS lymphoma are given intravenously (IV). This means the medicine is slowly infused through a tube into a vein in your arm or another part of your body. The medicine travels in the bloodstream to reach cells throughout the body. Some chemotherapy drugs are taken by mouth as a tablet or capsule. Chemotherapy is given in cycles. One cycle involves a few treatment days followed by several days of rest. Different chemotherapy drugs have different cycles. Common cycles are 14, 21, or 28 days long. Having chemotherapy in cycles gives your body a chance to recover after receiving the treatment. The retina converts what you see into signals, which it sends through the optic nerves to the brain. Lymphoma cells can also invade the vitreous, the clear gel that fills the eye. Title: . Content: 590: or as part of specific treatment program for primary CNS lymphoma. Intraocular chemotherapy In rare cases, primary CNS lymphoma may occur in the eye. In these situations, the chemotherapy may be infused into a vein or directly into the eye. Possible side effects from intraocular chemotherapy include eye irritation, infection, inflammation, and cataracts. Cataracts can be treated with a routine operation by an eye surgeon. Side effects of chemotherapy Like other therapies, the side effects of chemotherapy depend on many factors. These include the drug, the dose, and the person. Chemotherapy, especially in high doses, may not be the right treatment for people who are frail or older. These individuals may have a difficult time dealing with the harsh side effects. The main chemotherapy drug used to treat primary CNS lymphoma is high-dose methotrexate. Methotrexate is one of the most effective drugs for treating many kinds of cancers. But when given in high doses, methotrexate may cause damage to the kidneys, liver, and other organs. In severe cases, kidney failure is possible. Your multidisciplinary team When all of your doctors, specialists, and allied health providers are working and communicating as a team to help you, it’s called multidisciplinary care. Be clear about your treatment goals when you talk with your multidisciplinary team. Key points h A recommended treatment option for primary CNS lymphoma is participating in a clinical trial. Other treatment options include corticosteroids, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and stem cell rescue. Often, some of these therapies are combined to treat primary CNS lymphoma. Chemotherapy is a drug treatment that damages and destroys rapidly dividing cells throughout the body. The main chemotherapy drug used to treat primary CNS lymphoma is methotrexate. Whole-brain radiation therapy (WBRT) is the most commonly used radiation technique for primary CNS lymphoma. Targeted therapy drugs attack specific parts of cancer cells to slow their growth and spread. Immunotherapy uses your body’s immune system to fight cancer. The main immunotherapy drug for primary CNS lymphoma is rituximab. High-dose chemotherapy and stem cell rescue uses your own blood-forming stem cells to jumpstart the bone marrow to make more healthy

Title: . Content: 606: Ask your care team if there is a clinical trial you may be eligible for. If you don’t want to join a clinical trial or none are available for you, the recommended induction treatment is high-dose methotrexate chemotherapy, often given with other chemotherapies. High-dose chemotherapy The most effective chemotherapy drug for primary CNS lymphoma is methotrexate. Methotrexate has been used for many years to treat a variety of cancers. It works by blocking the body’s use of folate, a form of vitamin B. Lymphoma cells can’t multiply and spread as quickly without folate. High doses of methotrexate are needed to overcome the blood-brain barrier and still have enough strength to kill lymphoma cells. The blood-brain barrier is a protective layer around the brain that prevents germs, infections, and other toxins from getting in. contexts: Title: . Content: 593: Radiation therapy uses high-energy x-rays or other radiation to kill cancer cells. Like x-rays used for imaging, you won’t see or feel anything during treatment. The total dose of radiation is usually divided into small doses given over several weeks. By giving a little every day, the radiation damages the tumor while better preserving the healthy tissue. The most commonly used radiation technique for primary CNS lymphoma is treatment of the entire brain, called whole-brain radiation therapy (WBRT). Because primary CNS lymphoma can occur in multiple spots anywhere in the brain, WBRT is used to treat the entire brain all at once. WBRT can also reach the upper part of the spine and a part or all of the eyeballs. WBRT even treats microscopic tumors in the CNS that aren’t visible on an MRI scan. You’ll need to remain as motionless as possible during each scan. You may be fitted with a mask or supports to help you keep still. Symptoms usually develop over several weeks. Primary CNS lymphoma can cause a variety of symptoms. Symptoms are often related to the lymphoma’s location in the central nervous system. The most common location is in the central part of the brain. A lymphoma located here may cause specific nerve changes such as leg or arm weakness, or problems with coordination or movement. As the lymphoma tumor grows, it puts pressure on the CNS. This pressure often leads to neurological symptoms and difficulties, including headaches, nausea, vomiting, or seizures. Changes in eyesight, such as blurry vision or double vision, can also occur. There’s no single drug or procedure that’s best for treating primary central nervous system (CNS) lymphoma. The best treatment is the one that works best for you. Treatment options include corticosteroids, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and stem cell rescue. results.info_summary:
**Summary: Main Stages of Cutaneous Squamous Cell Carcinoma (CSCC)**

CSCC staging is based on TNM scores and ranges from **stage 0 to stage 4**, with stage 4 being the most advanced (also written as stage 0, I, II, III, IV). Not all stage 4 cancers are metastatic.

Key staging categories relevant to CSCC:

- **Local CSCC**: Cancer that has not spread to nearby lymph nodes. Usually treated with surgery; risk-stratified as low-risk, high-risk, or very high-risk.
- **Regional CSCC**: Cancer that has spread to nearby lymph nodes.
- **Metastatic/very advanced disease**: Cancer that has spread to distant parts of the body, including lung and distant lymph nodes.

Additional staging terminology:
- **Resectable**: Tumor can be completely removed with surgery.
- **Unresectable**: Tumor cannot be completely removed completely with surgery (may involve major vessels or critical structures).

Note: The source also describes mouth cancer TNM staging (for SCC of the mouth/lip mucosa), which is distinct from cutaneous CSCC and treated differently.

analysis.current_understanding: Actinic keratosis (AK) is a precancerous skin lesion that can progress to cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC). AK is caused by sun exposure and presents as scaly or rough skin, often red, white, tan, or pink, and may appear as small scaly spots or bumps resembling warts. Having AK increases the risk of developing squamous cell skin cancer. Additionally, CSCC can also arise from damaged, inflamed, or scarred skin, such as in Marjolin's ulcer (scars or chronic wounds), though this is not typically classified as a precancerous lesion.

Most colon cancers occur for unknown reasons. While rare, some people are born with a disorder that makes them more likely to get colon and other cancers. These are called inherited cancer syndromes. Two such conditions include Lynch syndrome and familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP). People born with Lynch syndrome are at high risk of developing colon, endometrial, and ovarian cancers. Lynch syndrome is caused by inherited mutations of the MMR genes. For cancers found to have the dMMR/MSI-H biomarker, testing for Lynch syndrome is recommended. FAP causes hundreds to thousands of polyps to form in the colon and rectum. The polyps start as benign growths, but over time can become invasive colon cancer. Cancer often develops by age 50 in people with classic FAP. A milder form (attenuated FAP) causes fewer polyps and usually starts later in life. Surgery is the preferred treatment for low-risk, local CSCC (squamous cell skin cancer that has not spread to lymph nodes). The recommended surgical options are:

- **Curettage and electrodesiccation (C&E) or shave excision** — usually considered for early, small CSCC on the surface of the skin. If the tumor is deeper than expected during the procedure, standard surgical or shave excision should be performed instead.

- **Mohs surgery or another form of PDEMA** — a recommended treatment option for low-risk CSCC that has not spread to lymph nodes.

If the patient is not a candidate for surgery, **radiation therapy** is recommended if they can have it.

For high-risk or very high-risk local CSCC (not spread to lymph nodes), surgery is the preferred treatment. Surgical options include:
- **Mohs surgery or another form of PDEMA** — preferred for very high-risk CSCC
- **Standard surgical excision** — with a wider margin of normal tissue removed for high-risk or very high-risk CSCC

A sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) may be considered before or during PDEMA.

If surgery is not an option, **radiation therapy** is typically used, with **systemic therapy** possibly added. Platinum-based chemotherapy is recommended with radiation. If radiation is not expected to kill the cancer completely or may damage critical organs, **systemic therapy alone** is recommended; immunotherapy with an immune checkpoint inhibitor is preferred if eligible. Clinical trials for systemic therapy are also an option.

If surgery removes the cancer but concerning features are noted, a multidisciplinary discussion is recommended, and radiation therapy will be considered. If PDEMA does not remove all cancer, another surgery is often tried first; otherwise, radiation is recommended, with systemic therapy (e.g., platinum-based chemotherapy) possibly added.

**Summary: Treatment of Regional CSCC with Lymph Node Involvement**

- Regional CSCC = squamous cell skin cancer that has spread to nearby lymph nodes.
- **Preferred treatment:** Surgery to remove the tumor and nearby lymph nodes (excision).
  - For head and neck tumors, lymph nodes may be removed from one or both sides of the neck; extent depends on number, location, and size of involved nodes.
- **After surgery:** Radiation therapy is often given to kill leftover cancer cells and reduce recurrence risk.

- **If surgery is not possible or not recommended:** Radiation therapy with or without systemic therapy; platinum-based chemotherapy is a recommended option with radiation.

analysis.current_understanding: Regional CSCC with lymph node involvement is typically treated with surgery to remove the tumor and affected lymph nodes. For head and neck tumors, this may involve removing lymph nodes from one or both sides of the neck, with the extent depending on the number, location, and size of involved nodes. After surgery, radiation therapy is often given to eliminate residual cancer cells and reduce recurrence risk. Systemic therapy, particularly platinum-based chemotherapy, may be added to post-surgery radiation if lymph nodes were not fully removed or if extranodal extension is present; multidisciplinary discussion is recommended in these cases. If surgery is not feasible, radiation therapy with or without systemic therapy is used, with platinum-based chemotherapy as a recommended option. If radiation is unlikely to be curative or may damage healthy organs, systemic therapy alone may be considered. Immunotherapy may also be an option for eligible patients.

results.info_summary:
**Systemic therapies for advanced CSCC:**

Systemic therapy is recommended for advanced CSCC (including recurrent or metastatic disease) when surgery and/or radiation cannot remove the cancer or are not possible/successful. Categories include:

1. **Immunotherapy (preferred first-line)** — PD-1 inhibitors (immune checkpoint inhibitors): **Cemiplimab (Libtayo)** and **pembrolizumab (Keytruda)**. Preferred if the patient is eligible.
2. **Targeted therapy** — EGFR inhibitors: **Cetuximab (Erbitux)**. Used if not eligible for immunotherapy or a clinical trial.
3. **Chemotherapy** — Platinum-based: **cisplatin** (generally preferred) or **carboplatin** (if cisplatin is too harsh or cannot be given). For recurrent/metastatic cancer, infusions typically given once every 3 weeks. May be combined with radiation (chemoradiation).
4. **Clinical trials** — May involve chemotherapy, targeted therapy, or immunotherapy.

If the patient is not eligible for an immune checkpoint inhibitor or a clinical trial, options are platinum-based chemotherapy and targeted therapy.

**Therapies for Actinic Keratoses and Superficial CSCC:**

**Superficial treatments** (affecting only the top layer of skin) are used for Bowen's disease (the earliest form of squamous cell skin cancer) and actinic keratoses (pre-cancerous lesions), especially when lesions are in the same general area.

- **Photodynamic therapy (PDT):** A light-sensitive drug is applied to the area and activated by red or blue light (in the doctor's office) or shaded outdoor light, killing cancer cells. results.info_summary:
After CSCC treatment, regular skin exams by a doctor are recommended, with frequency depending on whether cancer has spread to nearby lymph nodes.

**For local CSCC:**
- Very high-risk local CSCC: exams every 3 to 6 months during the first 2 years, then every 6 months for the next 3 years, then every 6 to 12 months (once or twice a year) for life (per NCCN experts).
- An annual exam once a year for life is recommended by NCCN experts.
- Imaging tests may be used to monitor some people with local CSCC.

**For regional CSCC:**
- Physical exams with skin checks every 2 to 3 months for 1 year, every 2 to 4 months for the second year, every 4 to 6 months for another 3 years, then every 6 to 12 months for life.
- CT scans may be recommended regularly to look for signs of cancer in nearby lymph nodes or other parts of the body.

Patients should also take preventive steps, as they are at higher risk of getting CSCC again and other types of skin cancer.

For local cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), risk assessment involves evaluating several features of the cancer to classify it as low-risk, high-risk, or very high-risk. This classification matters because high- or very high-risk disease is treated differently from low-risk disease. A high-risk CSCC has an increased risk of local recurrence; a very high-risk CSCC has an increased risk of both local recurrence and metastasis. The risk level is usually based on the highest risk factor found. Factors used to determine risk level include:
- Tumor location and size—CSCC on the head or neck is more likely to return after treatment than tumors on the trunk, arms, or legs.
- Perineural invasion (growth into a nerve or group of nerves, usually seen under the microscope), which makes the cancer high-risk or very high-risk.
- Tumor grade, which rates how fast the cancer is expected to grow and spread.

The newly retrieved information does not add further details on CSCC risk assessment; it focuses on general guidance about patient involvement in care, medical and family history, clinical trials, and questions to ask care teams, which are not specific to CSCC risk stratification.

There’s no single drug or procedure that’s best for treating primary central nervous system (CNS) lymphoma. The best treatment is the one that works best for you. Treatment options include corticosteroids, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and stem cell rescue. Receiving treatment in a clinical trial is also a recommended option. Therapies are often combined to treat cancer. For example, chemotherapy may be given with an immunotherapy drug, or several chemotherapy drugs may be given together. Chemotherapy is also an essential part of having a stem cell rescue. Surgery is not normally an option. Because primary CNS lymphoma usually develops deep within the brain tissue, removing it with surgery is risky and may be more harmful than helpful. Clinical trials are a recommended option for everyone with cancer, including patients with cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC). NCCN experts specifically recommend that everyone with primary CNS lymphoma consider joining a clinical trial for treatment; this principle of considering clinical trials as a recommended option applies broadly to cancer management, including CSCC.

Talk to your treatment team about whether a clinical trial makes sense for you, and start the conversation yourself rather than waiting for your doctor to bring it up. Ask whether you meet a trial's eligibility criteria, which may involve age, cancer type and stage, treatment history, or general health; these rules ensure participants are alike in specific ways and that the trial is as safe as possible. Patients who have already started standard treatment may not be eligible for certain clinical trials; try not to be discouraged, as new trials are always becoming available.

Clinical trials are managed by a research team that reviews the study in detail, including its purpose and the risks and benefits of joining, all provided in an informed consent form—read it carefully and ask questions before signing. Title: . Content: 50:. Categories of systemic therapy are described below. Chemotherapy Chemotherapy uses drugs to kill fast-growing cancer cells. For clinical management risk assessment in cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), doctors consider several features of the cancer to classify it as low-, high-, or very high-risk. This matters because high- or very high-risk disease is treated differently than low-risk disease. A high-risk CSCC has an increased risk of local recurrence, while a very high-risk CSCC has an increased risk of both local recurrence and metastasis. The risk level is usually based on the highest risk factor found. Factors used to determine risk level include **location and size**—for example, CSCC on the head or neck is more likely to return after treatment than tumors on the trunk, arms, or legs.

The newly retrieved information does not add further specific factors included in clinical management risk assessment for CSCC; it primarily concerns general cancer care guidance (e.g., patient advocacy, medical/family history, clinical trials, and questions to ask care teams) rather than CSCC risk stratification. Therefore, the existing summary remains the relevant answer, and no additional CSCC-specific risk factors can be integrated from the new information.

For regional CSCC (cancer spread to nearby lymph nodes), surveillance consists of physical exams with skin checks every 2 to 3 months for 1 year, every 2 to 4 months for the second year, every 4 to 6 months for another 3 years, and then every 6 to 12 months for the rest of life. Regular CT scans may also be used to look for cancer in nearby lymph nodes or other parts of the body.

For very high-risk local CSCC, exams should occur every 3 to 6 months during the first 2 years, then every 6 months for the next 3 years, then every 6 to 12 months (once or twice a year) for life, per NCCN experts. Imaging tests may be used to monitor some people with local CSCC.

results.info_summary: Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) is a type of blood cancer. It is caused by a specific abnormal gene called BCR::ABL1, formed when pieces of chromosome 9 and chromosome 22 break off and trade places, creating the Philadelphia (Ph) chromosome. CML arises from blood stem cells that produce an increased amount of myeloid progenitor cells (which form myeloblasts and other non-lymphoid blood cells).

Mutation testing looks for these changes or abnormalities that are unique to AML cells. Examples of such changes are called deletion, insertion, inversion, amplification, translocation (rearrangement), and point mutation. Amplification – When a part or whole chromosome or gene is increased (for example, duplicated) Deletion – When part of a chromosome or gene is missing such as del(5q) Insertion – When a new part of a chromosome or gene is included Inversion – Switching of parts within one chromosome such as inv(16) and inv(3) Point mutation – When part of a gene is changed Chromosome translocation and gene rearrangement – Switching of parts between 2 chromosomes. When described at the chromosome level, it is called a translocation. When described at the gene level, it is called rearrangement. results.info_summary: The Philadelphia chromosome (Ph) is an abnormal, shortened chromosome 22 that is the hallmark of chronic myeloid leukemia (CML). It forms when a piece of chromosome 9 and a piece of chromosome 22 break off and trade places (a translocation), creating a fused gene called BCR::ABL1 on the new chromosome 22. If the Ph chromosome or the BCR::ABL1 gene is absent, the patient does not have CML. BCR::ABL1 is not found in normal blood cells and is not inherited from birth parents to children. The BCR::ABL1 gene produces a new protein that drives uncontrolled blood cell growth, ultimately leading to CML. Treatment for CML aims to stop the activity of the BCR::ABL1 protein. The type of blast phase cell (lymphoid or myeloid progenitor) in blast phase CML (BP-CML) affects treatment. The cause of CML can be traced to a single, specific abnormal gene called BCR::ABLThis fused gene occurs when a piece of chromosome 9 and a piece of chromosome 22 break off and switch places. This creates a new, abnormal chromosome 22 that contains a small part of chromosome This new chromosome is referred to as the Philadelphia chromosome (Ph) and is the hallmark of CML. If you do not have the Ph chromosome or the BCR::ABL1 gene, you do not have CML. BCR::ABL1 is not found in normal blood cells. It is not passed down from birth parents to children. The BCR::ABL1 gene makes a new protein that leads to uncontrolled blood cell growth. This growth ultimately leads to CML. Treatment for CML aims to stop the activity of the BCR::ABL1 protein. Those with CML should be treated at centers experienced in this type of cancer. What can you do to get the best care? Advocate for yourself.

**Blast phase CML (BP-CML)** is an advanced form of chronic myeloid leukemia (CML). Key facts:

- CML is a blood cancer caused by the abnormal **BCR::ABL1** fused gene, formed when pieces of chromosome 9 and chromosome 22 break off and switch places, creating the **Philadelphia (Ph) chromosome**. Without the Ph chromosome or BCR::ABL1 gene, a patient does not have CML.
- CML typically arises from blood stem cells producing increased **myeloid progenitor cells**.
- In **BP-CML**, there is an increased amount of **either lymphoid or myeloid progenitor cells** (blast cells), whereas standard CML primarily involves myeloid progenitors.
- The **type of blast phase cell** (lymphoid vs. myeloid) **affects treatment** in BP-CML.
- Blasts are the very immature cells (myeloblasts or lymphoblasts).
- Treatment for CML aims to stop the activity of the BCR::ABL1 protein. Patients should be treated at centers experienced with this cancer and are encouraged to **seek the opinion of a CML specialist**.

In CML, the main white blood cell subtypes involved are **granulocytes** (which include **neutrophils**, **eosinophils**, and **basophils**). CML usually produces too many white blood cells, specifically granulocytes. 

CML is thought to arise from blood stem cells that produce an increased amount of **myeloid progenitor cells** (which form myeloblasts and other non-lymphoid blood cells). However, in advanced **blast phase CML (BP-CML)**, there can be an increased amount of either **lymphoid** or **myeloid progenitor cells** (lymphoblasts or myeloblasts, collectively called "blasts").

**Summary: Diagnostic Tests for Detecting the BCR::ABL1 Fusion Gene**

The newly retrieved information is drawn from NCCN Guidelines for Patients on CML (chronic myeloid leukemia) — the cancer most directly associated with the BCR::ABL1 fusion gene — but the retrieved excerpts do not themselves name BCR::ABL1 or describe the specific assays used to detect it. They confirm only that CML care "starts with testing," including "Testing for CML biomarker and genetic changes," blood tests, and bone marrow tests. The prior summary's test descriptions therefore remain the best available basis for answering the question:

- **Polymerase chain reaction (PCR)** — Detects gene rearrangements; used for diagnosis and monitoring response to targeted therapy. (Note: RT-PCR for BCR::ABL1 transcripts is the standard assay for this fusion.)
- **Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH)** — Dye-labeled DNA probes detect known abnormalities too small to be seen by other methods; performed on blood or bone marrow without culturing cells.
- **Karyotype (cytogenetics)** — Chromosome picture revealing defects, extra copies, or deletions; identifies the Philadelphia chromosome (t(9;22)).

analysis.current_understanding: The diagnostic tests used to detect the BCR::ABL1 fusion gene include: (1) Polymerase chain reaction (PCR), particularly RT-PCR for BCR::ABL1 transcripts, which is the standard assay; it detects gene rearrangements and is used for diagnosis and monitoring response to targeted therapy. (2) Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), which uses dye-labeled DNA probes to detect known abnormalities too small to be seen by other methods, performed on blood or bone marrow without culturing cells. (3) Karyotype (cytogenetics), a chromosome picture that reveals defects, extra copies, or deletions and identifies the Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22). Although the retrieved NCCN excerpts do not name BCR::ABL1 or these specific assays, they confirm that CML care starts with testing for a CML biomarker and genetic changes. Title: . Content: 169: of myeloid blasts in the bone marrow or blood. The number of blasts required to be diagnosed with AML can vary. In general, the number of blasts must be 20 percent or more of all cells found in the bone marrow. This means that at least 1 out of every 5 bone marrow cells are blasts. However, a diagnosis of AML is possible with any number of blasts, particularly if certain gene mutations or abnormal chromosomes are also present. Unlike other cancers of organs, like lung cancer or breast cancer, AML does not have stages. Many cancers spread from the location where they originate, and the extent or severity of cancer is determined by how far it has spread. AML arises from the bone marrow, which is present in nearly all of our bones. Because AML cells arise from multiple bones and flow in the blood all over the body, traditional staging is not useful. Instead, AML testing looks for specific gene mutations or abnormal chromosomes, which can tell your care team how aggressive your leukemia might be. Overview Accurate testing is needed to diagnose and treat AML. A diagnosis of AML is based on the presence of myeloid blasts in the bone marrow or blood. The number of blasts required to be diagnosed with AML can vary. In general, the number of blasts must be 20 percent or more of all cells found in the bone marrow. This means that at least 1 out of every 5 bone marrow cells are blasts. However, a diagnosis of AML is possible with any number of blasts, particularly if certain gene mutations or abnormal chromosomes are also present. Unlike other cancers of organs, like lung cancer or breast cancer, AML does not have stages. Many cancers spread from the location where they originate, and the extent or severity of cancer is determined by how far it has spread. AML arises from the bone marrow, which is present in nearly all of our bones. Because AML cells arise from multiple bones and flow in the blood all over the body, traditional staging is not useful. Instead, AML testing looks for specific gene mutations or abnormal chromosomes, which can tell your care team how aggressive your leukemia might

The Philadelphia chromosome and the BCR::ABL1 fusion gene are directly related and are both hallmarks of chronic myeloid leukemia (CML):

- The BCR::ABL1 fusion gene is created when a piece of chromosome 9 and a piece of chromosome 22 break off and trade places.
- This fusion results in two things: (1) a fused gene called BCR::ABL1, and (2) a shortened, abnormal chromosome 22 called the Philadelphia (Ph) chromosome.
- The Philadelphia chromosome contains a small part of chromosome 9 and is considered the hallmark of CML.
- If you do not have the Ph chromosome or the BCR::ABL1 gene, you do not have CML.
- The BCR::ABL1 gene is not found in normal blood cells and is not inherited from birth parents to children.
- The BCR::ABL1 gene makes a new protein that leads to uncontrolled blood cell growth, which ultimately leads to CML. Treatment aims to stop the activity of the BCR::ABL1 protein.

**Summary: Stages of NSCLC Considered Locally Advanced**

According to the NCCN Guidelines for Patients (Early and Locally Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer, 2024):

- **Stage 1** NSCLC is considered **early** NSCLC.
- **Stage 2 and Stage 3** are generally considered **locally advanced** NSCLC.
- Early and locally advanced NSCLCs have **not spread to the tissue lining around the lung or to other organs**. They have grown from the airway into lung tissue, and some have spread to nearby lymph nodes.
- **Stage 4** is metastatic cancer at diagnosis and is **not** considered locally advanced.

**Answer:** Stages 2 and 3 of NSCLC are considered locally advanced.

Supportive care refers to a range of care and resources often needed by patients with metastatic cancer. Hospice care, access to pain specialists, and emotional and spiritual support are all components of supportive care. Because metastatic cancer cannot be cured, the main goal of supportive care is to make you more comfortable and to help keep the cancer under control. Supportive care may also help you live longer and feel better overall. When used for advanced cancers, supportive care is often called palliative care. You may also consider enrolling in a clinical trial. Ask your treatment team if there is an open clinical trial that you can join. Advance care planning Talking with your doctor about your prognosis can help with treatment planning. If the cancer cannot be controlled or cured, a care plan for the end of life can be made. There are many benefits to advance care planning, including: Knowing what to expect Making the most of your time Lowering the stress of caregivers Having your wishes followed Having a better quality of life

CT scan A CT scan is a more detailed kind of -ray. It takes a lot of pictures, or images, from different angles. A computer then combines the images to make 3-D pictures. PET CT or MRI are sometimes combined with positron emission tomography (PET). A PET scan shows how your cells are using a simple form of sugar, which can be helpful for identifying cancer. A sugar radiotracer is put into your body through a vein. The radiotracer puts out a small amount of energy that is detected by the machine that takes pictures. Cancer cells appear brighter because they use sugar faster than normal cells. PET is very good at showing small groups of cancer cells. This test may also be useful for showing if ovarian cancer has spread. Chest x-ray A chest -ray can show if cancer has spread to your lungs. It may be ordered with other tests when ovarian cancer is first suspected or found. It may also be used to check treatment results. results.info_summary: Lung cancer screening is recommended for people at high risk for developing lung cancer, not for everyone. Screening is based on an individual's risk factors, and people should ask their health care provider if they qualify. The biggest risk factor is smoking tobacco, with risk increasing the more times and longer a person smokes; exposure to secondhand smoke also increases risk. Other risk factors include exposure to radon, asbestos, arsenic, beryllium, cadmium, chromium, nickel, coal smoke, soot, silica, diesel fumes, and air pollution (fine particulates, ozone, nitrogen oxides, sulfur dioxide). Screening aims to find lung cancer early, before symptoms start, when treatment is most successful. Patients are encouraged to play an active role in their care by asking questions and making shared decisions with their care team.

Screening is not for everyone; it is based on individual risk factors, and people should ask their health care provider if they qualify. Title: . Content: 55: always becoming available. Frequently asked questions There are many myths and misconceptions surrounding clinical trials. The possible benefits and risks are not well understood by many with cancer. Will I get a placebo? Placebos (inactive versions of real medicines) are almost never used alone in cancer clinical trials. It is common to receive either a placebo with a standard treatment or a new drug with a standard treatment. You will be informed, verbally and in writing, if a placebo is part of a clinical trial before you enroll. Clinical trials are available for both lung cancer treatment and prevention. For treatment, clinical trials test new ways of fighting cancer, and patients are encouraged to ask their care team if a trial is a good fit. For prevention, researchers are studying chemopreventive agents to prevent lung cancer caused by smoking, and patients can ask their care team about trials on preventing lung cancer. Clinical trials offer hope to all people with lung cancer.

results.info_summary:
Follow-up care after lung cancer treatment includes:

- **Monitoring for cancer return and late effects**: Patients should ask about the chances the cancer will return or they will develop another type of cancer, what late effects are caused by treatment, and how these will be screened.
- **Scheduling and frequency**: Patients need to know whom to see for follow-up care, how often, and for how many years. They should also ask who is responsible for scheduling monitoring tests.
- **Tests to monitor health**: Specific tests will be used to monitor the patient's health after treatment.
- **Financial concerns**: Patients should ask what to do if they have trouble paying for follow-up visits and tests.
- **Support resources**: Survivor support groups and other resources can be recommended.
- **Continuity of care**: If a patient moves after treatment and must change doctors, they should ask whether their care team will help them find a new doctor.

Additionally, follow-up care relates to the broader topic of "Planning follow-up care" and "Types of follow-up care," which are listed among lung nodule topics in the source material.

To assess whether a nodule is malignant, a team of board-certified experts—including a pulmonologist, thoracic radiologist, and thoracic surgeon—evaluates the nodule by: (1) assessing the patient's risk for lung cancer, (2) reviewing lung images and requesting additional imaging if cancer is suspected, and (3) performing a biopsy if needed. A biopsy removes a tissue or fluid sample, which is sent to a pathologist who examines cells under a microscope (cytology) to confirm cancer and determine the tumor histology (cancer subtype). Needle-based biopsy methods include fine-needle aspiration (FNA), fine-needle biopsy (FNB), and core needle biopsy (CNB), sometimes guided by ultrasound or CT scan. Biomarker tumor testing may also be used to identify gene mutations or proteins that inform treatment. The biggest risk factor for lung cancer is smoking tobacco.

results.info_summary:
**Indication for Lung Cancer Screening:**

Lung cancer screening is **not recommended for everyone**. It is indicated for **people at high risk for developing lung cancer**, based on their risk factors. The goal is to find lung cancer at an early stage, before symptoms appear, when treatment is most likely to be successful and help prevent death.

**Key risk factor:** The biggest risk factor is **smoking tobacco** (more than 50 cancer-causing compounds in tobacco smoke); risk increases with the amount and duration of smoking. Secondhand smoke exposure also increases risk.

**Other cancer-causing agents** (especially relevant for smokers): radon, asbestos, arsenic, beryllium, cadmium, chromium, nickel, coal smoke, soot, silica, diesel fumes, and air pollution (fine particulates, ozone, nitrogen oxides, sulfur dioxide).

**Note:** Individuals should discuss with their health care provider whether they qualify for screening based on their personal risk factors.

results.info_summary:
**Summary: Main Treatments for NSCLC**

There is no single best treatment for NSCLC—the best treatment is the one that is right for each person. Treatment recommendations are based on the latest research and current practices at leading cancer centers, such as the NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology (NCCN Guidelines®), which are updated frequently and used by health care providers worldwide. Often, multiple treatments are used together to get the best results.

When possible, **surgery** is used as the primary treatment for early or locally advanced NSCLC. Other types of cancer treatment are often combined with surgery to improve results.

For patients who cannot have surgery, other good options include:
- **Radiation therapy** (for some early cancers)
- **Chemoradiation** (a combination of 2 types of treatment, used for other cancers)

**Supportive care** is also important—it addresses the challenges of cancer and has been shown to extend and enhance life for people with lung cancer. Patients should tell their care team about symptoms and other needs to get the best supportive care.

**Clinical trials** offer hope to all people with lung cancer by testing new ways of fighting cancer; patients should ask their care team if a trial is a good fit.

Physical exams Physical exams performed by your oncologist are an important part of surveillance, especially in the first 5 years after treatment. At these follow-up visits, tell your doctor about any changes in your health. Such changes include new or worsening symptoms and other health conditions or concerns. The recommended time frames for these follow-up visits are as follows: Years 1 and 2: Every 3 to 6 months Years 3, 4, and 5: Every 6 to 12 months After year 5: Once a year or as agreed upon with your doctor Time frame ranges are used to allow for differences in individual risk of recurrence and in patient and provider preference. Those considered at higher risk of recurrence may benefit from more frequent exams than those with a lower risk. After the fifth year, visits are generally spaced out to once per year. Or you and your doctor may agree on a different schedule after discussing your personal risk of recurrence. Imaging Unlike physical exams, imaging is generally not needed at regular intervals for an extended time after treatment. Imaging is typically ordered if you have new or worsening symptoms, or if other findings suggest recurrence or spread. Follow-up imaging

results.info_summary: Biopsy is essential in diagnosing nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC). It removes a sample of tissue or fluid, which is sent to a pathologist—an expert in examining cells microscopically (cytology)—to confirm the presence of cancer and determine the cancer subtype (tumor histology). Biopsy methods include fine-needle aspiration (FNA), fine-needle biopsy (FNB), and core needle biopsy (CNB), using needles of different sizes; ultrasound or CT scan may guide a lymph node biopsy. If metastasis is suspected (e.g., to lymph nodes or lung), a biopsy of the metastasis may be needed, and each site may be biopsied if there is more than one. Biopsy results, along with medical history, physical examination, and imaging studies, are used to determine the treatment plan.

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) is classified by extent of disease using the TNM staging system:

- **T (Tumor)**: Size and extent of the primary tumor. T0 = no tumor found (but EBV-positive nodes); Tis = carcinoma in situ; T1 = tumor confined to nasopharynx or extending to oropharynx/nasal cavity, not parapharyngeal space. Tumors may also grow into nearby structures such as the base of the skull, jaw, roof of the mouth, or carotid artery.
- **N (Node)**: Whether cancer has spread to nearby (regional) lymph nodes, and if so, how many and where. NPC often spreads to neck lymph nodes.
- **M (Metastasis)**: Whether cancer has spread to distant organs (e.g., lungs, liver, distant lymph nodes). Metastatic disease may be referred to as "very advanced disease," though not all stage 4 cancers are metastatic.

Staging is further categorized as:
- **Anatomic staging** – based on TNM.
- **Prognostic staging** – includes anatomic TNM plus EBV levels in blood; divided into clinical and pathologic.
- **Clinical stage (c)** – determined before treatment,

results.info_summary:
The initial evaluation of NPC (nasopharyngeal carcinoma) includes the following diagnostic methods:

- **Medical history**: Record of health issues, treatments, tobacco/alcohol use; list of medications and supplements.
- **Physical exam**: Including a complete head and neck exam; mirror exam if needed. May check temperature, blood pressure, pulse, breathing rate, height/weight, listen to lungs/heart, examine eyes/ears/nose/throat, and palpate organs.
- **Screening for depression**.
- **Nasopharyngeal fiberoptic exam**.
- **Biopsy** of tumor or neck.
- **Imaging**: MRI with contrast of collarbone to skull base; CT of skull base and neck may also be done; FDG-PET/CT and/or chest CT with contrast for distant metastases.
- **As needed**: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) DNA testing, dental exam, nutrition/speech/swallowing evaluation, hearing test (audiogram), eye and endocrine evaluation.

General health tests (e.g., blood tests such as CMP) and biomarker testing are also mentioned.

results.info_summary: In NPC, the cancer subtype is determined through biomarker testing (also called molecular or genomic testing, tumor profiling, tumor sequencing, or gene expression profiling). This testing examines a sample of the tumor and/or blood for specific DNA mutations, protein levels, or other molecular features—such as MSI-H/dMMR mutations—that might suggest treatment options. Mutation testing uses methods such as next-generation sequencing (NGS) and polymerase chain reaction (PCR); NGS can find mutations other methods might miss, and PCR is highly sensitive, able to find 1 abnormal cell among more than a million. Most nasopharyngeal cancers are EBV-related (caused by the Epstein-Barr virus); EBV DNA is tested in tumor and/or blood samples before and after treatment. The AJCC staging system incorporates subtype information as part of determining the cancer stage; staging describes the extent of the cancer (tumor size and local growth, lymph node spread, and distant metastasis) and helps predict prognosis and guide treatment decisions.

**Summary: Types of biopsy used for NPC diagnosis**

For diagnosing nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC), several biopsy methods may be used to remove tissue or fluid samples, which are then examined by a pathologist via cytology to confirm cancer and determine tumor histology:

- **Fine-needle aspiration (FNA), fine-needle biopsy (FNB), and core needle biopsy (CNB)** — use needles of different sizes to sample tumor or lymph nodes. Ultrasound or CT imaging may guide lymph node biopsies.
- **Incisional biopsy** — removes a small amount of tissue through a cut in the skin or body.
- **Excisional biopsy** — removes the entire abnormal area; not preferred but may be necessary when other methods aren't possible or results don't match expectations.
- **Biopsy of metastasis** — may be needed to confirm cancer spread to areas like lymph nodes or lungs; each metastatic site may be biopsied depending on location.

Biomarker/molecular testing of biopsy samples may also be performed to identify mutations or proteins that guide treatment selection.

For NPC (nasopharyngeal cancer), prognostic factors include:

- **Anatomic staging factors (TNM):** tumor size/extent (T), lymph node involvement (N), and distant metastasis (M).
- **Prognostic stage:** includes anatomic TNM plus **Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) levels in the blood**; it assumes treatment with standard-of-care approaches.
- **Clinical vs pathologic staging:** clinical stage is based on physical exam, biopsy, and imaging before treatment; pathologic stage is based on tissue removed during surgery and provides more specific/accurate details on tumor size and lymph node status.
- Staging helps predict prognosis and guide treatment decisions.

results.info_summary: Before starting NPC therapy, patients should be informed that treatment such as chemotherapy can affect fertility (the ability to have children) temporarily or permanently. Those who want children in the future should be referred to a fertility specialist to discuss fertility preservation options **before starting cancer treatment**, as actions to preserve fertility may need to be taken beforehand. results.info_summary: Head and neck cancer and its treatment can affect the health of the jaw, teeth, and gums, as well as the mouth more broadly. Radiation therapy to the neck area commonly causes dry mouth, thick saliva, changes in taste, and problems swallowing; chemotherapy can cause mouth sores, loss of appetite, and increased risk of infection. Some side effects appear during treatment and stop shortly after, while others can be long-term, occur years later, or be life-long and irreversible. Patients should inform their dentist about their head and neck cancer and maintain regular dental cleanings and checkups. If dental work or procedures are needed, they may be recommended before starting certain treatments. Patients should also tell their care team about all medicines, over-the-counter drugs, herbals, and supplements they take, as some can interact with cancer treatment.

results.info_summary:
The AJCC TNM system stages nasopharyngeal cancer (NPC) using three main components:

- **T (tumor)** – Size and extent of the main (primary) tumor; whether it has grown into nearby areas.
- **N (node)** – Whether cancer has spread to nearby (regional) lymph nodes, and if so, how many and where.
- **M (metastasis)** – Whether cancer has spread to distant sites/organs.

Each component is assigned a number based on imaging and pathology results—the higher the number, the larger the tumor or the more the cancer has spread. These scores are combined to assign a final stage (e.g., T1N0M0). The AJCC staging system also accounts for subtype, and for throat/NPC staging, p16 (HPV) testing is an important part of staging.

Colon cancer basics 5 6 6 The colon Polyps Key points Colon cancer is common and treatable. Many cancers that start in the colon can be cured, especially when found early. The colon The colon makes up most of the large intestine (bowel). In the colon water is absorbed from eaten food, turning it into feces or stool. After leaving the colon, stool moves into the rectum. The rectum is the last 6 inches or so of the large bowel. Stool is held here until it leaves the body through an opening called the anus. The colon The start of the colon is a pouch called the cecum. Sticking out from the cecum is the appendix. This skinny tube is about the size of a finger and is closed at one end. The rest of the colon has 4 main sections: the ascending, transverse, descending, and sigmoid colon. The term colorectal cancer is used to describe cancers that form in either the colon or rectum. While these cancers are similar, their treatment is different. The focus of this guide is colon cancer. For information on rectal cancer treatment, see the NCCN Guidelines for Patients: Rectal Cancer at NCCN.org/

Colon cancer basics 5 6 6 The colon Polyps Key points Colon cancer is common and treatable. Many cancers that start in the colon can be cured, especially when found early. The colon The colon makes up most of the large intestine (bowel). In the colon water is absorbed from eaten food, turning it into feces or stool. After leaving the colon, stool moves into the rectum. The rectum is the last 6 inches or so of the large bowel. Stool is held here until it leaves the body through an opening called the anus. The colon The start of the colon is a pouch called the cecum. Sticking out from the cecum is the appendix. This skinny tube is about the size of a finger and is closed at one end. The rest of the colon has 4 main sections: the ascending, transverse, descending, and sigmoid colon. The term colorectal cancer is used to describe cancers that form in either the colon or rectum. While these cancers are similar, their treatment is different. The focus of this guide is colon cancer. results.info_summary: A colostomy in colon cancer treatment diverts the flow of stool when it is not safe to reconnect the remaining sections of colon after cancer removal. The remaining upper part of the colon is attached to an opening on the abdomen called a stoma; stool exits through the stoma into a bag attached to the skin. It is typically needed only for a short time and can often be reversed with another operation. It may also be used to relieve a bowel blockage caused by a tumor, either as colectomy with colostomy, or as a first surgery followed by a second surgery to remove the cancer. In some cases (e.g., abdominoperineal resection for lower rectal tumors involving the anus), a permanent colostomy is needed.

Unlike Stage 2, where there is no cancer in nearby lymph nodes, Stage 3 involves lymph node involvement. Stage 4, by contrast, involves spread to areas outside the colon and nearby lymph nodes (most often the liver and/or lungs).

results.info_summary: The key biomarker guiding immunotherapy in colon cancer is **mismatch repair deficiency (dMMR)** and its related status **MSI-H** (microsatellite instability-high). All colon cancers should be tested for mismatch repair (MMR) gene mutations. Immunotherapy with checkpoint inhibitors (e.g., pembrolizumab, nivolumab with or without ipilimumab) is preferred for dMMR/MSI-H colon cancers, including before colectomy. For pMMR/MSS cancers, chemotherapy is recommended instead. Other biomarkers where pembrolizumab is preferred include **TMB-H** and **PD-L1–positive**.

contexts: Title: . Content: 612: your biological (related by blood) family members. Those with a first-degree relative with colorectal cancer are more likely to have this cancer compared to the average person. Most colon cancers occur for unknown reasons. While rare, some people are born with a disorder that makes them more likely to get colon and other cancers. These are called inherited cancer syndromes. Two such conditions include Lynch syndrome and familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP). People born with Lynch syndrome are at high risk of developing colon, endometrial, and ovarian cancers. Lynch syndrome is caused by inherited mutations of the MMR genes. For cancers found to have the dMMR/MSI-H biomarker, testing for Lynch syndrome is recommended. FAP causes hundreds to thousands of polyps to form in the colon and rectum. The polyps start as benign growths, but over time can become invasive colon cancer. Cancer often develops by age 50 in people with classic FAP. A milder form (attenuated FAP) causes fewer polyps and usually starts later in life. If an inherited syndrome is suspected, your doctor will refer you to a genetic counselor. This expert can speak with you and your family about testing for syndromes related to colon cancer

results.info_summary:
**Summary:**

Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) is a protein found in the blood and is the biomarker used for monitoring colon cancer. CEA levels are often higher than normal in people with colon cancer, particularly if the cancer has spread to other organs. Monitoring CEA can be helpful even when cancer is only in the colon and levels are normal, because the level will rise if the cancer later spreads. However, monitoring CEA is not helpful for everyone, even if the cancer has spread. Pregnant people and tobacco users may have higher CEA levels.

Other biomarkers mentioned include mismatch repair deficiency (dMMR)/microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H), which is used for treatment planning rather than monitoring, and circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA), which is still being studied in clinical trials.

results.info_summary: CT (computed tomography) with contrast is the main imaging test for staging and surveillance of colon cancer, used to determine the extent of disease in the body. A CT scan of the chest and abdomen is recommended as part of initial testing and can show if the cancer has spread to the liver, lungs, or other organs. During the scan, contrast is injected into the vein and mixed with a liquid to drink to make pictures clearer; patients should inform their doctor of any prior contrast reactions. MRI is not often used to plan treatment for colon cancer, though it may be ordered to better view the liver or rectum or if CT results are unclear. If a pelvic MRI cannot be performed (e.g., due to a pacemaker) or MRI images are unhelpful, an endorectal ultrasound may be used instead. There is growing interest in circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) testing, also called a liquid biopsy, which looks for small pieces of DNA released by tumor cells into the blood and can detect microscopic disease remaining after colectomy; however, at this time ctDNA testing is only recommended as part of a clinical trial.
