**Summary: Treatment for Localized Thyroid Cancer**

Surgery is the main treatment for localized thyroid cancer. Treatment specifics depend on the cancer type and extent of disease:

- **Active surveillance** may be an option for very-low-risk cancers.
- **Total thyroidectomy** is recommended if the cancer is invasive; **RAI (radioactive iodine) therapy** may follow to kill remaining cancer cells.

- **External beam radiation therapy (EBRT)** is used for more aggressive, recurrent, or metastatic cancers that can't be removed surgically.
- **Targeted therapy** is generally reserved for cancers that can't be treated with surgery or RAI, have returned, or have metastasized

results.info_summary:
**Summary: Treatment for Regional Thyroid Cancer with Lymph Node Involvement**

For thyroid cancer that has spread to nearby lymph nodes (regional involvement):

- **Surgery is the primary treatment.** Total thyroidectomy is recommended for cancers that have grown or spread beyond the thyroid, including to nearby lymph nodes, or for tumors larger than 4 cm.
- **Lymph nodes near the thyroid that are known to have cancer are removed during surgery.**
- **Radioactive iodine (RAI) therapy** is usually recommended after total thyroidectomy if the cancer had spread significantly beyond the thyroid, or if there were large or more than 5 lymph nodes with cancer.
- **If a concerning amount of cancer remains after surgery,** options include: another surgery (preferred, if possible), RAI therapy, radiation therapy, systemic therapy, or monitoring.
- **After treatment, hormone replacement therapy with levothyroxine is started** to keep TSH low or normal.

results.info_summary:
The primary method for detecting recurrence in thyroid cancer involves **blood tests and neck ultrasound**. Specifically:

- **Thyroglobulin (Tg) blood testing**: Tg is only made by thyroid tissue. After total thyroidectomy, there shouldn't be any Tg in the blood, so checking Tg levels can monitor for cancer return. If Tg rises, further testing is needed.
- **Anti-thyroglobulin antibodies (Tg ab)**: A small number of people make antibodies in response to Tg, which can interfere with Tg level readings. If antibody levels go down, treatment may be working; if they go up, further testing should be done.
- **Neck ultrasound**: Used to monitor for the return of thyroid cancer.
- **Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) blood tests** are also part of follow-up.
- If recurrence is suspected, additional lab work, neck ultrasounds, TSH-stimulated testing, or imaging procedures such as CT or MRI may be used.
- **Note**: After lobectomy, Tg testing isn't helpful; follow-up involves physical exam, TSH blood test, and neck ultrasound 6 to 12 months after surgery.

Primary bone cancer originates in the bone or cartilage itself, distinguishing it from secondary (metastatic) bone cancer that spreads from other organs (breast, lungs, kidney). Most primary bone cancers are sarcomas—bone sarcomas—which start in the cells that form bone. Specific types and their origins include:

- **Osteosarcoma** – starts in cells most commonly in rapidly growing areas of bone (metaphysis), near the growth plates.
- **Ewing sarcoma** – starts in the bone marrow, commonly in the diaphysis of long bones or flat bones (pelvis, scapula).
- **Chondrosarcoma** – starts in the cells that form cartilage.
- **Chordoma** – starts in notochordal cells that form the spine and vertebrae (usually lower spinal column/sacrum or base of skull).
- **Giant cell tumor of bone (GCTB)** – an overgrowth of cells in the metaphysis extending into the epiphysis.

Osteosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma, and chondrosarcoma are the most common types of bone cancer (except multiple myeloma). Bone tumors often occur in areas of rapid bone growth (metaphysis).

Ewing sarcoma A cell must make a copy of its chromosomes before dividing into two cells. Sometimes, there are mistakes in the copies. One type of mistake is when parts (DNA) of two chromosomes break off and switch with each other. This is called a translocation. It can result in a fusion of two genes. A translocation between chromosomes 11 and 22 is written as t(11;22) and is common in Ewing sarcoma. Ewing sarcoma is characterized by the fusion of the EWS gene (EWSR1) on chromosome 22 with various members of the ETS gene family (FLI1, ERG, ETV1, ETV4, and FEV), with FLI1 being the most common. Almost everyone with Ewing sarcoma will have one of the possible gene fusions. This is not inherited from your birth parents but results from an error of cell division while your tissues were growing. This is called a somatic mutation or somatic change. Bone is a living tissue made of cells (osteocytes, osteoblasts, and osteoclasts), calcium, phosphate, hydroxyapatite (a bone mineral), and collagen. New bone formation, known as ossification, starts in the womb and ends during adolescence, between 10 and 19 years of age. Ossification is complete when the skeleton is done growing. Once ossification is complete, bone is continuously being replaced by a process called remodeling. Remodeling breaks down and rebuilds bone and helps maintain normal calcium levels in the body. When calcium is needed, cells called osteoclasts break down bone. This releases calcium into the bloodstream. At the same time, bone-forming cells called osteoblasts create bone from calcium in the bloodstream. Some types of bone cancer can interrupt this process. What causes primary CNS lymphoma? Every person diagnosed with cancer wants to know how they got it. Although no one knows exactly what causes a lymphoma, we do know that lymphomas often start with a genetic abnormality (mutation) in certain lymphocytes. This abnormality causes these lymphocytes to grow out of control (become cancerous). The abnormality occurs on its own. It’s not a mutation that occurs in other cells or organs in your body. And it’s not typically passed down in families (hereditary mutation). Although primary CNS lymphoma is rare, it could happen to almost anyone. However, some people with certain risk factors have a greater chance. Risk factors A risk factor is something that increases your chance of developing a disease. For example, having a reduced immune system increases the risk of developing primary CNS lymphoma. results.info_summary:
A diagnosis of bone cancer is confirmed using a **core needle or surgical biopsy**.

Key details:
- **Core needle biopsy** removes tissue samples with a hollow needle that grabs a piece of tissue; frequently performed under light sedation by an interventional radiologist, or by the surgeon in the office.
- **Surgical (open) biopsy** removes a sample of the tumor through a small incision; performed by the treating surgeon and requires a trip to the operating room.
- The **placement of the biopsy is critical**, so it is recommended that the biopsy be performed by an experienced surgeon at the center where the patient will receive treatment.
- A biopsy sample might also be tested to look for **biomarkers or proteins**, and the provider might refer the patient for **genetic testing**.
- **Bone marrow tests** (aspirate and biopsy) might be done in certain cases.
- While imaging tests (X-ray, bone scan, FDG-PET/CT) can detect cancer deposits, the biopsy is what confirms the diagnosis.

results.info_summary:
**Blood tests used in the evaluation of bone cancer:**

- **Alkaline phosphatase (ALP):** An enzyme found in blood; high levels can indicate bone tumors, liver disorders, or pregnancy. A bone scan may be performed if ALP levels are high.
- **Complete blood count (CBC):** Measures red blood cells (RBCs), white blood cells (WBCs), and platelets (PLTs).
- **Comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP):** Measures 14 substances in blood, providing information on kidney and liver function, blood sugar, calcium, and electrolyte levels. Specifically looks for hypercalcemia (higher-than-normal calcium levels), which can occur when bone damage from cancer causes bones to release calcium into the bloodstream.
- **Liver function tests (LFTs):** Measure chemicals made or processed by the liver; abnormal levels can signal liver problems or cancer spread to the liver.
- **Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH):** Measures an enzyme involved in converting food into energy; high levels can indicate cell damage caused by cancer.
- **Pregnancy test:** Given to those who can become pregnant before treatment begins.

Your bone marrow is like a sponge holding liquid and cells. An aspirate takes some of the liquid and cells out of the sponge, and a biopsy takes a piece of the sponge. The samples are usually taken from the back of the hip bone (pelvis). You will likely lie on your belly or side. Your doctors will first clean and give sedation and/or numb your skin and outer surface of your bone. For an aspirate, a hollow needle will be pushed through your skin and into the bone. Ewing sarcoma A cell must make a copy of its chromosomes before dividing into two cells. Sometimes, there are mistakes in the copies. One type of mistake is when parts (DNA) of two chromosomes break off and switch with each other. This is called a translocation. It can result in a fusion of two genes. A translocation between chromosomes 11 and 22 is written as t(11;22) and is common in Ewing sarcoma. Ewing sarcoma is characterized by the fusion of the EWS gene (EWSR1) on chromosome 22 with various members of the ETS gene family (FLI1, ERG, ETV1, ETV4, and FEV), with FLI1 being the most common. Almost everyone with Ewing sarcoma will have one of the possible gene fusions. This is not inherited from your birth parents but results from an error of cell division while your tissues were growing. This is called a somatic mutation or somatic change. results.info_summary: The TNM (tumor, node, metastasis) system is used to stage most bone cancers. In this system, T describes the size and depth of the primary tumor, N indicates whether cancer has spread to nearby lymph nodes, and M indicates whether cancer has metastasized to distant parts of the body. A grade (G) score is also used, which describes how abnormal the tumor cells look under a microscope (GX–G3). The T, N, M, and G scores are combined to assign a numbered stage from stage I to stage IV, with stage IV being the most advanced. Staging may be done twice: clinical stage (c) before treatment and pathologic/surgical stage (p) after surgery.

Metastasis Unlike normal cells, cancer cells can spread and form tumors in other parts of the body called metastases. In this process, cancer cells break away from the first (primary) tumor and travel through blood or lymph vessels to distant sites. Once in other sites, cancer cells may form secondary tumors. Since cancer cells can spread through the blood, it is still possible to develop metastases even when the axillary lymph nodes are negative for cancer. Cancer that has spread to a nearby body part such as the axillary lymph nodes is called a local metastasis. It might be referred to as locoregional disease or locally advanced. Cancer that has spread to a body part far from the primary tumor is called a distant metastasis. Breast cancer can metastasize almost anywhere but most commonly spreads to the bone (including spine), lungs, liver, brain, or distant lymph nodes. Breast cancer that has metastasized to other parts of the body is still called breast cancer. results.info_summary:
Mouth cancer staging is based on the TNM system, created by the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC). TNM stands for Tumor, Node, Metastasis and describes:

- **T**: The extent (size) of the tumor — how large it is and whether it has grown into nearby areas.
- **N**: Spread to nearby lymph nodes — whether cancer has spread to lymph nodes, and if so, how many and where.
- **M**: Metastasis to distant sites — whether cancer has spread to distant organs such as the lung and distant lymph nodes.

Staging is determined from a physical exam, biopsy, and imaging tests. The clinical stage is based on imaging and biopsy results before any treatment, while the pathologic (surgical) stage is determined by examining tissue removed during surgery. Numbered stages (0 to 4, with 4 being most advanced) are based on TNM scores. The staging information applies to squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of the mouth, including the mucosa of the lip.

results.info_summary: In the TNM system for staging mouth cancer, T refers to the size and extent of the main (primary) tumor. A higher T number indicates a larger tumor or greater spread. T1 is the lowest numbered T category and indicates a small tumor. According to the newly retrieved information, T1 in mouth cancer is defined as a tumor that is 2 cm or less with a depth of invasion (DOI) of 5 mm or less. Depth of invasion measures how deep the tumor has grown into tissue layers, not tumor thickness; it can be calculated using imaging such as MRI, and increased DOI raises the risk of regional lymph node metastases. By comparison, T2 includes a tumor 2 cm or less with DOI greater than 5 mm, or a tumor between 2 cm and 4 cm with DOI of 5 mm or less.

Oral mucosa The oral mucosa is the mucous membrane lining the inside of the mouth and lips. It is made up of 2 layers. Epithelium – The surface layer containing stratified squamous cells, which are thin, flat cells. Lamina propria – The bottom layer of connective tissue. A tumor can grow through the layers of the oral mucosa. A measure of how deep the tumor has grown is called depth of invasion (DOI). Depending on the region of the mouth, the epithelium may be nonkeratinized or keratinized. Nonkeratinized squamous epithelium covers the soft palate, inner lips, inner cheeks, the floor of the mouth, and area underneath the tongue. Keratinized squamous epithelium is present on rough surfaces caused by chewing such as the gums (gingiva) and hard palate as well as the top of the tongue. Smoking and vaping nicotine increases the risk of head and neck, lung, and other cancers; can limit how well cancer treatment works; impairs wound healing; and greatly increases side effects during and after surgery. Cannabis use may also affect the amount of anesthesia needed during surgery. Nicotine is the chemical in tobacco that drives continued smoking and vaping, and nicotine withdrawal is challenging for most people—stress from cancer can make quitting even harder. Smoking or heavy alcohol use worsens treatment outcomes and increases treatment toxicity.

results.info_summary: Depth of invasion (DOI) is a measure of how deep a tumor has grown into the layers of tissue of the oral mucosa (not tumor thickness). The oral mucosa consists of two layers: epithelium (surface layer of stratified squamous cells) and lamina propria (connective tissue below). A tumor can grow through these layers, and DOI quantifies this depth. Imaging scans such as MRI can be used to calculate DOI. As DOI increases, the risk of regional lymph node metastases also increases. DOI is a key component of TNM staging for mouth cancer (squamous cell carcinoma): T1 – tumor ≤2 cm with DOI ≤5 mm; T2 – tumor ≤2 cm with DOI >5 mm, or tumor 2–4 cm with DOI ≤10 mm; T3 – tumor 2–4 cm with DOI >10 mm, or tumor >4 cm with DOI ≤10 mm; T4a – tumor >4 cm with DOI >10 mm, or tumor invades nearby structures.

Ovarian transposition Cervical cancer treatment may involve external beam radiation therapy (EBRT). Radiation damages the ovaries and causes them to stop producing hormones needed for natural pregnancy. Ovarian transposition is a surgery that moves one or both ovaries out of the range of the radiation beam. The medical name for this procedure is oophoropexy. Ovarian transposition before starting EBRT may be an option if you are premenopausal and have the most common type of cervical cancer, squamous cell carcinoma. Egg freezing Unfertilized eggs can be removed, frozen, and stored for later use. The medical term for this is oocyte preservation. Surrogacy If you have frozen embryos or frozen eggs (oocytes), you may consider using a surrogate. A surrogate (often a relative or friend) volunteers to have the embryos inserted into their uterus. They carry the pregnancy and give birth. Cancer and its treatment, such as chemotherapy and radiation therapy, can affect fertility—the ability to have children—in mouth cancer patients. Treatment may cause fertility to be temporarily or permanently impaired or interrupted. The degree of fertility loss is related to:
- Age at time of diagnosis
- Treatment type(s)
- Treatment dose
- Treatment length

Radiation therapy, for example, can damage the hormone-making function of the ovaries and testicles, potentially causing the inability to conceive. Damage to the ovaries is known as premature ovarian insufficiency (POI) or radiation-induced premature menopause. Cancer and cancer treatment can also affect the ovaries and damage sperm.

Patients who want children in the future, or who are unsure, should be referred to a fertility specialist before starting cancer treatment to discuss fertility preservation options. Fertility preservation involves taking action before treatment begins to keep options open. Fertility and reproductive specialists can help determine what may be best for each situation. Fertility preservation options may include sperm banking (semen cryopreservation), egg freezing (oocyte cryopreservation), ovarian transposition (oophoropexy), embryo freezing, and consideration of possible surrogate pregnancy in the future.

Preventing pregnancy during treatment is also important. More information

Oral mucosa The oral mucosa is the mucous membrane lining the inside of the mouth and lips. It is made up of 2 layers. Epithelium – The surface layer containing stratified squamous cells, which are thin, flat cells. Lamina propria – The bottom layer of connective tissue. A tumor can grow through the layers of the oral mucosa. A measure of how deep the tumor has grown is called depth of invasion (DOI). Depending on the region of the mouth, the epithelium may be nonkeratinized or keratinized. Nonkeratinized squamous epithelium covers the soft palate, inner lips, inner cheeks, the floor of the mouth, and area underneath the tongue. Keratinized squamous epithelium is present on rough surfaces caused by chewing such as the gums (gingiva) and hard palate as well as the top of the tongue. results.info_summary:
The clinical evaluation of mouth cancer patients includes the following assessments:

- **Medical history** – a record of all health issues and treatments, including current and past medications, OTC medicines, herbals, and supplements; also includes reporting symptoms.
- **Physical exam** – checking temperature, blood pressure, pulse, breathing rate, height, weight; listening to lungs and heart; examining eyes, ears, nose, and throat; palpating body parts to assess organ size, texture, and pain; and feeling for enlarged lymph nodes in the neck, underarm, and groin.
- **Complete head and neck exam** – includes palpation of the oral cavity and use of a special mirror or fiberoptic scope to view areas of the mouth and throat not easily seen.
- **Dental exam** – regular dental cleanings and checkups; telling the dentist about head and neck cancer, as treatment can affect the jaw, teeth, and gums; dental work may be recommended before certain treatments.
- **Distress screening** – assessing emotional and psychological feelings related to the cancer diagnosis.
- **Fertility assessment (all genders)** – discussing fertility concerns and preventing pregnancy during treatment.

Performance status (PS) is a person's general level of fitness and ability to perform daily self-care tasks. In mouth/head and neck cancer, it is rated using the Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) scale, though the Karnofsky Performance Status (KPS) may also be used. ECOG PS is one factor considered when choosing a treatment plan, alongside patient preferences, which are always important. In head and neck cancer, PS might be referred to as good or poor; good PS is usually PS 0 or PS 1.

ECOG PS scores range from 0 to 5:
- PS 0: fully active
- PS 1: able to perform light to moderate activity, but with some limitations
- PS 2: limited to chair or bed less than half the time, still able to care for self
- PS 3: limited to chair or bed more than half the time
- PS 4: totally confined to bed or chair and completely unable to care for self
- PS 5: not alive

Title: . Content: 152: the genetic information in a cell. Normal human cells contain 23 pairs of chromosomes for a total of 46 chromosomes. Each chromosome contains thousands of genes. Genes are coded instructions for the proteins your cells make. Most genes contain information about a specific protein. A mutation is when something goes wrong in the genetic code. Biomarker tumor testing includes tests of genes or their products (proteins). It identifies the presence or absence of mutations and certain proteins that might suggest treatment. This information may be helpful when choosing the best treatment for you. It is sometimes called molecular testing or tumor profiling, tumor sequencing, gene expression profiling, or genomic testing. These tests are generally used in advanced or widely spread (metastatic) cancers. However, in comparison to other cancers, molecular testing has limited value in the treatment of mouth cancers since there are few drugs that specifically target the genetic mutations causing mouth cancers to grow and spread. Most stomach cancers begin in the mucus-secreting cells lining the inside of the stomach wall and are called adenocarcinomas. The stomach wall has 5 main layers: mucosa, submucosa, muscle, subserosa, and serosa. - Metastatic: has spread to distant parts of the body, most commonly the liver, abdominal lining (peritoneum), and distant lymph nodes; it may also spread to the lungs or bone.

It most commonly spreads to the liver, abdominal lining (peritoneum), and distant lymph nodes; it may also spread to the lungs or bone. Stomach cancer can spread to distant parts of the body through the blood or lymphatic system, and this distant spread is what defines metastatic stomach cancer. This contrasts with early-stage stomach cancer (confined to the mucosa, often small at 2 centimeters or less, with no lymph node involvement) and locoregional/locally advanced stomach cancer (invading deeper layers of the stomach wall and/or spreading to nearby lymph nodes or organs near the stomach).

- **General health tests** and **nutrition assessment**
- **Blood tests**
- **Imaging tests**
- **Endoscopy procedures**
- **H. pylori tests**
- **Biopsy** (including **biomarker testing**)
- **Genetic risk testing**
- **Performance status** evaluation
- **Physical exam** — checking vital signs (temperature, blood pressure, pulse, breathing rate), height and weight, listening to lungs and heart, examining eyes/ears/nose/throat, palpating body parts for organ size/texture/pain, and feeling for enlarged lymph nodes in neck, underarm, and groin
- **Family history** — gathering health history of blood relatives, including cancer type, location, age at diagnosis, and whether they had genetic testing

Results from **imaging studies and biopsy (including biomarker tests)** are used to determine the treatment plan.

What causes pancreatic cancer? Many people with cancer wonder how they got it. Experts don’t know exactly what causes pancreatic cells to become cancer cells. But they do know several factors that increase the chance of developing pancreatic cancer. Such risk factors include: Lifestyle factors, such as smoking tobacco, heavy alcohol use, and a less healthy diet Major contact with cancer-causing chemicals, such as pesticides Health conditions, such as diabetes and chronic inflammation of the pancreas Close blood relatives with pancreatic, breast, ovarian, or colorectal cancers or melanoma About 1 in 10 pancreatic cancers are hereditary. This means that a higher risk was passed down to you by your parents through your genes. The genetic cause of hereditary pancreatic cancer is unknown in most families. Hereditary health conditions that are known to increase risk of pancreatic cancer include: Hereditary breast-ovarian cancer syndrome (HBOC) Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, Lynch syndrome, and Li-Fraumeni syndrome Familial malignant melanoma syndrome, also known as melanoma-pancreatic cancer syndrome or

Title: . Content: 612: your biological (related by blood) family members. Those with a first-degree relative with colorectal cancer are more likely to have this cancer compared to the average person. Most colon cancers occur for unknown reasons. While rare, some people are born with a disorder that makes them more likely to get colon and other cancers. These are called inherited cancer syndromes. Two such conditions include Lynch syndrome and familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP). People born with Lynch syndrome are at high risk of developing colon, endometrial, and ovarian cancers. Lynch syndrome is caused by inherited mutations of the MMR genes. For cancers found to have the dMMR/MSI-H biomarker, testing for Lynch syndrome is recommended. FAP causes hundreds to thousands of polyps to form in the colon and rectum. The polyps start as benign growths, but over time can become invasive colon cancer. Cancer often develops by age 50 in people with classic FAP. A milder form (attenuated FAP) causes fewer polyps and usually starts later in life. If an inherited syndrome is suspected, your doctor will refer you to a genetic counselor. This expert can speak with you and your family about testing for syndromes related to colon cancer

The stomach wall is made up of **5 main layers**:  
1. **Mucosa** – innermost membrane in contact with food; consists of surface epithelium, lamina propria, and muscularis mucosae.  
2. **Submucosa** – connective tissue with blood vessels, nerve cells, and lymph vessels.  
3. **Muscle layer** (muscularis propria) – soft tissue that moves food through the stomach.  
4. **Subserosa** – connective tissue supporting the serosa.  
5. **Serosa** – outer membrane covering the stomach, allowing smooth movement against other organs.

results.info_summary:
**Local Spread Pattern of Stomach Cancer:**

- Most stomach cancers (adenocarcinomas) start in the innermost layer (mucosa) of the stomach wall and grow **outward through the layers** of the stomach wall (mucosa → submucosa → muscle → subserosa → serosa).
- **Early-stage:** Cancer has not grown beyond the first layer (mucosa); tumor is often small (2 cm or less) and not in any lymph nodes.
- **Locoregional/locally advanced:** Cancer has invaded the second layer (submucosa) or beyond, and may spread to nearby (regional) lymph nodes or organs near the stomach.
- **Local spread structures:** Cancer can spread to nearby lymph nodes, veins, arteries, and organs such as the **liver, pancreas, and spleen**. It may also grow into nearby lymphatic or blood vessels.
- **Inward growth:** Cancer can also grow inward, forming an ulcer or mass that causes symptoms.
- **Metastatic (distant) spread:** Via blood or lymphatic system, most commonly to the liver, abdominal lining (peritoneum), and distant lymph nodes; may also spread to lungs or bone.

results.info_summary: The mucosa is the innermost layer of the stomach wall and the site where most stomach cancers begin. Most gastric cancers start in the cells lining the inside of the stomach that secrete mucus; these are called adenocarcinomas. Stomach cancer starts in the mucosa and grows outward through the other layers (submucosa, muscle, subserosa, serosa). Before cancer develops, pre-cancerous changes often occur in the mucosa, and these early changes rarely cause symptoms, so they often go undetected. Early-stage stomach cancer has not grown beyond the mucosa; the tumor is often small (2 centimeters or less) and has not reached lymph nodes. In locoregional or locally advanced cancer, the cancer has invaded the submucosa or beyond.

results.info_summary: Gliomas are classified using three main approaches: histology (how tumor cells look under a microscope), grade (how abnormal the cells are and how quickly the tumor is likely to grow), and biomarkers (molecular characteristics such as genetic mutations). A glioma is diagnosed via stereotactic biopsy, in which a thin, hollow needle removes a tumor sample for lab testing, including molecular testing. Each glioma type has its own biomarker or set of biomarkers; for example, an astrocytoma with a mutation in the IDH gene is called an "astrocytoma IDH-mutant." When classifications are combined, they provide a full description, such as "astrocytoma IDH-mutant grade 2," naming the cell type, biomarker, and growth rate. Grade ranges from 1 to 4: grades 1–2 are low-grade, and grades 3–4 are high-grade; higher-grade tumors grow and spread faster, and all high-grade tumors require additional therapy after surgery. IDH is a commonly tested glioma biomarker, though it is not the only one. Biomarker testing looks for changes in genes, proteins, and other markers—many of which are mutations—to improve diagnostic accuracy, predict prognosis, and guide targeted treatment

results.info_summary:
Glioma diagnosis involves several methods:

1. **Imaging**: MRI is typically used; CT scan is an alternative if MRI is unavailable or not recommended. A radiologist analyzes the images and conveys results to the care team.

2. **Biopsy**: The only way to get an accurate diagnosis. Types include:
   - **Surgical resection**: Removes a piece of tissue (doubles as biopsy and treatment).
   - **Stereotactic biopsy**: A thin, hollow needle is inserted into the brain to remove a sliver of the tumor.

3. **Lab testing**: Tissue samples are sent to a laboratory for analysis by a neuropathologist, who examines the tissue under a microscope. Results indicate whether the tumor is malignant or benign and may include preliminary diagnosis (type and grade).

4. **Molecular (genetic) testing / Biomarker testing**: Performed on biopsy samples. Identifies tumor type, growth rate, and specific molecular characteristics such as genetic mutations. Can improve diagnostic accuracy and guide targeted treatment options. Commonly tested biomarkers provide specific information about the glioma.

Treatment eligibility for glioma is determined by:

results.info_summary:
Tissue sampling for glioma diagnosis involves a biopsy, which is the only way to get an accurate diagnosis. Methods include:

- **Resection**: A surgical procedure that removes the entire tumor or as much as safely possible; serves as both biopsy and treatment, and provides the largest sample for pathology. Used when the tumor is accessible.
- **Standard biopsy**: Used when resection isn't possible (tumor in a hard-to-reach or vital brain area). Two types:
  - **Stereotactic biopsy**: A precise procedure using a thin, hollow needle inserted into the brain to remove a sliver of tumor, often for hard-to-reach/vital areas; aims to remove only enough tissue for diagnosis. Performed by a neurosurgeon with a head frame or markers and anesthesia.
  - **Open biopsy**.

After sampling, tissue is sent to a lab and examined by a neuropathologist (microscopic and molecular/genetic testing), sometimes immediately during surgery. If no neuropathologist is available on-site, the biopsy can be sent to one.

Generally, 20 percent or more of all cells in the bone marrow must be blasts (at least 1 out of every 5 bone marrow cells). However, diagnosis is possible with any number of blasts if certain gene mutations or abnormal chromosomes are present. Diagnosis is confirmed using a bone marrow aspirate and bone marrow biopsy. Genetic and biomarker tests identify the AML subtype, guide treatment, and determine prognosis. results.info_summary:
**Molecular and cytogenetic tests used in AML workup:**

- **Karyotype (cytogenetics):** Detects chromosome changes/abnormalities in AML cells from blood or bone marrow samples; requires growing cells.
- **Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH):** Uses special dye probes that attach to DNA to detect abnormalities too small to be seen with other methods; only detects known changes; does not require growing cells, so it can be performed on bone marrow or blood samples.
- **Next-generation sequencing (NGS):** Looks for gene/chromosome changes or abnormalities unique to AML cells.
- **Polymerase chain reaction (PCR):** Also used to detect mutations/abnormalities unique to AML cells.

These tests are performed on a sample of blood or bone marrow to identify specific mutations in AML cancer cells; some mutations determine the type of treatment given. They are used to determine the AML subtype, target treatment, and establish prognosis. This testing looks only at changes in leukemia cells (not inherited/family risk changes) and is sometimes called molecular testing, tumor profiling, gene expression profiling, or genomic testing. Note: a bone marrow sample is sometimes needed to get all the information required to plan treatment.

results.info_summary:
**Summary: Imaging Modalities for Assessing Extramedullary Disease in AML**

- **FDG-PET/CT** is recommended if leukemia outside the blood and bone marrow (extramedullary disease) is suspected.
- **Brain CT without contrast** is used if central nervous system (CNS) bleeding is suspected.
- **Brain MRI with contrast** is used if leukemic meningitis is suspected.
- Imaging tests can detect leukemia spread outside the bloodstream to lymph nodes, liver, spleen, and skin; it rarely spreads to the lining of the brain and spinal cord.
- Imaging can also reveal areas of infection or bleeding that may impact care.

In short, the primary imaging modality for extramedullary AML assessment is **FDG-PET/CT**, with brain CT and MRI reserved for suspected CNS involvement.

Chemotherapy is the standard of care for AML and is often given as multi-agent regimens. Commonly used chemotherapy agents include:

- **Antimetabolites:** Cladribine (Mavenclad), clofarabine (Clolar), cytarabine (Ara-C), fludarabine, methotrexate

results.info_summary:
Targeted therapy in AML is a form of systemic therapy that focuses on specific or unique features of cancer cells. It seeks out how cancer cells grow, divide, and move in the body, and these drugs stop the action of molecules that help cancer cells grow and/or survive. Examples of targeted therapies for AML include:

- **CD33:** Gemtuzumab ozogamicin (GO) is a targeted therapy linked to a chemotherapy drug. It attaches to a cell surface protein called CD33, then enters the cell, where chemotherapy is released. Many leukemic blasts have CD33 proteins; mature blood cells do not have CD33 and are not affected. GO may delay blood count recovery and cause liver issues.

- **Core binding factor (CBF):** CBF creates a shortage of all types of mature blood cells. Gemtuzumab ozogamicin (GO) might be used in combination with daunorubicin and cytarabine to treat AML with CBF or other genetic abnormalities.

- **FLT3:** Gilteritinib, quizartinib, midostaurin, or sorafenib is used to treat AML with certain FLT3 mutations such as FLT3-ITD and FLT3-T

analysis.current_understanding: Targeted therapy in AML uses drugs that target specific features of leukemic cells, such as CD33, core binding factor (CBF), and FLT3 mutations. Examples include gemtuzumab ozogamicin (GO) for CD33-positive AML, which delivers chemotherapy to leukemic blasts while sparing mature blood cells, though it may delay blood count recovery and cause liver issues. For CBF AML, GO may be combined with daunorubicin and cytarabine. For FLT3-mutated AML (e.g., FLT3-ITD, FLT3-TKD), inhibitors like gilteritinib, quizartinib, midostaurin, or sorafenib are used. These therapies seek out how cancer cells grow, divide, and move, and stop molecules that help cancer cells grow and/or survive.

results.info_summary:
**Summary: Common Genetic Alterations in AML**

AML cells frequently contain acquired (somatic) genetic changes in genes and chromosomes—unique to the leukemia cells, not inherited. These are detectable via mutation testing (also called molecular testing, tumor profiling, gene expression profiling, or genomic testing).

**Types of genetic changes:**
- **Amplification** – part or whole chromosome/gene is increased/duplicated
- **Deletion** – part of a chromosome or gene is missing, e.g., del(5q)
- **Insertion** – a new part of a chromosome or gene is included
- **Inversion** – switching of parts within one chromosome, e.g., inv(16) and inv(3)
- **Point mutation** – part of a gene is changed
- **Translocation (chromosome level) / Rearrangement (gene level)** – switching of parts between 2 chromosomes, e.g., t(8;21)(q22;q1), with gene rearrangement written as RUNX1::RUNX1T

**Testing methods:** karyotype (cytogenetics), fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), next-generation sequencing.

**Note:** Some hereditary cancer/leukemia predisposition

analysis.current_understanding: AML cells commonly acquire somatic genetic alterations in genes and chromosomes, which are not inherited. These alterations include amplifications (duplications of gene/chromosome regions), deletions (e.g., del(5q)), insertions, inversions (e.g., inv(16), inv(3)), point mutations, and translocations/rearrangements (e.g., t(8;21)(q22;q1) leading to RUNX1::RUNX1T). Testing methods such as karyotype, FISH, and next-generation sequencing can detect these changes. Some hereditary cancer/leukemia predisposition may also be relevant, but the summary primarily addresses acquired alterations.

results.info_summary: Hematopoietic cell transplant (HCT) is one of the treatment types for AML, alongside systemic therapy (chemotherapy, targeted therapy), clinical trials, and supportive care. AML treatment is given in phases, with the initial goal of achieving remission, and the treatment plan is selected based on the patient's AML subtype. For an allogeneic (donor) HCT to be a treatment option, a very good HLA match between the patient and donor is required; HLA typing is a blood test performed before transplant, and blood or tissue samples from the patient and blood relatives are tested first. Otherwise, the body will reject the donor cells or the donor cells will react against the body. However, the available information—including newly retrieved content from NCCN Guidelines for Patients materials covering Hodgkin lymphoma, NSCLC, primary CNS lymphoma, and general guidance on cancer staging and treatment planning—does not specify exactly when hematopoietic cell transplant is considered in AML. The newly retrieved information focuses on cancer staging (anatomic and prognostic, clinical and pathologic stages) and treatment planning for other cancer types, and does not address the timing or indications for HCT in AML.

results.info_summary:
AML treatment selection is influenced by:

- **AML subtype** – determined by genetic and biomarker tests (gene mutations, abnormal chromosomes), which help target treatment and determine prognosis.
- **Test results** – blood tests, bone marrow aspirate and biopsy, and imaging studies guide the treatment plan.
- **Treatment goals** – regular discussions with the care team about the patient's goals shape the plan; treatment is given in phases with the goal of remission.
- **Multidisciplinary team (MDT) input** – treatment decisions involve a team of health care and psychosocial professionals with expertise in the patient's cancer type.
- **Cancer features and health circumstances** – some therapies work best for people with specific cancer features or health circumstances.
- **Evidence and safety** – therapies are categorized as preferred (most evidence, may work better and be safer), other recommended, or used in certain cases.
- **Clinical trial availability** – patients should ask whether a clinical trial might be right for them.

Note: Chemotherapy is the standard of care for AML, with dosing based on body weight and given in cycles.

Ovarian transposition Cervical cancer treatment may involve external beam radiation therapy (EBRT). Radiation damages the ovaries and causes them to stop producing hormones needed for natural pregnancy. Ovarian transposition is a surgery that moves one or both ovaries out of the range of the radiation beam. The medical name for this procedure is oophoropexy. Ovarian transposition before starting EBRT may be an option if you are premenopausal and have the most common type of cervical cancer, squamous cell carcinoma. Egg freezing Unfertilized eggs can be removed, frozen, and stored for later use. The medical term for this is oocyte preservation. Surrogacy If you have frozen embryos or frozen eggs (oocytes), you may consider using a surrogate. A surrogate (often a relative or friend) volunteers to have the embryos inserted into their uterus. They carry the pregnancy and give birth. results.info_summary:
**Fertility discussion before starting systemic therapy for AML:**

- Chemotherapy and other systemic treatments can affect fertility (the ability to have children) in all genders. Cancer and cancer treatment can affect the ovaries (damaging hormone-making function and causing premature ovarian insufficiency/radiation-induced premature menopause) and damage sperm.
- Before starting therapy, patients should ask their care team how cancer and cancer treatment might affect their fertility and whether they are at risk for impaired fertility. This applies to people of any gender. A doctor will discuss any fertility-related risks of the treatment plan.
- Patients who want to have children in the future—or who are unsure—should be referred to a fertility specialist (reproductive endocrinologist) to discuss options **before starting treatment**, since fertility preservation may require action before treatment begins.
- Fertility preservation keeps options open. Common methods include sperm banking (semen cryopreservation), egg freezing (oocyte cryopreservation), and embryo freezing; other options may include ovarian transposition (oophoropexy) and consideration of surrogacy in the future. Fertility and reproductive specialists can help determine the best approach and explain how a patient may be able to have a baby during or after treatment.

It also notes that fertility preservation (e.g., sperm or egg freezing) may require action before treatment begins. However, it does not specify how particular AML treatments (e.g., specific chemotherapy agents, targeted therapies, or stem cell transplants) affect fertility, nor does it provide details on the extent or mechanisms of fertility impairment for each treatment type. Supportive care is a recognized treatment type for AML, alongside systemic therapy (chemotherapy, targeted therapy), clinical trials, and hematopoietic cell transplant. It is also called palliative care and is intended to relieve symptoms of cancer, side effects of cancer therapies, and other cancer-related health issues. It is given at any stage of disease, not just at the end of life; it is not meant to treat the cancer itself, but to relieve symptoms and improve comfort. One treatment goal is controlling cancer, but this should be balanced with maintaining quality of life.

results.info_summary:
**Tests used for immunophenotyping in AML diagnosis:**

- **Flow cytometry** is the primary test used for immunophenotyping. It passes dyed cells through a beam of light to measure cell number, size, and shape, and can detect subtle differences between blood cancer types that a standard blood test cannot. It may be used on peripheral blood or bone marrow aspirate samples.
- **Immunophenotyping** specifically uses antibodies to detect the presence or absence of white blood cell antigens (biomarkers)—proteins found on the surface of or inside white blood cells. Certain biomarkers are targeted in AML treatment.
- **Immunohistochemistry (IHC)** is a related special staining process that adds a chemical marker to cells, which are then examined under a microscope. IHC looks for the immunophenotype of cells from a biopsy or tissue sample (e.g., bone marrow aspirate and biopsy).

**Purpose of Genetic and Biomarker Tests in AML:**

Genetic and biomarker tests in AML are used to:
1. **Learn more about your subtype of AML**
2. **Target treatment** — certain biomarkers are targeted in AML treatment

Gleason patterns After studying your biopsy sample under a microscope, the pathologist will assign a number based on the “pattern” of cancer cells (Gleason pattern) in the sample. A cancer cell pattern that looks more like normal and healthy cells is given a lower number. A cell pattern that looks more abnormal is assigned a higher number. Gleason patterns range from 1 to However, patterns 1 and 2 are so rarely found that they are no longer used. So the lowest (most normal) pattern number is Gleason score If prostate tumors contained only one pattern of cancer cells, estimating risk would be much easier. But prostate biopsies often contain more than one pattern of cells. To account for this, the two most common Gleason patterns found in the biopsy sample are combined into a single Gleason score. The pattern of cancer cells that takes up the largest area in the sample is assigned the first number. The pattern that accounts for the secondlargest area is given the second number. results.info_summary:
**Summary: Hereditary Syndromes as Major Risk Factors for Ovarian Cancer**

- About 1 in 6 ovarian cancers is caused by inherited (germline) gene mutations passed from parent to child — this is called hereditary ovarian cancer. It usually starts at a younger age than non-hereditary ovarian cancer.
- The most common cause is mutations in **BRCA1 (breast cancer gene 1)** or **BRCA2 (breast cancer gene 2)**, known as hereditary breast-ovarian cancer syndrome (HBOC). Everyone has BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes; when working properly they repair damaged cells, but mutations increase the risk of ovarian, breast, and some other cancers.
- **Lynch syndrome** is another major cause of hereditary ovarian cancer. It is the most common cause of hereditary colon and uterine cancers but can also cause ovarian and other cancers. Families with a history of Lynch syndrome may be at risk for ovarian and other cancers.
- **Li-Fraumeni syndrome** is also known to increase ovarian cancer risk (as well as pancreatic cancer), alongside Lynch syndrome and HBOC.

results.info_summary: Fertility-sparing surgery may be considered for some very early ovarian cancers that haven't spread beyond the ovaries. It involves removing one or both ovaries and fallopian tubes but leaving the uterus in place. A unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (USO) is only an option if the cancer is in one ovary and is appropriate for this procedure; natural pregnancy may still be possible if menopause hasn't occurred. If cancer is in both ovaries, a bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (BSO) without hysterectomy may be an option, though natural pregnancy isn't possible—assisted reproductive approaches like IVF (using your own eggs removed before surgery or donor eggs) may allow pregnancy. Patients should play an active role in their care by asking questions and making shared decisions with their care team, and can use suggested questions from the NCCN Guidelines for Patients to get more information on all aspects of their care.

Surveillance after ovarian cancer treatment includes:

- **Regular oncologist visits** for physical and pelvic exams when there are no signs of cancer:
  - First 2 years: every 2 to 4 months
  - Next 3 years: every 3 to 6 months
  - After 5 years: once a year
- **CA-125 (or other tumor marker) testing** on a regular basis if the level was high originally.
- **Blood and imaging tests** may be ordered if symptoms develop or if there are other reasons to suspect relapse.

Patients should report symptoms that may indicate recurrence, including pain or bloating in the pelvis or belly, unexplained weight loss, upset stomach, constipation, trouble eating or feeling full fast, fatigue, and needing to urinate often or urgently.

results.info_summary: Platinum-sensitive recurrent ovarian cancer is defined as cancer that returns more than 6 months after complete remission from platinum-based chemotherapy. Because platinum-based drugs worked well before, platinum-based chemotherapy is typically recommended for recurrent platinum-sensitive disease, especially for the first recurrence. The targeted therapy bevacizumab may be added to chemotherapy. In certain circumstances, secondary cytoreductive surgery may be suggested before starting recurrence treatment to remove all visible cancer. If recurrence treatment with platinum-based chemotherapy works well or very well, maintenance therapy is an option: bevacizumab can be continued alone if it was part of the recurrence regimen, and a PARP inhibitor may be an option if the patient hasn't already been treated with one and has a BRCA mutation. After successful chemotherapy for recurrent cancer, maintenance therapy with a PARP inhibitor can be continued until the cancer grows or spreads.

results.info_summary:
**Maintenance Therapy for Ovarian Cancer**

Maintenance therapy is systemic therapy given after successful initial treatment (surgery and platinum-based chemotherapy) to reduce the risk of cancer returning or extend time until it returns/worsens. It is an option for **stage 2, 3, and 4** cancers that respond well to initial treatment.

**PARP inhibitors (PARPi)** are oral targeted therapies used for maintenance, working best in **homologous recombination deficiency (HRD)-positive** cancers, including BRCA-mutated cancers.

PARP inhibitors used for maintenance after initial treatment:
- **Olaparib (Lynparza)** — with bevacizumab, given up to 15 months, with olaparib continued up to 2 years total
- **Niraparib (Zejula)** — alone, up to 3 years
- **Rucaparib** — alone, up to 2 years

Notes:
- Maintenance therapy is stopped if cancer grows/spreads or side effects become unsafe.
- Little research exists on PARPi maintenance for **stage 2** ovarian cancer; patients should discuss options with their provider.
- Recommendations may change with ongoing research.

results.info_summary:
**Genetic Alterations Tested for in Ovarian Cancer:**

**Germline (inherited) testing** — done on normal tissue (blood, saliva, or cheek swab):
- Everyone diagnosed with ovarian cancer should have genetic testing for inherited (germline) BRCA mutations.
- Testing typically covers BRCA and other genes involved in hereditary cancer, including many hereditary syndromes beyond BRCA and Lynch syndrome (e.g., Lynch syndrome is associated with increased ovarian cancer risk).
- About 1 in 6 ovarian cancers is caused by inherited gene mutations.

**Somatic (tumor) testing / biomarker testing** — done on removed tumor tissue or blood samples:
- Everyone diagnosed with ovarian cancer should have their tumor tested for mutations in BRCA genes and other genes important in DNA repair (BRCA is the most important biomarker for treatment planning).
- BRCA mutations are a form of homologous recombination deficiency (HRD); tumors can be HRD-positive with or without a BRCA mutation. BRCA and HRD status guide maintenance therapy decisions.
- Other biomarkers tested (generally recommended for recurrent ovarian cancer): microsatellite instability (MSI), mismatch repair (MMR), HER2 expression, tumor mutational burden (TMB), BRAF V600E mutation, folate receptor

The main risk factors for ovarian cancer identified in the information are:

**Genetic/hereditary factors:**
- About 1 in 6 ovarian cancers is caused by inherited gene mutations (hereditary ovarian cancer)
- Mutations in BRCA1 (breast cancer gene 1) or BRCA2 (breast cancer gene 2) increase risk of ovarian, breast, and some other cancers
- Lynch syndrome — the most common cause of hereditary colon and uterine cancers — can also cause ovarian cancer
- Ovarian cancer associated with BRCA mutations or Lynch syndrome usually starts at a younger age than non-hereditary ovarian cancer
- Some cancers and other diseases can run in families; family history of cancer among blood relatives, including the specific type of cancer and age at diagnosis, is relevant to risk assessment

**Assessment:** Doctors assess hereditary ovarian cancer likelihood using age, health history, and family history; genetic testing is recommended for everyone diagnosed with ovarian cancer.

(Note: The information provided focuses primarily on genetic risk factors and does not list other potential risk factors such as age, reproductive history, or hormone use.)

results.info_summary:
The FIGO (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics) system is the most commonly used staging system for ovarian cancer, though a similar AJCC system also exists. In the FIGO system, stage is defined by three main areas of cancer growth: the extent of the primary tumor (T), spread to nearby lymph nodes (N), and spread to distant sites/metastasis (M). Stages are numbered I, II, III, and IV, and are divided into substages for more detail. Staging is often done twice—clinical stage (before treatment, based on physical exam, biopsy, and imaging) and pathologic/surgical stage (after surgery, based on tissue removed during surgery), with the pathologic stage providing the most accurate picture of how far the cancer has spread and guiding post-surgery treatment. Staging helps predict prognosis and guides treatment decisions.

- **Stage I**: Cancer is confined to one or both ovaries.
  - **1A**: Cancer in one ovary; capsule intact, no cancer on outer surface, no cancer cells in ascites or washings.
  - **1B**: Cancer in both ovaries; capsules intact, no cancer on outer surface, no cancer cells in ascites or washings.

**Summary: Common symptoms of ovarian cancer listed in the ontology**

Ovarian cancer may cause no symptoms until the tumor has grown large or the cancer has spread. Common symptoms include:

- Feeling bloated
- Heartburn and indigestion
- Pain or pressure in the pelvis or belly
- Trouble eating or feeling full fast
- Having to urinate often or urgently
- Pain during sex

These symptoms may also result from hormonal changes or other common health problems. Ovarian cancer is more likely to be the cause if symptoms: began less than 1 year ago, occur more than 12 days per month, and are becoming more severe over time.

- Platinum-based chemotherapy is typically recommended for recurrent disease, especially for the first recurrence

results.info_summary:
Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is a type of blood cancer that occurs in the lymphocytes—a type of white blood cell—specifically abnormal B cells. It grows slowly, and treatment may not be needed for years; some patients may never need treatment. The specific cause of CLL isn't currently known other than that there is a change within the bone marrow. It can be tied to several factors, including older adults developing mutations over time and blood relatives of someone with CLL having a higher chance of getting it themselves.

CLL is the same cancer as small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL)—the only difference is where the abnormal cells are found. CLL is mostly found in the blood and bone marrow; SLL is mostly found in the lymph nodes and spleen. If a person has fewer than 5,000 cancerous cells in their blood, it is considered SLL; anything more than that is considered CLL. Because the cancer cells are the same, treatment of CLL and SLL is the same, and the disease is often referred to as CLL/SLL.

results.info_summary:
CLL/SLL is diagnosed through blood tests and, if needed, biopsy:

**Blood tests:** A blood sample is sent to a lab and examined by a hematopathologist (a specialist in diagnosing blood and immune cell cancers). Tests include:
- **Blood smear:** A drop of blood examined under a microscope; the appearance of abnormal cells can indicate the cancer type.
- **Flow cytometry:** Detects common patterns of proteins on the outside of cells (the immunophenotype). CLL cells have proteins such as CD200 and LEF1 (unlike mantle cell lymphoma).
- **Diagnostic threshold:** A CLL diagnosis requires at least 5,000 or more monoclonal B lymphocytes per microliter in the blood.

**Biopsy:** If blood results aren't clear, a lymph node or bone marrow biopsy confirms CLL. Lymph node testing also confirms small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL). Biopsy types include excisional (whole lymph node removed), incisional (part of a lymph node removed), and needle biopsy (small sample, used when other biopsies aren't safe). Removing a lymph node does not impair the ability to fight infections.

results.info_summary:
Common symptoms of CLL may include:

- Swollen glands in the neck or swelling in the stomach
- Fatigue or feeling tired more easily
- Excessive sweating or night sweats (sometimes drenching sheets)
- Fever (including fevers when not sick)
- Infections that keep coming back despite treatment
- Loss of appetite or early satiety (feeling full too quickly)
- Unintentional weight loss

Note: CLL usually doesn’t cause symptoms at first and may be found through routine blood testing.

results.gold_answer: CLL may be asymptomatic and discovered incidentally on routine blood testing.
results.answer: Yes.

results.info_summary:
**Risk Factors for Developing CLL:**

- **Age:** Older adults tend to develop changes or mutations over time that could cause cancer like CLL to form.
- **Family history/Genetics:** Blood relatives of someone with CLL have a higher chance of developing CLL themselves. Relatives are **7 to 8 times more likely** to develop CLL if there is a family history. First- and second-degree relatives (siblings, parents, grandparents) are relevant.
- **Lifestyle factors** (discussed with your doctor): diet, physical activity level, cigarette smoking, and alcohol consumption.

Note: The specific cause of CLL is not currently known, other than that there is a change within the bone marrow.

Bone marrow tests are not often needed for diagnosis but may be done to investigate low blood cell counts.

results.info_summary: CLL cells often exhibit a characteristic immunophenotype—a common pattern of surface proteins on the outside of cells—detected by flow cytometry, which identifies markers on cells via antibodies against white blood cell antigens (biomarkers). Key examples include CD20 (which helps identify the correct type of cancer), CD200, and LEF1; these help distinguish CLL from other lymphomas, as mantle cell lymphoma lacks CD200 and LEF1. The immunophenotype acts like a silhouette or shape that identifies the cell type. A CLL diagnosis requires at least 5,000 monoclonal B lymphocytes per microliter of blood. Beyond surface proteins, CLL cells also have other biomarkers detectable by FISH (e.g., 17p deletion), DNA sequencing (e.g., TP53 and IGHV mutations), and karyotype analysis, which help guide treatment selection.

This oversupply of abnormal B cells prevents healthy B cells from performing their duties effectively. This results in fewer healthy blood cells and a higher risk of infection. What are the symptoms of CLL? Usually, CLL doesn’t cause symptoms at first. It may be found due to routine blood testing. Symptoms of CLL may include the following. Family history significantly increases CLL risk. Blood relatives of someone with CLL have a higher chance of developing it themselves, and relatives are 7 to 8 times more likely to develop CLL when there is a family history. Because of this, health history taking for CLL includes family history: patients are asked to discuss the health of their close blood relatives—siblings, parents, and grandparents (first- and second-degree relatives). Doctors may ask about the specific type of cancer or where it started, whether it occurred in multiple locations, and whether relatives had genetic testing.

These inherited mutations occur in every cell in the body, can be passed on to children, and may put a person at risk for more than one type of cancer. results.info_summary:
Before starting CLL treatment in women of reproductive age, key considerations include:

- **Pregnancy testing**: A pregnancy test is required before treatment, as some cancer treatments can harm an unborn baby. Treatment options depend on the results.
- **Fertility preservation**: Chemotherapy and other treatments can temporarily or permanently impair fertility. Women who want children in the future—or are unsure—should be referred to a fertility specialist before starting treatment. Collecting and freezing eggs is a common method.
- **Preventing pregnancy during treatment**: Preventing pregnancy during treatment is important, as cancer and cancer treatment can affect the ovaries and damage sperm. Hormonal birth control may be an option.
- **Factors affecting fertility loss**: Loss of fertility is related to age at diagnosis, treatment type(s), treatment dose, and treatment length.
- **Resources**: More information on fertility preservation is available in the NCCN Guidelines for Patients®: Adolescent and Young Adult Cancer at NCCN.org/patientguidelines and on the NCCN Patient Guides for Cancer app.

These discussions should occur before treatment begins to keep future reproductive options open.

contexts: Title: . Content: 854: Abnormal levels may mean your kidneys and liver are not working as they should. Beta-2 microglobulin is a small protein found on most cells. It is released by cells into the blood by B cells. High levels of beta-2 microglobulin may suggest CLL is growing. Bone marrow tests Bone marrow tests are not often needed to diagnose CLL. However, they may be done to find out what’s causing low blood cell counts. Biomarker tests CLL cells have unique features that can be used to plan treatment specifically for you. These features are called biomarkers. Biomarkers are found with lab tests using either a blood or bone marrow sample: Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) can show missing parts and extra copies of genetic material called chromosomes. **Summary: Genetic Alterations Relevant in CLL Biomarker Testing**

Biomarker tests in CLL use blood or bone marrow samples to identify genetic features that guide treatment selection. Relevant tests and alterations include:

- **FISH (fluorescence in situ hybridization):** Detects missing or extra copies of chromosomes, notably the **17p deletion** biomarker.
- **DNA sequencing:** Identifies mutations in the **TP53** and **IGHV** genes, which control how unhealthy cells die.
- **Karyotype:** Reveals chromosomal defects; a **complex karyotype** is defined as 3 or more unrelated changes or deletions in more than one cell.

These biomarkers are used specifically to select treatment for CLL patients.

Refined summary:
CLL (chronic lymphocytic leukemia) is a slow-growing blood cancer that occurs in lymphocytes, specifically abnormal B cells, which grow out of control and crowd out healthy B cells. B cells are made in the bone marrow. The primary site of CLL is the blood and bone marrow, but the disease can also be found in the lymph nodes, and the lymph nodes and spleen may become swollen due to a buildup of CLL/SLL cells. CLL and SLL (small lymphocytic lymphoma) are often referred to together as CLL/SLL because the cancer cells are the same, and treatment is the same for both.

A risk assessment is a process for identifying potential problems and then considering what would happen if those problems occurred. In the case of early-stage prostate cancer, a risk assessment considers how likely the cancer is to remain within the prostate or to spread to outside the prostate. A risk assessment also considers whether the cancer may come back after treatment (recurrence) and, if so, whether it can be controlled with a different type of treatment. A complex karyotype in CLL is defined as 3 or more unrelated chromosomal changes or deletions present in more than one cell, detected via karyotype testing—a technique that produces a picture of a cell's chromosomes. Because karyotyping requires growing cells, a bone marrow or blood sample must be used; it can reveal extra, missing, rearranged, or abnormal chromosome pieces (normal human cells contain 23 pairs of chromosomes, or 46 total). This biomarker is relevant to CLL assessment and treatment planning.

The newly retrieved information does not provide additional facts about complex karyotype in CLL. Instead, it discusses unrelated topics, including risk assessment and prognosis in early-stage prostate cancer (using risk groups, life expectancy, nomograms, and molecular biomarker tests; risk groups ranging from very low to very high risk; PSA level, biopsy results), cancer staging (anatomic TNM, prognostic stage including tumor grade, clinical vs. pathologic staging before and after surgery, biomarker testing for genes or mutations such as p16 that might suggest treatment), and staging for nasopharyngeal cancer (AJCC staging system). Therefore, the CLL-specific definition above remains unchanged.

How is CLL treated? Treatment of CLL depends on your body. You may not need treatment right away. But treatment may be needed if your white blood cell count is rising rapidly, if you have low numbers of other normal blood cells (anemia, low platelets, or low neutrophils), if you have large or uncomfortable lymph nodes, or if you have symptoms listed above. Many treatment options are available and should be discussed with your doctor at your first visit and as your condition is followed. These range from pills you take every day to a combination of IV infusions and pills taken for a specific amount of time. You may live for years without needing treatment. This rare condition can lead to a more aggressive cancer called diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) or another cancer called Hodgkin lymphoma. Is there a cure for CLL? There is currently no cure for CLL, but you can get effective treatment so your blood cells will be mostly healthy ones and a full life is possible. This is a condition called minimal residual disease. We’ll describe this in a later chapter. While the goal of treatment is not to cure CLL, the goal is to prevent the disease from causing problems and from becoming life-threatening. What is SLL? Small lymphocytic lymphoma, or SLL, is the same cancer as CLL. The only difference between the two is where the abnormal cells are found. CLL is mostly found in the blood and bone marrow. SLL is mostly found in lymph nodes and the spleen. If a person has fewer than 5,000 cancerous cells in their blood, it is considered SLL. Anything more than that is considered CLL. Oral medications are an important part of CLL treatment. Treatment may not be needed right away (watch and wait), and some patients may never need treatment. When treatment is needed—for example, if the white blood cell count is rising rapidly, if other normal blood cell counts are low (anemia, low platelets, or low neutrophils), if lymph nodes are large or uncomfortable, or if symptoms occur—options “range from pills you take every day to a combination of IV infusions and pills taken for a specific amount of time.” A more intense or aggressive treatment plan may be needed if Richter transformation develops, a rare condition that can lead to diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) or Hodgkin lymphoma. Treatment of CLL and SLL is the same because the cancer cells are the same; the difference is mainly where abnormal cells are found (CLL mostly in blood and bone marrow; SLL mostly in lymph nodes and spleen, with fewer than 5,000 cancerous cells in the blood considered SLL). There is currently no cure for CLL, but effective treatment can help keep blood cells mostly healthy, prevent problems, and extend life.

results.info_summary: Throat cancer belongs to a group called **head and neck cancers**. Specifically, throat cancer starts in the **oropharynx** (the middle part of the throat near the mouth), making it a type of head and neck cancer. Most head and neck cancers, including throat cancer, are **squamous cell carcinomas (SCCs)**.

Content: 262: Human papillomavirus (HPV) is a group of viruses that infect the cells on the surface of skin or on the moist surfaces or inner linings of some organs and body cavities, such as the cervix, vagina, vulva, penis, anus, mouth, and throat. HPV infection usually clears on its own. However, HPV infections can cause abnormal tissue growth (warts) and sometimes cancer. Cancer caused by HPV is called HPV-related cancer. HPV is the main cause of squamous cell carcinomas of the throat (oropharynx), particularly cancers of the tonsils and base of the tongue. HPV type 16 is responsible for 9 out of 10 throat cancers. The remaining cancers are caused by HPV18, 33, and HPV-positive throat cancer is a distinct disease with specific tumor features that can be targeted during treatment. p16 HPV16 is detected using a test to look for p is a protein that slows cell division. It is produced by a gene located on chromosome 9 (shown as 9p3). Human cells have 23 pairs of chromosomes or 46 chromosomes in total. Testing to look for the presence (expression) of p16 is called biomarker testing.

It primarily covers general guidance on patient advocacy, medical and family history, clinical trials, and questions to ask care teams—topics applicable to cancer care broadly but not specific to imaging modalities for throat cancer.

The existing summary remains accurate and complete for answering the question. Minor refinements for conciseness and clarity:

---

Imaging tests take pictures of the inside of the body to show the primary tumor and detect cancer elsewhere. Specific imaging studies include CT (computed tomography/CAT) scans, which use x-rays. Scoping procedures (endoscopy) involve inserting a thin, tube-shaped tool with a light and camera lens through the mouth or nose to examine the oropharynx, determine tumor size and spread, take pictures, and guide biopsy. Fiberoptic nasopharyngolaryngoscopy is used to examine the larynx and nearby structures. A radiologist interprets imaging tests and sends a report to the health care provider. Results from imaging studies and biopsy are used to determine the treatment plan and cancer staging (TNM scores).

Mouth cancer starts in the squamous cells that form the surface lining of the mouth. Normally, these are thin, flat cells and are similar to the top layer of skin and surface lining some other parts of the body such as the lungs and esophagus. Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is the most common type of mouth cancer and is the focus of this book. Mouth cancer can develop in the parts that make up the mouth such as: Lips (mucosal lip) Gums (gingiva) Lining inside the cheeks and lips (buccal mucosa) Front two-thirds of the tongue Roof of the mouth (hard palate) Bony, raised areas that hold the teeth sockets (alveolar ridge) h Floor of the mouth (under the tongue) Small area of the gum behind the wisdom teeth (retromolar trigone) Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma of the vermilion lip is not included in this book. The vermillion lip is the area where the skin and the lip meet on the outside of the mouth. The AJCC TNM staging system components include:

- **T (Tumor)**: Describes the extent (size) of the tumor and whether it has grown into nearby areas.
- **N (Node)**: Describes the spread to nearby lymph nodes, including how many and where.
- **M (Metastasis)**: Describes the spread to distant sites/organs such as the lungs or liver.

Additional components in the AJCC staging system:
- **G (Grade)**: How much the cancer cells look like normal cells.
- **Biomarker testing**: Whether the cancer has genes, proteins (such as p16), or mutations that might suggest treatment.

For throat cancer: Tis = carcinoma in situ, with cancerous cells only in the squamous cell layer. T1 = tumor ≤2 cm with DOI ≤5 mm. T2 = tumor ≤2 cm with DOI >5 mm, or tumor 2–4 cm with DOI ≤5 mm. T3 = tumor 2–4 cm with DOI >5 mm, or tumor >4 cm with DOI ≤5 mm. T4a = moderately advanced local disease: tumor >4 cm with DOI >5 mm, or tumor invading nearby structures only, such as through the cortical bone of the mandible.

results.info_summary: Pathologic stage (p), also called surgical stage, is determined by examining tissue removed during surgery—specifically the tumor and nearby lymph nodes. It is based on information gained after surgery to remove all or part of the tumor and nearby lymph nodes, giving a more accurate picture of how far the cancer has spread, and is used to determine treatment options after surgery. Pathologic staging is more specific and accurate than clinical staging (which is based on physical exam, biopsy, and imaging before treatment) regarding tumor size and lymph node status. Staging uses the TNM system (T = tumor size/extent, N = spread to nearby lymph nodes, M = metastasis to distant body parts), with higher numbers indicating larger tumor or more spread; scores are combined to assign a stage. If cancer drug therapy is given before surgery, a "y" is added (e.g., ypT). Testing for p16 (HPV) is also an important part of staging throat cancer.

A risk assessment also considers whether the cancer may come back after treatment (recurrence) and, if so, whether it can be controlled with a different type of treatment. results.info_summary:
The oropharynx (often referred to as the throat) includes the following main anatomical sites related to throat cancer:

- **Soft palate** – the back of the roof of the mouth
- **Tonsils**
- **Side and back walls of the throat**
- **Base (back) of the tongue**, found in the throat

Throat cancer most commonly starts in the oropharynx, with squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) being the most common type. The oropharynx is one of three parts of the pharynx, along with the nasopharynx and hypopharynx. Tumors in this area can grow into nearby structures such as the larynx (voice box).

Scoping procedures used as diagnostic methods for throat cancer include:

- **Fiberoptic nasopharyngolaryngoscopy** – examines the larynx and nearby structures.
- **Nasolaryngoscopy** – a small flexible scope passed through the nose into the throat; typically takes less than 1 minute.

- **Esophagoscopy** – a device guided down the throat into the esophagus under anesthesia to examine for abnormal growths.
- **Bronchoscopy** – a device inserted through the nose or mouth under anesthesia to examine the trachea and bronchi; may detect cancer or perform treatment procedures.
- **Panendoscopy** – different endoscopes passed down the mouth or nose to perform laryngoscopy, pharyngoscopy, esophagoscopy, or bronchoscopy; thoroughly examines the mouth, oropharynx, larynx, esophagus, trachea, and bronchi. The main prognostic factors for squamous cell carcinoma of the throat (oropharynx) are assessed primarily through cancer staging, which predicts prognosis and guides treatment decisions. The AJCC TNM system evaluates:

- **Tumor extent (T):** size of the cancer and whether it has grown into nearby areas
- **Lymph node spread (N):** whether the cancer has spread to nearby lymph nodes, and if so, how many and where
- **Metastasis (M):** spread to distant organs such as the lungs, bones, or liver

Additional prognostic factors include:

- **Grade of the cancer (G):** how much the cancer cells look like normal cells; the more different they look, the higher the grade and the faster the cancer is expected to grow and spread (low grade = slow growing; high grade = fast growing)
- **p16 (HPV) status:** p16 is a protein that slows cell division, produced by a gene on chromosome 9 (9p3). For throat cancer, biopsy samples are routinely tested for p16 as a surrogate marker for HPV infection (p16 testing differs from direct HPV testing). results.info_summary: Cutaneous B-cell lymphoma (CBCL) is a rare type of non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) that develops from abnormal B lymphocytes—white blood cells that produce antibodies to fight infection—and starts in the skin. It is not a type of skin cancer. CBCL commonly appears as nodules or lumps under the skin that may look like small pimples called papules; these skin lesions are caused by the abnormal lymphocytes. Main types include primary cutaneous marginal zone lymphoma (PCMZL, also called PCMZ lymphoproliferative disorder), primary cutaneous follicle center lymphoma (PCFCL), and primary cutaneous diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, leg type (PC-DLBCL, leg type). Most primary cutaneous B-cell lymphomas (PCBCLs) are indolent or slow-growing. Diagnosis involves tests such as a skin exam, general health tests, blood tests, imaging tests, biopsy, and immunophenotyping, as well as testing for CBCL biomarkers and genetic changes and TNM scores; accurate testing is needed to diagnose and treat lymphomas of the skin. **Diagnostic methods for CBCL (cutaneous B-cell lymphoma):**

Testing for CBCL includes:

- **General health tests** and a **skin exam**
- **Blood tests**
- **Imaging tests**
- **Biopsy** of the skin lesion
- **Immunophenotyping**
- **Biomarker and genetic testing** for CBCL
- **TNM scores** (staging)
- **Fertility testing** (for all genders)

Results from blood and tissue tests, imaging studies, and biopsy determine the treatment plan. Accurate testing is needed to diagnose and treat lymphomas of the skin.

CBCL is a primary cutaneous lymphoma (PCL)—a non-Hodgkin lymphoma found in the skin, not skin cancer—that develops from abnormal B cells and often appears as nodules or papules under the skin. Main types include PCMZL, PCFCL, and PC-DLBCL (leg type); most PCBCLs are indolent or slow-growing.

results.info_summary:
Cutaneous B-cell lymphoma (CBCL) is a type of primary cutaneous lymphoma (PCL)—a rare non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) of the skin, not a skin cancer—that develops from abnormal B cells, a type of lymphocyte (white blood cell) that produces antibodies to fight infection. CBCL often appears as nodules under the skin that may look like small pimples called papules. Its main subtypes include:

- Primary cutaneous marginal zone lymphoma (PCMZL), also called PCMZ lymphoproliferative disorder
- Primary cutaneous follicle center lymphoma (PCFCL)
- Primary cutaneous diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, leg type (PC-DLBCL, leg type)

Most primary cutaneous B-cell lymphomas (PCBCLs) are indolent or slow-growing.

**Summary:**

Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL) is a type of **primary cutaneous lymphoma (PCL)**, which is a **non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL)** found in the skin. It develops from **abnormal T cells** (a type of white blood cell/lymphocyte). PCL is not skin cancer. There are 2 types of PCL: CTCL and cutaneous B-cell lymphoma (CBCL). Basal cell skin cancer, also known as basal cell carcinoma (BCC), is the most common type of skin cancer. About 3 million cases of basal cell skin cancer are diagnosed every year in the United States. The good news is it can be cured in most cases. Treatment usually involves surgery to remove the cancer. Keep reading to find out more. What is basal cell skin cancer? Basal cell skin cancer is the most common of all skin cancer types. If caught early, it is easily treatable and curable. This is because it rarely metastasizes (spreads). Skin cancers often occur in the top layer of the skin (epidermis) and less commonly in the middle layer of the skin (dermis). The epidermis is made up of basal cells and other cells. Basal cell skin cancer occurs when some basal cells become abnormal and grow out of control. This cancer usually develops in areas exposed to the sun, including the face, head, neck, arms, legs, and trunk. But it can occur anywhere on the body.
