Your doctor or other health care provider will discuss the results with you. Be sure to ask any questions you have. Is blue light cystoscopy better? Cystoscopy commonly uses a white light to see inside the bladder. Some newer cystoscopes now use a blue light. When combined with a special dye injected into the bladder, blue light cystoscopy can identify tumors a little more distinctly than white light. Another technology called narrow-band imaging also helps detect tumors more clearly during cystoscopy but doesn’t require a dye. While both blue light cystoscopy and narrow-band imaging may potentially detect tumors better than standard white light, they’re relatively new and still in the “testing phase.” More research will show whether they can replace or be used with white light as the standard detection method. Title: . Content: 509: specialist before starting treatment. Imaging tests Imaging tests take pictures of the inside of your body. A radiologist, an expert in interpreting imaging tests, will write a report and send this report to your doctor. The doctor will discuss the results with you. Before the pictures are taken, the tracer will be injected into your vein. It can take a few hours for the tracer to enter your bones. However, the test is quick and painless. A special camera will take pictures of the tracer in your bones as it moves over your body. Areas of bone damage take up more radiotracer than healthy bone and show up as bright spots on the pictures. Inherited cancer risk Sometimes, mutations in genes inherited from your parents can increase the risk for different cancers. You can pass these genes on to your children. Other family members might also carry these mutations. If you have a family history of cancer or other features, your doctor might suggest genetic testing to find out if you have an inherited cancer risk. The goal of this type of genetic testing is to look for germline (inherited) mutations that occur in every cell in your body. Title: . Content: 649: implants. Biopsy A biopsy removes a sample of tissue or fluid. Samples removed during a biopsy or surgery will be sent to a pathologist, an expert in examining cells using a microscope (called cytology) to confirm the presence of cancer. The pathologist will determine the cancer subtype called tumor histology. A fine-needle aspiration (FNA), fine-needle biopsy (FNB), and core needle biopsy (CNB) use needles of different sizes to remove a sample of tumor or lymph node. An ultrasound or CT scan might be used to guide a lymph node biopsy. Biopsy of metastasis Metastasis is the spread of cancer to an area of the body such as lymph nodes or lung. A biopsy of the metastasis may be needed to confirm the presence of cancer. If there is more than one metastasis, each site may be biopsied. The type of biopsy used depends on the location of the suspected metastases and other factors. Biomarker testing Biomarker tumor testing includes tests of genes or their products (proteins). It identifies the presence or absence of mutations and certain proteins that might suggest treatment. This information is used to choose the best treatment for you. It is sometimes called molecular testing or tumor profiling, tumor sequencing, gene expression

Complete blood count A complete blood count (CBC) measures the levels of red blood cells (RBCs), white blood cells (WBCs), and platelets (PLTs) in your blood. Red blood cells carry oxygen throughout your body, white blood cells fight infection, and platelets control bleeding. Comprehensive metabolic panel A comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP) measures 14 different substances in your blood. It is usually done on the plasma part of your blood. A CMP provides important information about how well your kidneys and liver are working, among other things. Liver function tests Liver function tests (LFTs) look at the health of your liver by measuring chemicals that are made or processed by the liver. Levels that are too high or low signal that the liver is not working well or that cancer has spread to the liver. Supportive care refers to a range of care and resources often needed by patients with metastatic cancer. Hospice care, access to pain specialists, and emotional and spiritual support are all components of supportive care. Two common tests that look for prostate cancer are the prostate-specific antigen (PSA) test and digital rectal exam. PSA test This is a blood test that measures the amount of PSA in your bloodstream. PSA is a protein made inside the prostate gland. Its job is to help semen transport sperm. All prostate cells, both normal cells and cancer cells, make PSA. If there’s something wrong with the prostate— like prostate cancer—the prostate may make more PSA. While most PSA goes into semen, a little bit ends up in the bloodstream, too. An unusually high amount of PSA in the blood may be a sign of prostate cancer. Likewise, an increase in PSA after treatment may indicate that the treatment is losing effectiveness. However, age and other factors—such as an enlarged prostate or a urinary tract infection— can also cause high levels of PSA. This means that a PSA test by itself can’t provide a diagnosis of prostate cancer. That’s why a PSA test is often paired with imaging or a digital rectal exam, or both, to decide whether you need a biopsy. PSA level (also called total PSA) is measured in nanograms of PSA per milliliter (ng/mL) of blood

results.info_summary:
Imaging methods for detecting prostate cancer and assessing its extent include MRI, CT, PET, ultrasound, bone scan, or a combination of these. 

- **MRI**: Provides detailed views of cancer within the prostate and can show spread to nearby lymph nodes or pelvic bones. May be used before biopsy or after diagnosis.
- **CT**: Used for imaging, often combined with PET (PET/CT).
- **PET**: Used after diagnosis to determine the extent of cancer or detect metastasis; can also show treatment effectiveness. Often combined with CT or MRI (PET/CT or PET/MRI).
- **PSMA/PET**: A special PET imaging targeting prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA); especially useful for detecting spread to nearby lymph nodes or distant metastasis and monitoring recurrence.
- **Bone scan**: Detects whether cancer has spread to bones; used if bone pain, high risk of bone metastasis, or certain test changes. May also monitor treatment.
- **Ultrasound**: Commonly used as transrectal ultrasound (TRUS) to guide biopsy.

Imaging may not be needed for early-stage prostate cancer if risk of metastasis is low based on PSA, digital rectal exam, and biopsy results.

contexts: Title: . Content: 402: The biggest risk factor for prostate cancer is age. Prostate cancer is diagnosed most often in those aged 65 years and above. Your chances of getting prostate cancer increase as you become older. Family history Your family health history is information about the diseases and health conditions in your family. A family history reflects a pattern of certain diseases among family members. Having a close family member with prostate cancer (a sibling or parent) increases the chance of getting it yourself. Those with a family history of certain other cancers (breast, ovarian, colon, pancreatic, and other cancers) may also be at a higher risk for prostate cancer. Genetic factors When cancer “runs in the family,” genetic testing can be done to find specific genetic changes (mutations) known to be linked with prostate cancer or other cancers. For instance, having an inherited genetic change in the BRCA2 gene increases the risk of getting prostate cancer. But genetic abnormalities that aren’t inherited can occur, too. Race In the United States, Black males are more likely than white males to develop prostate cancer. Prostate cancer in Black males is also more likely to occur at an earlier age and be more aggressive and more advanced when diagnosed. Black males are also twice as likely to die from prostate cancer compared with white males.

Two common tests that look for prostate cancer are the prostate-specific antigen (PSA) test and digital rectal exam. PSA test This is a blood test that measures the amount of PSA in your bloodstream. PSA is a protein made inside the prostate gland. Its job is to help semen transport sperm. All prostate cells, both normal cells and cancer cells, make PSA. If there’s something wrong with the prostate— like prostate cancer—the prostate may make more PSA. While most PSA goes into semen, a little bit ends up in the bloodstream, too. An unusually high amount of PSA in the blood may be a sign of prostate cancer. Likewise, an increase in PSA after treatment may indicate that the treatment is losing effectiveness. However, age and other factors—such as an enlarged prostate or a urinary tract infection— can also cause high levels of PSA. This means that a PSA test by itself can’t provide a diagnosis of prostate cancer. That’s why a PSA test is often paired with imaging or a digital rectal exam, or both, to decide whether you need a biopsy. results.info_summary:
The grading systems used to estimate prostate cancer aggressiveness are the **Gleason score** and the **Grade Group** system.

- **Gleason score**: Based on Gleason patterns (ranging from 1 to 5, though patterns 1 and 2 are no longer used). The two most common patterns in the biopsy sample are combined by adding their numbers. Scores range from 6 to 10: 6 is lowest, 7 is intermediate-grade, and 8–10 is high-grade. A higher score means the cancer is more likely to grow and spread quickly.

- **Grade Group**: A simpler interpretation of the Gleason score, with five groups numbered 1 to 5. Higher Grade Group = more aggressive cancer. Gleason 6 = Grade Group 1 (lowest); Gleason 9 or 10 = Grade Group 5 (highest). Grade Groups 2 and 3 both have a Gleason score of 7, but Grade Group 3 is more serious because its first number is higher. Grade Group 1 = low risk; Grade Groups 2 and 3 = intermediate risk; Grade Groups 4 and 5 = high and very high risk.

They are determined by combining clinical characteristics—PSA level, Grade Group, tumor stage, and biopsy results—and classify disease into five categories from very low risk to very high risk. results.info_summary: The main treatment options for prostate cancer include surgery, radiation therapy, hormone therapy, chemotherapy, immunotherapy, targeted therapy, radiopharmaceuticals, and other therapies. For early-stage prostate cancer, active surveillance is an option—regular testing without immediate treatment unless the cancer grows or changes. For advanced-stage prostate cancer (which has spread to other areas of the pelvis or body and is usually a life-long disease), treatments include hormone therapy, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, immunotherapy, targeted therapy, radiopharmaceuticals, surgery, and other therapies. Hormone therapy (androgen deprivation therapy, or ADT) is often combined with one or more other therapies, as combining therapies can be more effective than using either alone. It also estimates how aggressive your prostate cancer is—how quickly it might grow and whether it will spread. Gleason patterns After studying your biopsy sample under a microscope, the pathologist will assign a number based on the “pattern” of cancer cells (Gleason pattern) in the sample. A cancer cell pattern that looks more like normal and healthy cells is given a lower number. A cell pattern that looks more abnormal is assigned a higher number. Gleason patterns range from 1 to However, patterns 1 and 2 are so rarely found that they are no longer used. results.info_summary:
Diagnostic methods for localized prostate cancer include:

- **Digital rectal exam (DRE):** Simplest way to check the size and texture of the prostate.
- **PSA blood test:** An unusually high amount of PSA in the bloodstream may be a sign of prostate cancer.
- **Biopsy:** The only way to confirm (diagnose) prostate cancer; removes samples of cells or tissue to test for cancer. Usually performed by a urologist, often guided by transrectal ultrasound (TRUS).
- **Imaging tests:** Used to see if cancer has spread beyond the prostate and to help plan treatment. Methods include MRI, CT, PET, PSMA/PET, ultrasound, bone scan, or a combination. Imaging can occur before, during, or after a biopsy.
- **Molecular biomarker testing:** Helps assess whether cancer is lower risk or higher risk.

Note: PSMA/PET is especially useful for detecting spread to lymph nodes or distant metastasis and for monitoring recurrence, so someone with early-stage prostate cancer may not need it at initial diagnosis. Bone scans detect spread to bones.

Genetic alterations associated with metastatic prostate cancer include:

- **Germline (hereditary) mutations**: inherited mutations present in every cell, tested via blood, urine, or saliva. Germline testing is recommended for those with metastatic prostate cancer, regardless of family history.
- **Somatic (acquired) mutations**: mutations that occur spontaneously and are found only in the tumor cells.
- **Specific genes implicated**: BRCA1, BRCA2, ATM, CHEK2, and others.

Germline testing is specifically recommended for individuals with high-risk, very-high-risk, regional, or **metastatic prostate cancer**, regardless of family history. Molecular biomarker testing (also called genomic testing, tumor profiling, or molecular tumor testing) can be considered for localized, regional, or metastatic prostate cancer to assess risk.

results.info_summary:
**Summary: Common Urinary Symptoms of Prostate Cancer**

Prostate cancer often grows slowly and typically shows no symptoms in its early stages—most patients diagnosed with early prostate cancer have no symptoms. Symptoms are more common with advanced prostate cancer. Urinary (and related) symptoms, if they occur, may include:

- Blood in the urine or semen
- Burning or pain while urinating
- Urinating frequently, especially at night
- Weak or intermittent urine stream
- Trouble urinating or straining to urinate
- Trouble holding in urine
- Feeling like the bladder hasn't fully emptied

**Important note:** Prostate cancer shares many symptoms with benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), also called enlarged prostate, which is much more common than prostate cancer. An enlarged prostate can push against the bladder and compress the urethra, slowing urine flow and causing a feeling of incomplete bladder emptying. It is difficult to distinguish the two conditions based on symptoms alone, so patients with these symptoms should tell their health care providers, as special testing may be needed.

Two common tests that look for prostate cancer are the prostate-specific antigen (PSA) test and digital rectal exam. PSA test This is a blood test that measures the amount of PSA in your bloodstream. PSA is a protein made inside the prostate gland. Its job is to help semen transport sperm. All prostate cells, both normal cells and cancer cells, make PSA. If there’s something wrong with the prostate— like prostate cancer—the prostate may make more PSA. While most PSA goes into semen, a little bit ends up in the bloodstream, too. An unusually high amount of PSA in the blood may be a sign of prostate cancer. Likewise, an increase in PSA after treatment may indicate that the treatment is losing effectiveness. However, age and other factors—such as an enlarged prostate or a urinary tract infection— can also cause high levels of PSA. This means that a PSA test by itself can’t provide a diagnosis of prostate cancer. A risk assessment is a process for identifying potential problems and then considering what would happen if those problems occurred. In the case of early-stage prostate cancer, a risk assessment considers how likely the cancer is to remain within the prostate or to spread to outside the prostate. A risk assessment also considers whether the cancer may come back after treatment (recurrence) and, if so, whether it can be controlled with a different type of treatment. To assess risk, your care providers use these tools: risk groups, life expectancy, nomograms, and molecular biomarker tests. results.info_summary: The risk group classification guides prognosis and treatment decisions. For early-stage prostate cancer, care teams classify disease into one of five risk groups (from very low to very high risk) based on clinical characteristics including PSA level, biopsy results, Grade Group, and tumor stage. The risk group is the basis for prognosis—which predicts the likely course and outcome of the disease—and prognosis guides treatment options. Patients with lower risk generally receive minimal or no treatment, while higher risk patients usually receive more aggressive treatment. Grade Groups also inform risk: Grade Group 1 indicates low risk; Grade Groups 2 and 3 correspond to intermediate risk; Grade Groups 4 and 5 predict high and very high risk.

Treatments for advanced-stage prostate cancer include hormone therapy as well as non-hormone therapies like chemotherapy, immunotherapy, targeted therapy, and radiation therapy. Often, hormone therapy is combined with one or more other therapies. Combining therapies can be more effective than using either therapy alone. key word in ADT is “deprivation”—this therapy “deprives” (starves) the cancer of its main fuel: androgens. This can shrink the tumor or slow tumor growth for a while. You might hear the term “castration” used when describing prostate cancer or its treatment. This term describes a drastic reduction of testosterone. Castration can be done with hormone-lowering medication or by surgical removal of one or both testicles (orchiectomy). Though orchiectomy is a surgical procedure, it’s still considered hormone therapy because it removes the primary source of testosterone: the testicles. While drug hormone therapy can be reversed when the medication is stopped, orchiectomy is permanent and can’t be reversed. Hormone therapies for prostate cancer include luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone (LHRH) agonists and LHRH antagonists, both of which cause the testicles to stop making testosterone. You may have heard of leuprolide (Lupron), a commonly used LHRH agonist or degarelix (Firmagon), a commonly used LHRH antagonist. Most LHRH agonists and LHRH antagonists are injections. These may be given monthly, or 2, 3, or 4 times a year. The exception is relugolix (Orgovyx), an LHRH antagonist that comes as a tablet taken once a day. results.info_summary:
The main hormonal therapy for advanced prostate cancer is **androgen deprivation therapy (ADT)**, which lowers testosterone to very low levels by stopping its production or blocking cancer cells from using it. ADT includes:

- **LHRH agonists** (e.g., goserelin, leuprolide/Lupron, triptorelin)
- **LHRH antagonists** (e.g., degarelix/Firmagon, relugolix/Orgovyx)
- **Anti-androgens** (e.g., nilutamide, flutamide, bicalutamide)
- **Surgical castration** (orchiectomy)

Hormone therapy has been the main treatment for advanced prostate cancer for several decades and is often combined with other therapies.

results.info_summary: Blood tests are used to detect signs of hormone secretion by adrenal tumors. Biochemical tests measure substances in the blood to identify hormone secretion, which helps diagnose functional adrenal tumors. These tumors can produce hormones such as aldosterone, which causes aldosteronoma, and cortisol, which causes Cushing syndrome. A comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP)—which measures 14 substances, including blood sugar, calcium, and electrolytes—can provide information about kidney and liver function and may identify hypercalcemia. Other blood tests, such as alkaline phosphatase (ALP), lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), complete blood count (CBC), liver function tests (LFTs), B12 and folic acid, iron, blood clotting tests, creatinine, and blood urea nitrogen (BUN), assess organ function and cancer spread. Imaging tests such as FDG-PET/CT and SSTR-PET/CT can also help locate and characterize adrenal tumors.

results.info_summary: Functional adrenal tumors produce hormones, which can cause hormone-related symptoms and conditions. They are usually benign but some can become cancerous and spread. Benign functional tumors can still produce hormones and may be found during tests for hormone-related symptoms. Adrenocortical carcinoma can be functioning or nonfunctioning; if functioning, it may produce more than one hormone.

Adrenocortical carcinoma (ACC) symptoms fall into two categories:

**Hormone-related symptoms** (affecting about half of patients, caused by hormones produced by the tumor):
- Weight gain
- Muscle weakness
- Pink or purple stretch marks on the skin
- Hormonal changes such as excess facial hair, hair loss on the head, irregular periods, enlarged breast tissue, and shrinking testicles

- Nausea
- Vomiting
- Abdominal bloating
- Back pain
- Fever
- Loss of appetite
- Loss of weight without trying

**Summary:**

Among adrenal tumors, **neuroblastoma** is the type specifically noted to metastasize (spread) to other parts of the body, **including the bones**. It is a rare, cancerous adrenal tumor affecting children ages 5 and under, most often found in infants.

Other adrenal tumors mentioned:
- **Benign adrenal tumors** (e.g., adenomas) do not metastasize.
- **Adrenocortical carcinoma (ACC)** is the most common adrenal gland cancer but very rare (1–2 per million); it can be functioning or nonfunctioning.
- **Pheochromocytoma** begins in the adrenal medulla; most are benign but can be cancerous.

Note: General bone cancer content clarifies that cancers spreading to bone from elsewhere are called metastatic (secondary) bone malignancies, but the specific adrenal tumor identified as spreading to bones is **neuroblastoma**.

Based on the provided information, the imaging methods included in the diagnosis of adrenocortical carcinoma (ACC) are:

- **CT scan** – used to detect adrenal tumors, often incidentally.
- **MRI scan** – also used to detect adrenal tumors.

Blood tests and biochemical tests are also mentioned but are not imaging methods.

results.info_summary:
**Role of biopsy in adrenal tumor diagnosis:**

- Biopsy is one of several testing methods used to diagnose adrenal tumors, alongside general health tests, imaging tests (CT or MRI), blood tests, and genetic tests. Testing is used both to diagnose and to plan treatment.
- Adrenal tumors often cause no symptoms and are found incidentally through imaging done for another reason. Most adrenal tumors are benign; adrenal cancer (adrenocortical carcinoma, ACC) is rare (about 1–2 per 1 million people; roughly 300–500 diagnoses per year in the U.S.).
- A biopsy removes a sample of tissue or fluid, which a pathologist examines under a microscope (cytology) to confirm cancer and determine the cancer subtype (tumor histology).
- Needle biopsy types include fine-needle aspiration (FNA), fine-needle biopsy (FNB), and core needle biopsy (CNB), using needles of different sizes to sample tumor or lymph node. Ultrasound or CT may guide the biopsy.
- If cancer has spread (metastasized) to sites such as lymph nodes or lung, biopsy of the metastasis may be needed to confirm cancer; if there are multiple metastases, each site may be biopsied

analysis.current_understanding: Biopsy techniques and procedures for adrenal tumors include various needle biopsy methods such as fine-needle aspiration (FNA), fine-needle biopsy (FNB), and core needle biopsy (CNB), which use needles of different sizes to remove samples from the tumor or lymph nodes. Imaging guidance like ultrasound or CT may be used during the procedure. The biopsy sample is sent to a pathologist for microscopic examination (cytology) to confirm cancer presence and determine the cancer subtype (tumor histology). If metastasis is suspected, biopsies of metastatic sites (e.g., lymph nodes, lung) may be performed, with the technique depending on the location and other factors. However, this information only partially addresses the broader question of biopsy's role in adrenal tumor diagnosis, and it is specific to the current dependency on techniques and procedures while other dependencies like indications, limitations, and guidelines are not yet covered.

- Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome
- Carney complex

Some of these conditions can also increase risk for kidney tumors.

Metastasis Unlike normal cells, cancer cells can spread and form tumors in other parts of the body called metastases. In this process, cancer cells break away from the first (primary) tumor and travel through blood or lymph vessels to distant sites. Once in other sites, cancer cells may form secondary tumors. Since cancer cells can spread through the blood, it is still possible to develop metastases even when the axillary lymph nodes are negative for cancer. Cancer that has spread to a nearby body part such as the axillary lymph nodes is called a local metastasis. It might be referred to as locoregional disease or locally advanced. Cancer that has spread to a body part far from the primary tumor is called a distant metastasis. Breast cancer can metastasize almost anywhere but most commonly spreads to the bone (including spine), lungs, liver, brain, or distant lymph nodes. Breast cancer that has metastasized to other parts of the body is still called breast cancer. results.info_summary:
Metastatic breast cancer (MBC) is breast cancer that has spread (metastasized) to distant parts of the body beyond the breast and nearby lymph nodes. Key details:

- **Definition**: MBC refers to cancer that has spread to distant sites (distant metastasis), as opposed to local/regional spread to nearby lymph nodes.
- **Staging**: In staging, M1 indicates distant metastasis is found — this is MBC. M0 means no evidence of distant metastasis.
- **Spread mechanism**: Cancer cells break away from the primary tumor and travel through blood or lymph vessels to distant sites, where they may form secondary tumors.

results.info_summary: Key biomarkers for breast cancer include HER2 status and hormone receptor status (estrogen and progesterone receptors), which are tested from biopsy samples to guide treatment. Biomarker testing also examines specific DNA mutations/alterations, protein levels, and molecular features such as PIK3CA mutations (targetable with specific therapies) and tumor mutational burden-high (TMB-H, defined as 10 or more mutations per million base pairs), which can predict response to immune checkpoint inhibitors targeting PD-1/PD-L1. results.info_summary:
**Summary: Biomarkers guiding immunotherapy use in breast cancer**

Biomarker testing of tumor samples can identify molecular features used to select the best treatment, including immunotherapy. Relevant biomarkers for guiding immunotherapy use include:

- **PD-L1 (programmed death-ligand 1):** PD-L1–positive status is a preferred biomarker for treatment with pembrolizumab (Keytruda), an immune checkpoint inhibitor.
- **TMB-H (tumor mutational burden-high):** Defined as 10 or more mutations per million base pairs of tumor DNA. TMB-H can predict response to immune checkpoint inhibitors targeting PD-1 and PD-L1.
- **MSI-H/dMMR (microsatellite instability-high/deficient mismatch repair):** Also a preferred biomarker for pembrolizumab.

Pembrolizumab (Keytruda) is an example of immunotherapy (immune checkpoint inhibitor) that may be given alone or with other treatments; it targets the "off switches" PD-1 and CTLA-4 to re-activate the immune system against tumor cells.

Diagnostic methods for breast cancer include:

- **Biopsy with pathology review**, required to confirm cancer and perform cancer cell tests.
- **Tumor status testing on the biopsy sample**: estrogen receptor (ER) and progesterone receptor (PR) hormone receptor (HR) status, HER2 status, and biomarker testing.
- **Genetic counseling and genetic cancer risk testing** if at risk for hereditary breast cancer.
- **Additional assessments**: fertility, birth control, and sexual health concerns; distress screening; performance status.

The breast The breast is an organ and a gland found on the chest. The breast is made of milk ducts, fat, nerves, lymph and blood vessels, ligaments, and other connective tissue. Behind the breast is the pectoral (chest) muscle and ribs. Muscle and ligaments help hold the breast in place. Breast tissue contains glands that can make milk. These milk glands are called lobules. Lobules look like tiny clusters of grapes. Small tubes called ducts connect the lobules to the nipple. The ring of darker breast skin is called the areola. The raised tip within the areola is called the nipple. The nipple-areola complex (NAC) is a term that refers to both parts. Lymph node involvement in breast cancer is assessed primarily through **sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB or SNB)**. The sentinel lymph node (SLN) is the first lymph node(s) to which cancer cells are most likely to spread from the primary tumor; there can be more than one SLN. During surgery (e.g., mastectomy or lumpectomy), a radioactive material and other dyes are injected into the area of the breast tumor; the dye travels through breast lymphatics to the lymph nodes, helping the surgeon identify the sentinel nodes. results.info_summary:
**Summary: Therapy for Hormone Receptor-Positive Breast Cancer**

Hormone receptor-positive (HR+) breast cancer is treated with **endocrine therapy** (sometimes called hormone therapy), which blocks estrogen and/or progesterone receptor signaling. This is distinct from hormone replacement therapy used for menopause.

Key details:
- HR+ breast cancer is defined by the presence of estrogen and/or progesterone hormone receptors found via IHC testing (estrogen receptors in at least 1 out of 100 cancer cells).
- Most breast cancers are hormone receptor-positive.
- Endocrine therapy stops the body from making hormones or blocks what hormones do, which can slow tumor growth or shrink the tumor for a period of time.
- Hormones that may be targeted include estrogen, progesterone, LHRH (GnRH), and androgen.
- One type of surgical endocrine therapy is bilateral oophorectomy.

Note: For ER-low–positive invasive breast cancer (receptors in only 1 to 10 out of 100 cells), endocrine therapy might not be recommended. Hormone receptor-negative (HR-) cancers are not treated with endocrine therapy.

results.info_summary: HER2-targeted therapy is the drug therapy used to treat HER2-positive breast cancer. It is most often given with chemotherapy, though it may also be used alone or combined with endocrine therapy. HER2-targeted therapies include three types: HER2 antibodies (which prevent growth signals from outside the cell and boost immune cell attack), HER2 inhibitors (which stop growth signals from within the cell), and HER2 antibody-drug conjugates (which deliver cell-specific chemotherapy). Examples include pertuzumab (Perjeta), trastuzumab (Herceptin) and its biosimilars (Kanjinti, Ogivri, Herzuma, Ontruzant, Trazimera), ado-trastuzumab emtansine (T-DM1/Kadcyla), fam-trastuzumab deruxtecan-nxki (Enhertu), lapatinib (Tykerb), margetuximab-cmkb (Margenza), neratinib (Nerlynx), tucatinib (Tukysa), and Phesgo (a substitute for trastuzumab combined with pertuzumab). Heart function (left ventricular ejection fraction) is monitored before and during trastuzumab treatment.

In inflammatory breast cancer (IBC), cancer cells block lymph vessels in the skin of the breast, causing the breast to look red and swollen and feel warm to the touch. Before starting breast cancer treatment, discuss fertility and reproductive health with your care team. Key points:

- **Fertility impact**: Chemotherapy and other treatments can temporarily or permanently impair fertility. Loss of fertility depends on age at diagnosis, treatment type(s), dose, and length.
- **Fertility specialist referral**: Those who want children in the future should be referred to a fertility specialist to discuss options **before starting treatment**. Fertility preservation keeps options open, even if unsure about future children. Fertility is a relevant topic for all genders.
- **Pregnancy planning**: Talk to your care team if you are planning a pregnancy. Consult your doctor for the best time to plan a pregnancy after treatment.
- **Pregnancy testing**: Those who can become pregnant will have a pregnancy test before starting treatment. Cancer treatment can harm a developing baby if you are or become pregnant during treatment.
- **If pregnant or breastfeeding**: Certain treatments must be avoided.
- **Preventing pregnancy during treatment**: Birth control is recommended during and after treatment. Non-hormonal methods (barrier methods, IUDs) are preferred after a breast cancer diagnosis; hormonal birth control may or may not be recommended. results.info_summary:
Follow-up for breast cancer includes:

- **Regular follow-up care visits** to monitor health after treatment, with frequency and duration determined by the care team (how often and for how many years should be discussed).
- **Tests to monitor health**, including blood tests and imaging tests, with a clear understanding of who is responsible for scheduling them.
- **Monitoring for cancer recurrence** or the development of another type of cancer.
- **Screening for late effects** caused by treatment and knowing how these will be screened.
- **Discussion of survivorship issues**, including what happens after treatment.
- **Support resources**, such as survivor support groups and other recommended resources.
- **Financial guidance** if there is trouble paying for follow-up visits and tests.
- **Help transitioning care** if the patient moves after treatment and needs to change doctors (including finding a new doctor).
- **Keeping copies of medical records**, including blood tests, imaging results, and pathology reports.
- **Communication with the care team**, including writing down questions, taking notes, and asking questions about test results and follow-up plans.

Metastasis Unlike normal cells, cancer cells can spread and form tumors in other parts of the body called metastases. In this process, cancer cells break away from the first (primary) tumor and travel through blood or lymph vessels to distant sites. Once in other sites, cancer cells may form secondary tumors. Since cancer cells can spread through the blood, it is still possible to develop metastases even when the axillary lymph nodes are negative for cancer. Cancer that has spread to a nearby body part such as the axillary lymph nodes is called a local metastasis. It might be referred to as locoregional disease or locally advanced. Cancer that has spread to a body part far from the primary tumor is called a distant metastasis. Breast cancer can metastasize almost anywhere but most commonly spreads to the bone (including spine), lungs, liver, brain, or distant lymph nodes. Breast cancer that has metastasized to other parts of the body is still called breast cancer. A patient with fair skin and a history of organ transplant is at particularly high risk for developing basal cell carcinoma for two distinct reasons:

1. **Fair skin:** People with lighter-colored skin, red or blond hair, or light eye color are at higher risk of skin cancer because melanin (skin pigment) filters out the sun's harmful UV rays. Less melanin means less protection against UV radiation, which can damage DNA inside basal skin cells and cause them to grow out of control.

2. **Organ transplant/immune suppression:** People with weakened immune systems from organ transplants are at higher risk for basal cell skin cancer. After organ transplantation, patients typically take immunosuppressant drugs to prevent the body from attacking the donated organ. These drugs reduce the body's ability to fight infection and disease, contributing to increased cancer risk.

Additionally, UV light exposure (from the sun or tanning beds) is the primary cause of basal cell skin cancer, so the combination of increased UV sensitivity (fair skin) and reduced immune surveillance (transplant) compounds the risk.

results.info_summary:
Recurrent basal cell carcinoma (BCC) management differs from initial treatment in several ways:

- **Treatment setting:** Initial BCC is most commonly treated with surgery; radiation therapy or systemic therapy may be used in some cases. For recurrence, treatment is guided by risk and recurrence considerations (Chapter 4 of the source; details not fully specified).
- **Radiation limitations:** The same area generally should not be treated with radiation more than once. If cancer grows in a previously radiated area, it usually requires surgery, though healing may be poorer because tissues were weakened by radiation.
- **Adjuvant therapy:** Radiation is sometimes used after surgery (adjuvant) to kill remaining cancer cells or prevent recurrence in patients with high-risk tumors.
- **Factors influencing treatment choice:** Tumor size and location (radiation effective for small tumors and head/neck areas); genetic conditions (e.g., basal cell nevus syndrome, xeroderma pigmentosum) that increase radiation-induced cancer risk; connective tissue diseases (e.g., lupus, scleroderma); prior radiation to the same site; and immune suppression.
- **General BCC risk factors:** Fair skin, red/blond hair (list truncated in source).

No new information retrieved directly addresses recurrent BCC management.

The epidermis is made up of basal cells and other cells. Basal cell skin cancer occurs when some basal cells become abnormal and grow out of control. For a patient treated for BCC on the neck, the recommended follow-up strategy is regular skin exams by a doctor to monitor for recurrence. These exams should include a complete check of the skin on the entire body, as well as the lymph nodes closest to the cancer site. The reason for this follow-up is that once a patient has had skin cancer, they are at higher risk of getting it again, as well as other types of skin cancer—and BCC, while rarely metastatic and usually curable with surgery, can recur, particularly since it commonly develops in sun-exposed areas such as the neck. Therefore, regular skin exams are very important to monitor for the return of the cancer.

The frequency of follow-up depends on whether the cancer was local (not in nearby lymph nodes) or regional (in nearby lymph nodes). For local CSCC, monitoring during the first 2 years after treatment is most important, with exams at least every 3 to 12 months (low risk) or every 3 to 6 months (high risk). **Summary: Immune Suppression, Radiation Therapy, and BCC Risk/Management**

**Risk factors for basal cell skin cancer (BCC):**
- **Prior radiation therapy** – Radiation treatment for other conditions, especially at a young age, can cause skin cancer.
- **Immune suppression** – People with weakened immune systems from organ transplants or autoimmune diseases are at higher risk for BCC.

**Management implications:**
- BCC is highly treatable and curable; early detection and treatment are key. Surgery is the most common treatment; radiation therapy or systemic therapy may be used in some cases.
- Radiation therapy should **not** be used in people with certain genetic conditions that increase risk of radiation-caused skin cancer (e.g., basal cell nevus syndrome, xeroderma pigmentosum), and may not be appropriate for some with connective tissue diseases (e.g., lupus, scleroderma).
- The same area generally should not be treated with radiation more than once. When cancer grows in a previously radiated area, it usually requires surgical removal, though healing is often poorer because tissues were weakened by radiation (especially on the scalp).
- A radiation oncologist should help determine whether radiation is appropriate.

Additionally, radiation therapy is contraindicated in certain genetic conditions that increase radiation-induced skin cancer risk (e.g., basal cell nevus syndrome, xeroderma pigmentosum) and may be inappropriate for some patients with connective tissue diseases (e.g., lupus, scleroderma). Title: . Content: 0:About basal cell skin cancer What is basal cell skin cancer? How is basal cell skin cancer treated? What can you do to get the best care? Basal cell skin cancer, also known as basal cell carcinoma (BCC), is the most common type of skin cancer. About 3 million cases of basal cell skin cancer are diagnosed every year in the United States. The good news is it can be cured in most cases. Treatment usually involves surgery to remove the cancer. Keep reading to find out more. What is basal cell skin cancer? Basal cell skin cancer is the most common of all skin cancer types. If caught early, it is easily treatable and curable. This is because it rarely metastasizes (spreads). Skin cancers often occur in the top layer of the skin (epidermis) and less commonly in the middle layer of the skin (dermis). The epidermis is made up of basal cells and other cells. Basal cell skin cancer occurs when some basal cells become abnormal and grow out of control. This cancer usually develops in areas exposed to the sun, including the face, head, neck, arms, legs, and trunk. But it can occur anywhere on the body. Title: . Content: 564: diagnosed? Primary CNS lymphoma is often found when a person develops symptoms. A symptom is a feeling or problem that may be a sign of disease. Symptoms usually develop over several weeks. Primary CNS lymphoma can cause a variety of symptoms. Symptoms are often related to the lymphoma’s location in the central nervous system. The most common location is in the central part of the brain. A lymphoma located here may cause specific nerve changes such as leg or arm weakness, or problems with coordination or movement. Other such symptoms may include changes in personality or behavior, depression, confusion, memory problems, loss of bladder control (incontinence), or difficulty speaking or swallowing. As the lymphoma tumor grows, it puts pressure on the CNS. This pressure often leads to neurological symptoms and difficulties, including headaches, nausea, vomiting, or seizures. Changes in eyesight, such as blurry vision or double vision, can also occur. You’ll need several tests to confirm whether you have primary CNS lymphoma or a lymphoma that started in another part of your body, or a different disease with similar symptoms. Important tests include a neurological exam, imaging (MRI or CT scan), and biopsies. A biopsy means taking a sample of fluid or tissue from your body to look for cancer
results.info_summary:
For a patient with primary CNS lymphoma presenting with blurry vision and suspected eye involvement, the prioritized diagnostic procedures are:

1. **Thorough eye examination** — Everyone diagnosed with primary CNS lymphoma should have this, performed by an ophthalmologist using a slit lamp (a microscope with a bright light). Pupils are dilated with drops first to allow better viewing of the retina, optic nerve, and other eye structures.

2. **Vitreous biopsy (vitrectomy)** — If the vitreous looks unusual or the patient has visual symptoms (such as blurry vision), a vitrectomy may be needed. The eye is numbed with anesthetic, and a thin needle removes a small amount of vitreous, which is tested for cancer cells. In some cases, vitrectomy alone can confirm primary CNS lymphoma without needing a brain biopsy.

3. **Lumbar puncture (spinal tap)** — Removes cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) to test for cancer cells, helping confirm diagnosis and plan treatment. It is done only if it can be performed safely and won't delay treatment.

4. **Additional MRI** — May be needed if cancer cells are found in spinal fluid or if symptoms are present, to identify any lesions.

Although there are different treatment options for primary central nervous system (CNS) lymphoma, the treatment approach is often a two-step process. The first step is the induction phase, which aims to wipe out all lymphoma cells or as many as possible. The goal of the second step, the consolidation phase, is to destroy any cancer cells that may remain in the body after the first phase. Consolidation is also for preventing the lymphoma from returning. Induction The first (induction) phase of treatment can last several months. Treatment typically requires multiple courses of chemotherapy, which are given while in the hospital. The options for induction treatment are listed in Guide 1 and discussed here: Clinical trial Clinical trials allow you to receive treatment while also helping researchers learn more about this uncommon cancer. Title: . Content: 589: Treatment may include a single chemotherapy drug or a combination of drugs. A combination of drugs is sometimes chosen because the drugs work better when they’re used together. Most chemotherapy drugs for primary CNS lymphoma are given intravenously (IV). This means the medicine is slowly infused through a tube into a vein in your arm or another part of your body. The medicine travels in the bloodstream to reach cells throughout the body. Some chemotherapy drugs are taken by mouth as a tablet or capsule. Chemotherapy is given in cycles. One cycle involves a few treatment days followed by several days of rest. Different chemotherapy drugs have different cycles. Common cycles are 14, 21, or 28 days long. Having chemotherapy in cycles gives your body a chance to recover after receiving the treatment. High-dose chemotherapy The most effective chemotherapy drug for primary CNS lymphoma is methotrexate. Methotrexate has been used for many years to treat a variety of cancers. It works by blocking the body’s use of folate, a form of vitamin B. Lymphoma cells can’t multiply and spread as quickly without folate. High doses of methotrexate are needed to overcome the blood-brain barrier and still have enough strength to kill lymphoma cells. The blood-brain barrier is a protective layer around the brain that prevents germs, infections, and other toxins from getting in. But it also blocks some chemotherapy drugs like methotrexate from reaching the brain. For induction therapy, high-dose methotrexate is given together with the immunotherapy drug rituximab (Rituxan). For an older adult with a history of organ transplant who develops primary CNS lymphoma, the relevant risk factors to consider are:

1. **Organ transplant** — requires medications that suppress the immune system, leading to a higher risk of infections and impaired immune function.
2. **Impaired immune system** — having a reduced or impaired immune system increases the risk of developing primary CNS lymphoma.

The treatment approach for primary CNS lymphoma is often a two-step process:

1. **Induction phase** — Aims to wipe out all lymphoma cells or as many as possible. It can last several months and typically requires multiple courses of chemotherapy, which are given while in the hospital. Clinical trials are also an option.

2. **Consolidation phase** — Aims to destroy any cancer cells remaining after induction and prevent the lymphoma from returning.

Treatment options overall include corticosteroids, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and stem cell rescue. The main chemotherapy drug used is methotrexate; the main immunotherapy drug is rituximab. Whole-brain radiation therapy (WBRT) is the most commonly used radiation technique. Surgery is not normally an option.

There’s no single drug or procedure that’s best for treating primary central nervous system (CNS) lymphoma. The best treatment is the one that works best for you. Treatment options include corticosteroids, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and stem cell rescue. Receiving treatment in a clinical trial is also a recommended option. Therapies are often combined to treat cancer. Essential lab tests for the initial workup of primary CNS lymphoma, especially with suspected immunodeficiency, include:

- **HIV blood test** — required for everyone with primary CNS lymphoma; HIV-related PCNSL needs specialized care with antiretroviral therapy plus cancer treatment.
- **Comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP)** — 14 blood tests covering blood sugar, calcium, electrolytes, and liver/kidney health.
- **Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) test** — high levels can indicate cell damage from cancer or other problems.
- **Hepatitis B testing** — necessary before immunotherapy if previously infected or at risk, since immunotherapy can "reawaken" the virus.

Additional relevant procedures (not strictly laboratory blood tests) include lumbar puncture for CSF testing for cancer cells and thorough eye examination. Bone marrow biopsy may be considered if imaging suggests bone involvement, though cancer cells there are uncommon.

**Summary: Imaging and Biopsy Methods for Confirming Primary CNS Lymphoma Localized to the Brain**

- **Imaging:** MRI of the brain is the most useful imaging technique for identifying primary CNS lymphoma. An MRI should be done early on if symptoms suggest a brain tumor, and it highlights primary CNS lymphoma in the brain (which may appear as one or multiple tumors). If MRI is unavailable or not recommended, a CT (CAT) scan may be used instead. A radiologist analyzes the images and conveys results to the care team.

- **Biopsy:** A biopsy is the only way to be certain of a cancer diagnosis. Although there are different treatment options for primary central nervous system (CNS) lymphoma, the treatment approach is often a two-step process. The first step is the induction phase, which aims to wipe out all lymphoma cells or as many as possible. The goal of the second step, the consolidation phase, is to destroy any cancer cells that may remain in the body after the first phase. Consolidation is also for preventing the lymphoma from returning. Induction The first (induction) phase of treatment can last several months. results.info_summary:
For suspected regional CSCC with lymph node involvement, necessary diagnostic procedures include:

1. **Imaging**: CT scan of lymph nodes near the CSCC to determine number, location, and size of involved nodes. PET/CT may be needed to assess for further spread or to plan treatment. Scans of the upper body, stomach, and pelvis may also be included to check for metastatic disease.

2. **Biopsy**: If lymph nodes feel swollen or appear abnormal on initial imaging, a biopsy is performed—either fine-needle aspiration (FNA) or core needle biopsy.

3. **Surgical evaluation**: Test results determine candidacy for surgery to remove the cancerous lesion and nearby lymph nodes.

These procedures establish how far the disease has spread and guide the treatment plan.

Actinic keratosis (AK) is an area of scaly or rough skin caused by long-term sun exposure that may become squamous cell skin cancer (CSCC). Having AKs means a person is at increased risk of developing CSCC. AKs vary in appearance—red, white, tan, or pink—and may appear as small scaly spots or bumps, sometimes resembling warts. Because of this risk, it is important to have skin examined by a doctor or dermatologist.

Although it helps to put gliomas into categories, it’s important to note that each glioma has its own molecular characteristics and behavior. That also means that each person’s glioma is unique. So your progress and experience will be unique to you. Gliomas often occur in the upper part of the brain where they can disrupt important brain functions. Few gliomas in adults have distinct and welldefined edges like the one in this illustration. Most gliomas blend deeply into normal brain tissue and have vague borders. This makes them very difficult to remove entirely. When the tumor is removed, some tumor cells must be left behind to avoid damaging nearby brain tissue. How are gliomas diagnosed? A glioma is often found when it starts causing symptoms. A symptom is a problem or feeling that may be a sign of disease. Gliomas cause symptoms when they put pressure on the brain or invade brain tissue. Some people have many symptoms while others don’t have any. **Summary: Risk Assessment Findings that Classify Local CSCC as High-Risk and Impact on Treatment**

**Risk assessment findings classifying local CSCC as high-risk:**
- **Location:** Tumors on the head or neck are more likely to recur after treatment than those on the trunk, arms, or legs.
- **Size:** Referenced as a factor (specific dimensions not detailed).
- **Perineural invasion:** Tumor growth into a nerve or group of nerves (usually seen under the microscope) classifies the CSCC as high-risk or very high-risk.
- **Tumor grade:** A rating of how fast the cancer is expected to grow and spread.
- **Depth of invasion:** The deeper the tumor has invaded into the skin, the higher the risk of recurrence after treatment.
- **Immune status:** Conditions that weaken the immune system (e.g., long-term corticosteroid use, HIV/AIDS, organ transplant) increase the risk of CSCC and of cancer returning after treatment.
- The risk level/category is usually based on the **highest risk factor found**.
- **High-risk CSCC** = increased risk of local recurrence; **very high-risk CSCC** = increased risk of local recurrence and likely other adverse

Conditions or factors that weaken the immune system include long-term corticosteroid use, HIV/AIDS, lymphoma, chronic lymphocytic leukemia, and having received an organ transplant (due to immunosuppressant drugs). For clinical management, immunosuppressed patients are generally treated as having higher-risk disease. Treatment options include standard surgical excision with wider margins for high-risk or very high-risk CSCC, Mohs surgery or other PDEMA, and radiation therapy when surgery is not an option. Systemic therapy may be added to radiation, with platinum-based chemotherapy recommended in that setting. If radiation is not expected to be curative or may damage critical organs, systemic therapy alone is recommended, and immunotherapy with an immune checkpoint inhibitor is preferred if the patient is eligible. Clinical trials for systemic therapy (chemotherapy, targeted therapy, or immunotherapy) may also be considered.

analysis.current_understanding: The patient has cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC) arising in a chronic wound (Marjolin's ulcer). Two risk factors are present: (1) the cancer originates in damaged, inflamed, or scarred skin; and (2) it develops in chronic nonhealing wounds such as ulcers or burns. These factors place the CSCC in a higher-risk category, making it more difficult to treat and more likely to recur after treatment. Therefore, staging should consider it as high-risk, and management should be adjusted accordingly (e.g., more aggressive treatment and closer follow-up).

**Genetic syndromes and increased CSCC risk:** NCCN recommends that people with genetic syndromes predisposing to skin cancer be referred to a cancer center with expertise in CSCC prevention and treatment, and receive counseling from someone with expertise in cancer genetics (e.g., genetic counselor, medical geneticist, endocrinologist, oncologist, surgeon, or oncology nurse) throughout treatment. Relevant inherited cancer syndromes include Lynch syndrome (caused by inherited MMR gene mutations), familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), and BRCA1/BRCA2 mutations (which increase risk of breast, ovarian, prostate, colorectal, pancreatic, and melanoma skin cancers, and can affect treatment response).

**Other conditions that weaken the immune system and increase CSCC risk:**
- Organ transplant recipients taking immunosuppressants
- Lymphoma (cancer of the lymph nodes)
- Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (cancer of white blood cells in bone marrow)
- HIV/AIDS

results.info_summary: A clinician would perform a skin biopsy when a patient has an area of abnormal-looking skin (called a lesion) that looks like it could be skin cancer. A skin biopsy—removing a sample of the lesion to test for cancer—is the only way to know for sure if cancer is present and is needed to diagnose squamous cell skin cancer (CSCC). The sample should be reviewed by a pathologist, who notes the overall appearance and the size, shape, and type of cells. The doctor chooses among several biopsy methods based on the size of the lesion. Testing for CSCC may also include a full health history, a close examination of the lesion(s), and imaging scans if cancer may be deep within the skin or has spread to other parts of the body. If spread to lymph nodes is suspected (e.g., lymph nodes near the CSCC feel swollen or look abnormal on initial imaging), the next step is a lymph node biopsy, using fine-needle aspiration (FNA) or core needle biopsy.

results.info_summary: The BCR::ABL1 fusion gene is formed when pieces of chromosome 9 and chromosome 22 break off and trade places, creating the Philadelphia (Ph) chromosome—the hallmark of CML. **Diagnosis:** If you do not have the Ph chromosome or the BCR::ABL1 gene, you do not have CML; BCR::ABL1 is not found in normal blood cells and is not inherited. Accurate testing is needed to diagnose and treat CML, and testing may include blood tests, bone marrow tests, and testing for the CML biomarker and genetic changes. **Treatment:** The BCR::ABL1 gene makes a new protein that leads to uncontrolled blood cell growth, causing CML, so treatment aims to stop the activity of the BCR::ABL1 protein. In blast phase CML (BP-CML), the type of blast phase cell (lymphoid or myeloid) affects treatment. Patients should be treated at centers experienced in this type of cancer, and seeking the opinion of a CML specialist should be considered. analysis.current_understanding: The BCR::ABL1 fusion gene is central to both diagnosing and treating CML. Diagnosis: the fusion gene arises from a translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22, forming the Philadelphia chromosome, which is the hallmark of CML. Its presence is required for CML diagnosis—without the Ph chromosome or BCR::ABL1, a patient does not have CML—and it is neither found in normal blood cells nor inherited, making it a specific biomarker that requires accurate laboratory testing (blood, bone marrow, and genetic/biomarker tests). Treatment: the fusion gene produces an abnormal protein that drives uncontrolled blood cell growth, so therapies aim to inhibit or stop the activity of the BCR::ABL1 protein. Treatment specifics can vary, such as in blast phase CML where the blast cell type (lymphoid vs. myeloid) influences the approach. Management should occur at experienced centers, with consideration of a CML specialist, and patients are encouraged to participate actively in shared decision-making. Overall, the information adequately explains that BCR::ABL1 is both the defining diagnostic marker and the primary therapeutic target in CML.

The BCR::ABL1 gene makes a new protein that leads to uncontrolled blood cell growth, ultimately causing CML. BCR::ABL1 is not found in normal blood cells and is not inherited. The very immature cells (myeloblasts or lymphoblasts) are referred to as blasts.

results.info_summary:
**Summary: Genetic and Chromosomal Events Leading to CML**

Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) is caused by a single, specific genetic abnormality:

1. **Chromosomal translocation**: A piece of chromosome 9 and a piece of chromosome 22 break off and trade (switch) places.
2. **Formation of the Philadelphia (Ph) chromosome**: This translocation creates a shortened, abnormal chromosome 22 that contains a small part of chromosome 9. This is called the Philadelphia chromosome and is the hallmark of CML.
3. **Formation of the fused gene**: The translocation fuses portions of the two chromosomes to create an abnormal fusion gene called **BCR::ABL1**.
4. **Protein production and uncontrolled growth**: The BCR::ABL1 gene produces a new protein that leads to uncontrolled blood cell growth, ultimately causing CML.

**Key details:**
- CML is thought to arise from blood stem cells that produce an increased amount of myeloid progenitor cells.
- In advanced blast phase CML (BP-CML), increased amounts of lymphoid or myeloid progenitor cells can occur.
- The BCR::ABL1 gene is not found in normal blood cells and is not inherited from birth parents to children.

results.gold_answer: BCR::ABL1 fusion gene and Philadelphia chromosome are tested, both resulting from the same chromosomal translocation.
results.answer: Philadelphia chromosome and BCR::ABL1 gene; the Philadelphia chromosome contains the BCR::ABL1 gene.

Many cancers spread from the location where they originate, and the extent or severity of cancer is determined by how far it has spread. AML arises from the bone marrow, which is present in nearly all of our bones. Because AML cells arise from multiple bones and flow in the blood all over the body, traditional staging is not useful. Instead, AML testing looks for specific gene mutations or abnormal chromosomes, which can tell your care team how aggressive your leukemia might be. In CML, the disease is caused by the Philadelphia chromosome — a fusion gene called BCR::ABL1 formed when pieces of chromosome 9 and chromosome 22 break off and trade places. This gene produces a protein that leads to uncontrolled blood cell growth. CML is thought to arise from blood stem cells that produce an increased amount of myeloid progenitor cells, which mature into myeloblasts and other non-lymphoid blood cells (granulocytes). Lung cancer screening is recommended for individuals at high risk of developing lung cancer, with tobacco smoking being the most significant risk factor (risk increases with more frequent and longer smoking). Other contributing factors include second-hand smoke exposure, radon, asbestos, arsenic, beryllium, cadmium, chromium, nickel, coal smoke, soot, silica, diesel fumes, and air pollution (fine particulates, ozone, nitrogen oxides, sulfur dioxide). Screening aims to detect lung cancer at an early stage, before symptoms appear, when treatment is most successful. It is not recommended for everyone; patients should ask their healthcare provider whether they qualify. The diagnostic process includes assessing risk factors (medical history, family history of cancer), reviewing lung images, and performing a biopsy if needed. Nodules found by imaging may prompt further scans; if unlikely to be cancer, patients may be referred for screening. Patients are encouraged to play an active role in their care by asking questions and making shared decisions with their care team, as this leads to greater satisfaction and better outcomes.

Talk to your doctor about whether a clinical trial may make sense for you. Phases Most cancer clinical trials focus on treatment. Treatment trials are done in phases. Phase 1 trials study the dose, safety, and side effects of an investigational drug or treatment approach. They also look for early signs that the drug or approach is helpful. Phase 2 trials study how well the drug or approach works against a specific type of cancer. Phase 3 trials test the drug or approach against a standard treatment. If the results are good, it may be approved by the FDA. Phase 4 trials study the long-term safety and benefit of an FDA-approved treatment. Who can enroll? Every clinical trial has rules for joining, called eligibility criteria. The rules may be about age, cancer type and stage, treatment history, or general health. These requirements ensure that participants are alike in specific ways and that the trial is as safe as possible for the participants. Informed consent Clinical trials are managed by a group of experts called a research team. results.info_summary:
The subtype of NSCLC is determined by histology (looking at cancer cells under a microscope), and each subtype originates from a different type of cell:

- **Adenocarcinoma**: Starts in the mucus-making cells that line the alveoli (small air sacs). It is the most common subtype (about 4 out of 10 lung cancers) and the most common type seen in those who don't smoke.
- **Squamous cell (epidermoid) carcinoma**: Starts in the flat cells that line the inside of the airways (bronchi). About 3 out of 10 lung cancers are this subtype.
- **Large cell (undifferentiated) carcinoma**: Starts in large cells that can grow anywhere in the lungs. Accounts for 5 out of 10 NSCLCs.

Other NSCLC subtypes include adenosquamous carcinoma and sarcomatoid carcinoma. NSCLC overall forms from cells lining the airways (bronchi, bronchioli, and alveoli). (SCLC, by contrast, is a fast-dividing cancer of the neuroendocrine cells, with small, oval- or oat-shaped cells.)

**Summary: Rationale for Using Both Imaging and Biopsy in Assessing a Lung Nodule**

- **Imaging** is used first to detect and characterize a lung nodule. A nodule may be found by chance on imaging, and additional scans (e.g., CT or MRI) may be requested to assess whether it may be cancer. Imaging reviews nodule size and other features to help determine whether further procedures are needed.

- **Biopsy** is performed when needed to remove samples of fluid or tissue for testing. Biopsy samples are sent to a pathologist—a physician expert in examining tissues and cells—who examines them under a microscope to determine whether the nodule is cancerous and, if so, the cancer type (tumor histology). A biopsy can also confirm metastasis if cancer has spread.

- **Rationale for both:** Imaging alone cannot always confirm whether a nodule is cancer. A team of experts (including a pulmonologist, thoracic radiologist, and thoracic surgeon) reviews lung images and requests more imaging if cancer is suspected, then performs a biopsy if needed. Some nodules don't need biopsy and are instead monitored with imaging.

In EBRT, radiation is delivered from outside (external to) the body using a large machine Anal canal cancer (stages I – III) called a linear accelerator. What makes IMRT unique compared to other forms of EBRT is that it uses many small beams of different intensities (strengths). This allows a high dose of radiation to be targeted at the tumor while limiting the amount of radiation to the surrounding normal tissue. Early NSCLC (stage 1) and locally advanced NSCLC (stages 2 and 3) have not spread to the tissue lining around the lung or to other organs; their distinction is based mainly on cancer stage. Stage 1 is early NSCLC, while stages 2 and 3 are generally considered locally advanced. At diagnosis, stages 1–3 have grown from the airway into lung tissue, and some have spread to nearby lymph nodes.

There is no single best treatment for NSCLC; the best treatment is the one that is right for each person, and often multiple treatments are combined for the best results. When possible, surgery is used as primary treatment for both early and locally advanced NSCLC, often combined with other treatments to improve results. Patients who cannot have surgery have other options: some early cancers are treated with radiation therapy, while other cancers are treated with chemoradiation (chemotherapy and radiation therapy given during the same time period). dependency_analysis.query: Definition of early-stage NSCLC

analysis.current_understanding: Early-stage NSCLC is defined as stage 1 NSCLC, where the cancer has not spread to the tissue lining around the lung or to other organs, but has grown from the airway into lung tissue. Some cases may involve spread to nearby lymph nodes. Treatment for early-stage NSCLC typically involves surgery when possible, often combined with other treatments; for patients who cannot have surgery, radiation therapy or chemoradiation may be used, and clinical trials may be an option.

dependency_analysis.query: Use of combined modality therapy in each stage

analysis.current_understanding: The available information states that when possible, surgery is used as primary treatment for both early and locally advanced NSCLC, often combined with other treatments to improve results. Patients who cannot have surgery have other options: some early cancers are treated with radiation therapy, while other cancers are treated with chemoradiation (chemotherapy and radiation therapy given during the same time period). However, the information does not specify the details of combined modality therapy separately for early versus locally advanced NSCLC, such as which combinations are standard for each stage. Therefore, the question about the main differences in treatment between early and locally advanced NSCLC cannot be fully answered with this information alone.

**Key risk factors (exposures):**

- Radon and asbestos exposure
- Carcinogens: arsenic, beryllium, cadmium, chromium, nickel

Recurrence This section discusses cervical cancer that does not improve with treatment (persistent) or that returns after treatment (recurrent). If your doctor suspects recurrence based on your symptoms or a physical exam, you will have imaging tests to check. This could include CT, PET, and/or MRI. Surgery to look inside the body (exploratory surgery) may be helpful in some cases. The goal is to learn the extent of the cancer. This can help guide treatment decisions. Biomarker testing Biomarkers are features of a cancer that can help guide treatment. Biomarkers are often mutations (changes) in particular genes. They can also be proteins that are made in response to the cancer. Biomarker testing is recommended for all recurrent cervical cancers. The results help determine whether treatment with certain targeted therapies is an option. The results can also be used to determine whether you can join certain clinical trials. results.info_summary:
To confirm nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) and determine its subtype, the necessary diagnostic methods are:

- **Biopsy** — confirms the diagnosis and identifies the cancer type (most commonly squamous cell carcinoma, SCC).
- **Biomarker testing** — examines specific DNA mutations, protein levels, or other molecular features, including Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) status, since most NPCs are EBV-related.
- **Imaging studies** — used alongside medical history and physical examination to determine tumor size, location, and whether the cancer has spread (staging).

Per the information, results from medical history, physical examination, imaging studies, and biopsy are combined to determine the treatment plan. Diagnosis specifically requires biopsy and biomarker testing, while staging uses TNM classification combined with imaging and biomarker information.

results.info_summary: Enlarged lymph nodes in a patient with nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) indicate that the cancer has spread to nearby (regional) lymph nodes, which is reflected in the "N" (node) category of the TNM staging system. The N score accounts for whether cancer has spread to nearby lymph nodes, how many are involved, and their location—and the higher the N number, the more the cancer has spread. Lymph node involvement is a key component of cancer staging, which describes tumor size and location and whether cancer has spread to lymph nodes or other parts of the body, and is used to reflect prognosis and guide treatment decisions. Staging is based on clinical assessment (physical exam, biopsy, and imaging) before treatment (e.g., cN2), and NPC can spread to nearby lymph nodes as well as areas such as the nasal cavity, oropharynx, hypopharynx, base of the skull, jaw, and roof of the mouth. Notably, in NPC, T0 can be assigned when no tumor is found but neck lymph nodes test positive for Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), and most nasopharyngeal cancers are EBV-related.

**Summary: Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma (NPC) — At-Risk Populations and Risk Factors**

**At-risk populations:**
- NPC is a rare cancer that most often occurs in people from parts of **Asia, Native America, and North Africa**.

**Risk factors / contributing factors:**
- **Epstein-Barr virus (EBV):** Most nasopharyngeal cancers are EBV-related.
- **Tobacco and alcohol use:** Known risk factors for developing head and neck cancers (the category that includes NPC); these can also limit how well treatment works and affect survival. Patients are advised to avoid tobacco and limit alcohol during treatment.
- **Genetic/molecular features:** Biomarker testing may identify specific DNA mutations, protein levels, or other molecular features; some mutations and proteins can be targeted with specific therapies. Note: head and neck cancers are not inherited from biological parents, though some cancers and other diseases can run in families; care teams collect family health history.

results.info_summary: Staging of nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) is based on physical exam, biopsy, and imaging (clinical stage is based on imaging and biopsy results). Imaging helps the care team stage the cancer and plan treatment; a radiologist interprets results and conveys them to the oncologist. For surveillance, imaging may be ordered if there is concern the cancer has returned or spread. Specific imaging modalities that may be used include computed tomography (CT), MRI, positron emission tomography (PET), PET/CT, ultrasound, and panoramic dental x-ray (Panorex). CT takes many x-rays from different angles, combined by computer into cross-sectional images; FDG-PET/CT can be done at the same time as a diagnostic CT, and PET/CT can be performed with one or two machines depending on the cancer center. MRI uses radio waves, a powerful magnet, and a computer, does not use radiation, and is safe for most people, though people with certain heart monitors, pacemakers, or some types of surgical clips generally cannot have MRI. Contrast dye may be used with both CT and MRI unless contraindicated (e.g., allergy or condition that could cause a harmful reaction); it may be injected into a vein and/or mixed with a liquid

results.info_summary:
Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is the most common type of nasopharyngeal cancer (NPC). It arises in the thin, flat squamous cells of the mucous membranes lining the nasopharynx—the upper part of the throat connecting the back of the nose to the back of the mouth. Within the cancer ontology, NPC is classified as a head and neck cancer, and most NPCs originate in the squamous cells forming the surface lining of the nasopharynx.

NPC is staged using the TNM system, which assesses tumor extent (T), regional lymph node involvement (N), and distant metastasis (M). T categories include T0 (no primary tumor found but neck lymph nodes test positive for Epstein-Barr virus), Tis (carcinoma in situ, with cancerous cells confined to the squamous cell layer), and T1 (tumor confined to the nasopharynx or extending into the oropharynx and/or nasal cavity but not the parapharyngeal space).

SCC is the primary focus of NPC diagnosis and treatment.

results.info_summary:
**Summary: Risk Factors Prompting Consideration of Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma (NPC)**

NPC is a rare cancer that most often occurs in people from parts of Asia, Native America, and North Africa. Most nasopharyngeal cancers are Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)-related (caused by EBV). The most common type is squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), arising in the squamous cells lining the nasopharynx.

Key point for differential diagnosis: NPC is often difficult to recognize because symptoms are similar to other less serious conditions, and many people have no symptoms until the cancer reaches an advanced stage. Cancer cells often spread to lymph nodes in the neck (and less frequently to the lungs).

Therefore, clinicians should consider NPC in the differential when risk factors include: origin from or ancestry in parts of Asia, Native America, or North Africa; EBV association; and/or presence of neck lymph node involvement—particularly given the nonspecific or absent symptoms in early disease.

The American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) created the TNM staging system, which determines how much cancer is in the body, where it is located, and what subtype the patient has. It is used to reflect prognosis and guide treatment decisions. For nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC), staging is based on a combination of information, and the TNM system assesses three aspects:

- **T (tumor):** Size and extent of the main (primary) tumor — how large the cancer is and whether it has grown into nearby areas (e.g., oropharynx, nasal cavity, parapharyngeal space). Head and neck tumors are measured in centimeters. T scores range from T0 (no tumor found but neck lymph nodes test positive for Epstein-Barr virus) and Tis (carcinoma in situ, cancerous cells only in the squamous cell layer) through higher numbers.
- **N (node):** Whether cancer has spread to nearby (regional) lymph nodes, and if so, how many and where.
- **M (metastasis):** Whether the cancer has spread to distant organs such as the lungs or liver.

results.info_summary: Dental health assessment is important in the management of nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) and other head and neck cancers because the cancer and its treatment can affect the health of the jaw, teeth, and gums. Patients should tell their dentist about their head and neck cancer diagnosis and keep up with regular dental cleanings and checkups. If dental work or procedures are needed, they may be recommended before starting certain treatments. This is particularly relevant because radiation therapy to the neck area—a common treatment for head and neck cancers—can cause side effects such as dry mouth, thick saliva, changes in taste, and skin rash or redness, some of which may occur years after treatment. For optimal care, patients with head and neck cancers are strongly recommended to be treated at a comprehensive cancer center with doctors who are experts in evaluating and treating NPC.

results.info_summary: Young adults with colon cancer should be counseled about fertility preservation before treatment because colon cancer is increasingly diagnosed in young adults, and some cancer treatments—such as chemotherapy and radiation therapy—can temporarily or permanently impair fertility or make it hard or impossible to have children. Radiation can damage the hormone-making function of the ovaries and testicles, causing inability to conceive; ovarian damage is known as premature ovarian insufficiency (POI) or radiation-induced premature menopause. Options include sperm banking (semen cryopreservation), egg freezing (oocyte cryopreservation), and ovarian tissue banking. Fertility preservation keeps options open, and loss of fertility is related to age at diagnosis, treatment type, dose, and length.

**Diagnostic Tests for Initial Evaluation and Staging of Colon Cancer**

**Initial Evaluation:**

- **Colonoscopy** – Most colon cancers are found during colonoscopy; a follow-up colonoscopy is common to thoroughly examine the colon.

results.info_summary:
Patients with a first-degree relative with colorectal cancer are at higher risk than the average person. Most colorectal cancers occur for unknown reasons, but rare inherited cancer syndromes should be considered:

- **Lynch syndrome**: Caused by inherited mutations in mismatch repair (MMR) genes; associated with high risk of colorectal, endometrial, and ovarian cancers. Testing for Lynch syndrome is recommended for cancers with dMMR/MSI-H biomarker.
- **Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP)**: Causes hundreds to thousands of polyps in the colon and rectum; polyps start benign but can become invasive cancer, often by age 50 in classic FAP. Attenuated FAP causes fewer polyps and starts later in life.

A detailed family history—including the specific type of cancer, where it started, and the age at diagnosis in blood relatives on both sides of the family—helps determine appropriate care and whether an inherited syndrome should be suspected. If an inherited syndrome is suspected, referral to a genetic counselor is recommended for testing.
