It can detect common patterns of proteins on the outside of cells. Most cells have an identifiable pattern of proteins, like a silhouette or a shape, called the immunophenotype. A CLL diagnosis requires at least 5,000 or more of the same white blood cells called monoclonal B lymphocytes to be found per microliter in your blood. Diagnosis by biopsy A biopsy is a procedure that removes samples from the body for testing. If the blood results aren’t clear, you’ll have a biopsy of your lymph nodes or bone marrow to confirm CLL. Tests of lymph nodes will also confirm small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL). An excisional biopsy is when a whole lymph node is removed by a surgeon, while an incisional biopsy removes only part of a lymph node. There are many lymph nodes throughout your body, so if you have a lymph node removed, you won’t lose your ability to fight infections and disease. results.info_summary:
**Summary: Key Components in Diagnosing Cutaneous B-cell Lymphoma (CBCL)**

Diagnosis of CBCL involves a comprehensive testing process. Key components assessed include:

- **General health tests** and a **skin exam**
- **Blood tests** (including flow cytometry, which detects protein patterns/immunophenotype on cells)
- **Imaging tests**
- **Biopsy** (e.g., excisional, incisional, or needle biopsy) to remove tissue samples for lab testing
- **Immunophenotyping**
- **Testing for CBCL biomarkers and genetic changes**
- **TNM scores** (staging)

Results from blood and tissue tests, imaging studies, and biopsy collectively determine the diagnosis and treatment plan. Accurate testing is essential to diagnose and treat CBCL, which develops from abnormal B cells (a type of lymphocyte/white blood cell) and often appears as nodules or papules under the skin.

**Summary: Diagnostic Methods and Criteria for Pediatric ALL**

**Primary Diagnostic Criterion:**
- In general, a diagnosis of ALL requires **20 percent or more lymphoblasts** present in the bone marrow (i.e., at least 1 out of every 5 marrow cells are lymphoblasts).
- In certain cases, ALL can be diagnosed with **less than 20 percent lymphoblasts**.

**Diagnostic Methods/Tests:**
- Blood tests
- Bone marrow tests (primary diagnostic tool)
- Imaging tests
- Lumbar puncture (to detect CNS involvement)
- Heart tests
- General health tests
- Fertility testing (all genders)
- Tissue tests
- Biomarker and genetic testing (including pharmacogenomic testing)
- Genetic risk testing

**Key Diagnostic Details:**
- ALL is a fast-growing blood cancer starting in lymphocytes (disease-fighting white blood cells).
- Bone marrow makes too many immature lymphocytes called lymphoblasts (blasts).
- ALL can be found in bone marrow, blood, and organs such as the testicles or central nervous system (CNS).
- ALL has 2 main types: B cell (B-ALL) and T cell (T-ALL), with subtypes based on lymphocyte type, genetic

**Summary: Treatment Approaches for Childhood ALL by Subtype/Special Cases**

**General treatment:** All patients with ALL receive steroids and multiagent chemotherapy; other systemic therapies may also be used. Treatment depends on the type of ALL, age at diagnosis, and other factors.

**By subtype/special case:**
- **BCR::ABL1-negative or BCR::ABL1-like B-ALL** (most common type of B-ALL): A clinical trial is the preferred treatment.
- **BCR::ABL1-positive B-ALL:** Treatment aims to stop the activity of the BCR::ABL protein caused by the BCR::ABL1 gene; usually an intensive combination of systemic therapies.
- **T-ALL** (less common than B-ALL; starts in T-cell lymphocytes): Treatment options include a clinical trial or chemotherapy.
- **Infant ALL** (infants are under 12 months of age): Treatment is different than for other age groups.

**Other relevant points:** Supportive care addresses side effects. Families are encouraged to seek an ALL specialist and treatment at an experienced pediatric leukemia center, ask questions, and make shared decisions with the care team.

results.info_summary:
The newly retrieved information does not contain facts about the disease sites or symptoms of pediatric ALL; it concerns general cancer-care guidance, medical/family history taking, clinical trials, and questions to ask care teams. Therefore, the refined summary remains focused on the existing ALL-specific information:

ALL in children is a fast-growing blood cancer that starts in lymphocytes (a type of white blood cell). In the bone marrow, too many immature lymphocytes called lymphoblasts (or blasts) are made, crowding out normal blood cell production. The two main types are B-cell (B-ALL) and T-cell (T-ALL). ALL can involve the bone marrow, blood, and organs such as the testicles or the central nervous system (CNS). B-cell lymphoblasts grow mostly in the lymph nodes, and T-ALL can cause an enlarged thymus, sometimes leading to breathing problems due to pressure on the windpipe and blood vessels. Diagnosis generally requires 20 percent or more lymphoblasts in the bone marrow, though in certain cases ALL can be diagnosed with less than 20 percent.

analysis.current_understanding: Pediatric ALL is a fast-growing blood cancer originating from lymphocytes. It primarily involves the bone marrow, where excessive immature lymphoblasts crowd out normal blood cell production, and can also involve the blood and specific extramedullary sites such as the central nervous system and testicles. B-cell ALL (B-ALL) commonly involves lymph nodes, while T-cell ALL (T-ALL) can cause thymic enlargement with potential breathing difficulties due to airway or vascular compression. Diagnosis typically requires ≥20% bone marrow lymphoblasts, though lower percentages may suffice in certain cases. However, the provided information does not specify the typical disease sites and symptoms associated with pediatric ALL in a comprehensive or systematic way.

**Summary: Influence of Age Group at Diagnosis on ALL Management and Treatment in Children**

- Treatment for ALL depends on the type of ALL, **age at diagnosis**, and other factors.
- **Infant ALL** (infants under 12 months of age) is treated **differently than other age groups**.
- The guideline covers treatment for ALL in **infants, children, and young adults**.
- **Pediatric** includes anyone **18 years of age or under**, and certain **adolescents and young adults (AYAs)** — those **15 to 39 years of age** at initial cancer diagnosis.
- An AYA may be treated in a **pediatric or adult center** depending on the type of cancer; this book applies to AYAs treated at a pediatric/children’s cancer center, while those treated at adult centers are directed to separate NCCN guidelines.
- For best care, consider seeking an **ALL specialist** and treatment at an **experienced children’s (pediatric) leukemia center**.
- Patients (or their families) should take an active role in care by asking questions and making **shared decisions** with the care team; each chapter of the NCCN Guidelines for Patients ends

Infant ALL (under 12 months) is treated differently than other age groups. The guideline covers infants, children, and young adults, emphasizing the importance of treatment at experienced pediatric leukemia centers and involvement of ALL specialists. results.question: What are the key differences in presentation and management between B-cell ALL and T-cell ALL in children?
results.gold_answer: B-cell ALL is more common and defined by B-cell biomarkers, while T-cell ALL often presents with an enlarged thymus and breathing problems, with both subtypes managed using steroids, multiagent chemotherapy, systemic therapy, and clinical trials.

- **Frequency:** B-ALL is more common than T-ALL.

Mature B-cell ALL (Burkitt leukemia) and infant ALL (under 12 months) are each treated differently from standard B-ALL.

**Diagnostic Methods:**
- Digital rectal examination (DRE) and anoscopy at 8–12 weeks post-chemoradiation to assess treatment response
- Imaging: MRI of the pelvis using a rectal cancer staging technique (shows extent of cancer in rectum and nearby lymph nodes); CT of the chest and abdomen (detects spread to liver, lungs, or other organs)
- Molecular testing: microsatellite instability (MSI) or microsatellite stable (MSS) status
- Medical history: record of all health issues and treatments, including any history of H. pylori infection/treatment, and a list of old and new medicines, OTC medicines, herbals, or supplements (some supplements interact with prescribed medicines)
- Family health history assessment for all rectal cancer patients, covering blood relatives on both sides of the family, including specific cancer types, sites of origin, and age at diagnosis
- Biopsy if follow-up examination 8–12 weeks after treatment finds disease progression
- Proctoscopy, endorectal ultrasound or MRI with contrast, and colonoscopy after transanal local excision

**Surveillance Strategies:**

*After chemoradiation (complete remission):*
- DREs every 3–6

**Summary:**

- **Polyp types associated with rectal cancer:** The most common type is the **adenoma**. While it may take many years, adenomas can become invasive rectal cancer; cancer forming in an adenoma is called an **adenocarcinoma** (the most common rectal cancer type). Polyps that **rarely** turn into cancer include **hyperplastic** and **inflammatory polyps**. Almost all rectal cancers start in a polyp. Polyps are also classified by shape: **pedunculated** (mushroom-like with a stalk) and **sessile** (flatter, no stalk); sessile polyps are more likely to return after treatment.

- **Impact of polypectomy on prevention:** Removing polyps can **prevent cancer before it starts**. Most polyps can be removed during a colonoscopy via a minor surgical procedure called a **polypectomy**. Polyps can also be tested to confirm cancer hasn't already started. Often no further treatment is needed; in other cases, resection of a larger piece of the rectum may be required, depending on polyp size/shape, polypectomy results, and tissue testing results. For sessile polyps, EUS or pelvic MRI is recommended to guide

Hyperplastic and inflammatory polyps rarely turn into cancer. For sessile polyps, EUS or pelvic MRI is recommended to guide treatment.

**Summary: Genetic and Biomarker Features of Rectal Cancer and Diagnostic Implications**

**Biomarkers (MMR/MSI testing):**
- All patients diagnosed with rectal cancer should have their tumor tested for mutations in mismatch repair (MMR) genes; this biomarker helps guide treatment.
- Testing is performed on a piece of the rectal tumor in a lab. Abnormal results are termed **mismatch repair deficient (dMMR)** or **microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H)**; tumors without these changes are **microsatellite stable (MSS)** or **mismatch repair proficient (pMMR)**.

**Inherited Genetic Syndromes:**
- Most rectal cancers occur for unknown reasons, but some are linked to inherited mutations.
- If a tumor is dMMR/MSI-H, the patient should also be tested for **Lynch syndrome** — an inherited condition caused by MMR gene mutations that raises risk of colorectal, endometrial, and ovarian cancers.
- **Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP)** is another rare inherited syndrome causing hundreds to thousands of polyps in the colon and rectum; these benign growths can become invasive rectal cancer over time.

results.question: How are treatment strategies for rectal cancer determined by tumor stage?
results.gold_answer: Treatment for rectal cancer is stage-dependent: T1 tumors are managed with endoscopic and transanal procedures, T2 and T3 tumors require transabdominal surgery, and locally advanced cases are treated with chemoradiation and chemotherapy regimens including oxaliplatin or irinotecan.
results.answer: Treatment is based on pathologic staging: stage 1 needs no further treatment; stages 2 and 3 almost always need more treatment, such as chemoradiation, chemotherapy, or both.

results.info_summary:
Treatment strategies for rectal cancer are determined by surgical (pathologic) staging, which assesses tumor depth and lymph node involvement:

- **Stage 1**: Tumor has grown into the second or third (muscle) layer of the rectal wall. No further treatment is needed.
- **Stage 2**: Tumor has grown through the rectal wall and possibly into nearby tissues or organs. More treatment is almost always needed.
- **Stage 3**: Cancer has spread to nearby lymph nodes. More treatment is almost always needed.

For stages 2 and 3, next treatments may include chemoradiation, chemotherapy, or both. Chemotherapy is given in cycles of treatment days followed by rest days, with cycle length varying by drug. Any regimen with "OX" in the name includes oxaliplatin, which can cause nerve damage (neuropathy) to fingers and toes—symptoms include numbness, cramping, tingling, or pain. Any regimen with "IRI" contains irinotecan.

results.question: What are the primary surgical procedures used in rectal cancer, and how do they relate to tumor location and stage?
results.gold_answer: Surgical procedures for rectal cancer include polypectomy, transanal local excision for early-stage or distal tumors, transabdominal surgery for more advanced stages, low anterior resection (LAR) for mid to upper rectal tumors, and abdominoperineal resection (APR) for lower rectal tumors.

- **Polypectomy** may be used for cancers arising in polyps; if cancer isn't fully removed, resection is needed. Sessile polyps are more likely to recur and may require EUS or pelvic MRI to guide surgery.

**Risk Factors and Genetic Syndromes Linked to Rectal Cancer**

**Risk factors:**
- **Family health history:** Having a first-degree relative with colorectal cancer increases risk compared to the average person. Doctors assess family history by asking about blood relatives on both sides of the family, including the specific type of cancer, where it started, and age at diagnosis.
- **Most rectal cancers occur for unknown reasons**, though a rare subset is linked to inherited gene mutations.

**Genetic syndromes:**
- **Lynch syndrome:** A rare inherited cancer syndrome caused by inherited mutations in mismatch repair (MMR) genes. People with Lynch syndrome are at high risk of colorectal (including rectal), endometrial, and ovarian cancers. Testing for Lynch syndrome is recommended for cancers found to have the dMMR/MSI-H biomarker (mismatch repair deficient / microsatellite instability-high).
- **Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP):** A rare inherited cancer syndrome causing hundreds to thousands of polyps in the colon and rectum. Polyps begin as benign growths but can become invasive rectal cancer, often by age 50 in classic FAP. A milder form (attenuated FAP) causes fewer polyps and usually starts later in life

Treatment should involve a team of digestive health experts with experience in chemotherapy, radiation, surgery, and imaging. Everyone with anal cancer is encouraged to consider enrolling in a clinical trial for treatment if available. Anal cancer most often starts in squamous cells lining the canal that leads from the skin surface into the rectum. Cancer that forms in squamous cells is known as squamous cell carcinoma. Squamous cells are found in the tissues that form the surface of the skin and in other areas of the body. Most colorectal cancers, in contrast, start in glandular cells and are called adenocarcinomas. This difference is important in determining treatment options. Title: . Content: 927: Anal cancer starts in either the anal canal or the perianal region. The anal canal connects the rectum and the anal opening. It is about 1 and a half inches (4 centimeters) long. The anal canal is surrounded by muscles (anal sphincters) that relax to allow stool to leave the body through the anus. The perianal region includes the anal opening and the skin directly surrounding it. In some cases, an anal tumor can involve both the anal canal and the perianal skin. Risk factors A risk factor is something that increases the risk of developing a disease. Some people with no known risk factors develop anal cancer. And, some people with risk factors never get anal cancer. Risk factors for anal cancer are described next. Human papillomavirus infection The risk factor most strongly linked with anal cancer is long-term infection with human papillomavirus (HPV). HPV is a sexually transmitted virus. HPV is extremely common. It affects almost everyone who has ever been sexually active. Most people are unaware that they are–or ever were–infected. In most people, the immune system gets rid of (“clears”) HPV from the body. In some people, however, the virus causes long-term cell changes that develop into cancer

results.info_summary:
Fertility preservation options for patients undergoing rectal cancer treatment include:

- **Sperm banking (semen cryopreservation):** Freezing and storing semen for later use.
- **Egg freezing (oocyte cryopreservation):** Removing, freezing, and storing unfertilized eggs for later use.
- **Ovarian tissue banking:** Removing part or all of an ovary, freezing the egg-containing tissue, and later reimplanting it.
- **Ovarian transposition (oophoropexy):** Surgery to move one or both ovaries out of the range of the radiation beam, since rectal cancer treatment may involve external beam radiation therapy (EBRT), which damages the ovaries and stops hormone production needed for natural pregnancy.

Patients interested in future fertility should tell their care team, who will discuss fertility-related risks and may refer them for counseling about these options.

Endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD) is a recommended option for all T1 tumors. This minimally invasive procedure removes small rectal cancers in one piece, often curing them. Another name for this procedure is endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR). First, an endoscope is used to locate the tumor in the rectal wall. A tool is guided through the scope to inject fluid between the tumor and the layer of muscle beneath it. This helps lift and separate the tumor, making it easier to cut off. During this time you will have flexible sigmoidoscopy about every 6 months. The first one may be as early as 3 months after ESD. This is called transanal local excision. The surgeon cuts through all layers of the rectal wall to remove the cancer and some surrounding normal rectal tissue. Lymph nodes are not removed. Advanced techniques for removing tumors higher in the rectum include transanal endoscopic microsurgery (TEM) and transanal minimally invasive surgery (TAMIS). contexts: Title: . Content: 871: in Chapter What causes bladder cancer? Many people wonder why they got cancer. Cancer experts don’t know exactly what causes bladder cells to grow out of control. What they do know is that bladder cancer and other cancers start with abnormal changes (mutations) in the genes of cells. Genes are tiny parts of a cell that carry the instructions for how cells behave. These instructions also control how new cells are made. Sometimes, mutations can mix up these instructions. This can turn normal cells into cancer cells. In most people with bladder cancer, these mutations aren’t passed down in families (hereditary mutation). They happen on their own and only in cancer cells. Still, you may have a higher risk for bladder cancer if another family member also had bladder cancer. In rare cases, mutations in these genes can be passed down in families. This results in an increased risk of getting bladder cancer. However, only some individuals with these genetic mutations go on to develop bladder cancer. What are the risk factors for bladder cancer? A risk factor is something that increases your chance of developing a disease. Risk factors don’t necessarily cause bladder cancer. But people with bladder cancer often have one or more of these risk factors: Smoking – Smoking is the greatest risk factor for bladder cancer. It accounts for about

Title: . Content: 872:. But people with bladder cancer often have one or more of these risk factors: Smoking – Smoking is the greatest risk factor for bladder cancer. Age – The risk of bladder cancer increases as you age. Family history – Your risk increases if you or anyone in your family has had bladder cancer. Also, people with an inherited condition called Lynch syndrome have a greater risk of cancer in the urinary tract, including bladder cancer. Chemical exposure – Some chemicals used in dyes, rubber, leather, printing materials, textiles, and paint products have been linked to an increased risk for bladder cancer. Title: . Content: 869: or feeling that may signal a disease or condition. The most common symptom of bladder cancer, and the one that usually appears first, is having blood in your urine (hematuria). How does blood get into urine? Bladder tumors are likely to release a little blood, which mixes with the urine in your bladder. The blood may turn your urine pink or bright red. Or, if there isn’t enough blood to be visible, your urine may look normal. But your clinical team can still detect blood by looking at a sample of the urine under a microscope. Blood in the urine can be caused by many other things besides bladder cancer. The most common cause is an infection in the urinary tract. So anyone with blood in their urine should see a health care provider to get their urine tested. - Blood and urine tests (general health tests)
- Imaging
- Inherited cancer risk testing

Title: . Content: 914: chemotherapy? The term dose-dense refers to a method of speeding up chemotherapy by shortening the amount of time in between treatments (doses). The most common systemic chemotherapy used to treat bladder cancer is a combination of medicines known as dose-dense methotrexate, vinblastine, doxorubicin, and cisplatin (or ddMVAC). A commonly used chemotherapy for bladder cancer is cisplatin, which contains the metal platinum. Platinum-based chemotherapy medicines can be effective against bladder cancer but can also damage the kidneys. People with kidney conditions or other health issues may not be able to have chemotherapy or, if possible, may receive non-platinum chemotherapy medicine. Chemotherapy is given in a sequence of treatments called a cycle. A cycle includes a period of treatments (such as once-a-day for a few days) followed by a time of rest (several days or weeks). This treatment cycle is then repeated a few times. For example, you might have 3 to 6 cycles of chemotherapy over 2 to 3 months. Immunotherapy Immunotherapy is a type of systemic therapy that uses your immune system (your body’s natural defense against infection and disease) to find and destroy cancer cells. Checkpoint inhibitors are one type of immunotherapy used to treat bladder cancer and other cancers. Checkpoint inhibitors block the natural braking mechanisms in the body to allow your immune system to better identify and fight the cancer. The checkpoint inhibitors for bladder cancer include: Keytruda (pembrolizumab) Opdivo (nivolumab) Bavencio (avelumab) Tecentriq (atezolizumab) Targeted therapy Targeted therapy is a systemic treatment that can pick out and attack certain types of cancer cells. Targeted therapy is more often used for people with specific gene mutations. If you don’t have the mutation that the medicine “targets,” this treatment is unlikely to help. Cisplatin, a platinum-based agent, is commonly used but can damage the kidneys; non-platinum alternatives may be given to patients with kidney conditions. **Surgical Procedures and Urinary Diversion Options for Bladder Cancer**

**Surgical Procedures:**

1. **Transurethral Resection of Bladder Tumor (TURBT):** Removes tumors through the urethra without cutting into the abdomen. The urologist guides an instrument with a small cutting device through the urethra into the bladder to examine and remove the tumor from the bladder lining. It is done in an operating room under anesthesia, and the tumor can be tested for a more detailed diagnosis. TURBT is also the first step in trimodal therapy (a "bladder-preserving" approach combining TURBT, radiation, and chemotherapy), which can be used instead of radical cystectomy in certain patients.

2. **Radical Cystectomy:** The most common surgery for muscle-invasive bladder cancer. It removes the entire bladder, nearby lymph nodes, and other organs in the pelvis.

3. **Partial Cystectomy:** Removes part of the bladder. It is rarely used for bladder cancer—fewer than 1 out of 20 people with bladder cancer are eligible. It can only be done if the cancer is in a spot that can be neatly removed without taking out the whole bladder.

Bladder cancer commonly recurs even after treatment—more so than almost any other cancer—and often returns in a different place and sometimes at a more advanced stage. Because of this, patients need regular follow-up tests for many years, potentially for the rest of their lives, to check whether the cancer has returned.

Follow-up and surveillance methods include:
- **Urine cytology:** A lab test in which a pathologist examines a urine sample under a microscope for cancer or precancerous cells. A sample can be collected by urinating into a container or during cystoscopy. If abnormal cells are found, cancer may be anywhere in the urinary tract, so cystoscopy is needed to check the urethra and bladder; if no cancer is found there, imaging tests are used to examine the ureters, kidneys, or other areas.
- **Urine tests for tumor markers/biomarkers:** Tumor cells shed cancer cells, and biomarker tests can identify these specific cells. Biomarker tests may provide helpful clues but are not reliable enough to diagnose bladder cancer; they are sometimes used for surveillance in people treated for non–muscle-invasive bladder cancer.
- **Cystoscopy and biopsy**, along with **imaging**, blood tests, and urine tests, are used

results.info_summary:
**Common Symptoms from Bladder Cancer Itself:**
- Blood in the urine (most common symptom)

**Side Effects by Treatment Type:**

- **Bladder removal surgery (radical cystectomy):** bleeding, blood clots, kidney problems, infection, sexual dysfunction, incontinence, problems caused by the urinary diversion
- **Intravesical therapy:** swelling (inflammation) of the bladder lining, frequent urination, pain or burning feeling when urinating, blood in the urine, infection
- **Chemotherapy:** nausea, vomiting, extreme tiredness (fatigue), fever, infection, tingling or numbness, rash, diarrhea
- **Immunotherapy:** autoimmune reaction, fatigue, fever, nausea, loss of appetite, infection, diarrhea, constipation

**Notable Side Effects More Common in Bladder Cancer Patients (especially after surgery):**
- Sexual dysfunction (including decreased desire to have sex, possibly due to lack of energy, body self-consciousness after surgery, stress, or depression)
- Trouble controlling urine flow (urinary incontinence)

**Additional Notes:**
- Most side effects appear soon after treatment starts and go away after treatment ends; others are long-term or appear years later.
- Side effects depend on treatment type and length

analysis.current_understanding: Bladder cancer patients experience side effects and symptoms from both the disease and its treatments. The most common symptom from the cancer itself is blood in the urine. Treatment-related side effects vary by type: radical cystectomy can cause bleeding, blood clots, kidney problems, infection, sexual dysfunction, incontinence, and issues with urinary diversion; intravesical therapy can cause bladder inflammation, frequent urination, painful/burning urination, blood in urine, and infection; chemotherapy can cause nausea, vomiting, extreme fatigue, fever, infection, tingling/numbness, rash, and diarrhea; immunotherapy can cause autoimmune reactions, fatigue, fever, nausea, loss of appetite, infection, diarrhea, and constipation. Notably, sexual dysfunction and urinary incontinence are more common in bladder cancer patients, especially after surgery. Side effects often appear soon after treatment and resolve after treatment ends, but some can be long-term or appear years later, depending on treatment type and duration.

Tumor removal For bladder cancer, a surgical procedure called a resection removes the tumor but leaves the rest of the bladder in place. The full name of the procedure is called a transurethral resection of bladder tumor (TURBT, sometimes pronounced tur-bit). Even though it has a complicated name, the concept of TURBT is simple. It’s a procedure that removes tumors through the urethra without having to cut into the abdomen. The tumor can then be tested to provide a more detailed diagnosis. TURBT is done in an operating room in a clinic or hospital. You’ll be given anesthesia to put you to sleep. The urologist then guides an instrument with a small cutting device through the urethra and into the bladder. The instrument is used to examine and remove the tumor from the bladder lining. Title: . Content: 874:: Surgery Chemotherapy Immunotherapy Radiation therapy Targeted therapy Surgery, by itself or with other treatments, can be used in many stages of bladder cancer. For less advanced cancer, a minor surgical procedure can be used to remove just the tumor. For more advanced cancer, the entire bladder can be surgically removed. In addition, you may receive chemotherapy or immunotherapy directly into the bladder. For people with metastatic bladder cancer, chemotherapy or immunotherapy is used to treat cancer anywhere in the body. Another treatment option is to join a clinical trial. You’ll also receive treatment for any side effects caused by cancer therapy. Can bladder cancer be cured? Bladder cancer in an early (non-invasive) stage can usually be cured. Treatment for more advanced stage (muscle-invasive) bladder cancer can be complicated but it may still get rid of the cancer. Metastatic bladder cancer is not typically curable, but it is still treatable. And treatments are improving all the time. For most people with bladder cancer, treatment provides a longer and more comfortable life with fewer symptoms. It’s important to know that bladder cancer commonly comes back even after treatment. results.info_summary:
Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is the most common type of kidney cancer, arising in cells lining the renal tubules. RCC is classified into subtypes by histology (microscopic examination of cancer cells):

- **Clear cell RCC (ccRCC):** Most common subtype, ~7 out of 10 people with RCC; cells appear very pale or clear under a microscope.
- **Non-clear cell RCC (nccRCC):** Includes several subtypes:
  - **Papillary RCC (PRCC):** Most common nccRCC subtype, ~1 out of 10 people with RCC; tumors look like long, thin finger-like growths.
  - **Chromophobe RCC:** Cells are pale but larger than clear cells and look different.
  - **Collecting duct RCC (cdRCC):** Forms in collecting duct/tubule cells.
  - **Renal medullary carcinoma (RMC):** Found in young people of African descent with sickle cell trait, sickle cell disease, or other sickling disorders.
  - **Translocation RCC:** Diagnosed across ages but tends to occur in children/younger adults; features unique gene fusions.

Treatment decisions for renal cell carcinoma (RCC) are based on:

- Tumor size and location
- Whether cancer has metastasized to distant sites (such as lungs, lymph nodes, bones, less frequently liver and brain)
- Presence of sarcomatoid features (sRCC), which can occur in almost any RCC subtype and occurs in less than 5% of RCC tumors

results.info_summary:
**Non-clear cell RCC (nccRCC): Histological Features and Subtypes**

**Papillary RCC (PRCC):** The most common nccRCC subtype (~1 in 10 people with RCC); tumors typically appear as long, thin, finger-like growths under the microscope.

**Chromophobe RCC:** Cells are pale but larger than clear cells and look different.

**Translocation RCC:** Found at all ages but tends to be diagnosed in children or younger adults; tumors have unique gene fusions that promote cancer.

**Unclassified RCC:** Cancer cells don't look like any subtype, or more than one subtype is present.

**Rare nccRCC types:**
- **Collecting duct RCC (cdRCC):** Forms in cells of the collecting ducts or tubules.
- **Renal medullary carcinoma (RMC):** Found in young people of African descent who carry the sickle cell trait, sickle cell disease, or other diseases causing red blood cell sickling.

**Recently defined RCC types:** Clear cell papillary renal cell tumor; fumarate hydratase-deficient RCC; ELOC (formerly TCEB1)-mutated RCC.

results.info_summary:
**Main Risk Factors for Anal Cancer:**

- **HPV infection** — the risk factor most strongly linked; long-term infection with high-risk strains (especially HPV16 and HPV18) is the primary cause. Progression to cancer often occurs decades after initial infection.
- **HIV infection**
- **Immunosuppressant use** (e.g., anti-rejection medicines after organ transplant)
- **History of cervical, vulvar, or vaginal cancer or precancer**
- **History of anal precancer**
- **History of blood cancers** such as lymphoma, chronic lymphocytic leukemia, or multiple myeloma
- **Certain autoimmune disorders** (e.g., Crohn's disease)
- **Smoking**
- **History of anal sex**
- **History of sexually transmitted infection (STI)**

**Biomarkers/Precancerous Lesions:**

- **Anal dysplasia** (pre-cancerous lesions), also known as:
  - Low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (LSIL) / mild dysplasia
  - High-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL) / moderate or severe dysplasia
  - Anal intraepithelial neoplasia (AIN)

**Other Relevant Facts:**

- Most common type is **squamous cell carcinoma**

results.info_summary:
**Diagnostic methods for detection and staging of anal cancer:**

- **Digital rectal exam (DRE):** Important for diagnosis, staging, and follow-up. The physician inserts a gloved, lubricated finger into the anus and rectum to detect or assess growths/other abnormalities in the anal canal and nearby areas.
- **High-resolution anoscopy (HRA):** Typically performed after a DRE by trained colorectal surgeons/providers. A numbing gel is applied, a short hollow anoscope is inserted a few inches into the anus, acetic acid is applied to anal canal tissue, and a colposcope (special magnifying instrument) is used to examine tissues. Acetic acid makes abnormal cells appear differently; suspicious areas are biopsied.
- **MRI:** Can show how deep into the rectal wall the cancer has grown and whether it has spread to nearby lymph nodes; may also be used to determine the extent of cancer in the pelvis and to look for cancer in the abdomen, especially the liver (e.g., if contrast agent for CT can't be used). Uses magnetic field and radio waves (no radiation). A gel may be inserted into the rectum before imaging; a coil device/blanket sends signals.

Title: . Content: 927: Anal cancer starts in either the anal canal or the perianal region. The anal canal connects the rectum and the anal opening. It is about 1 and a half inches (4 centimeters) long. The anal canal is surrounded by muscles (anal sphincters) that relax to allow stool to leave the body through the anus. The perianal region includes the anal opening and the skin directly surrounding it. In some cases, an anal tumor can involve both the anal canal and the perianal skin. Risk factors A risk factor is something that increases the risk of developing a disease. Some people with no known risk factors develop anal cancer. And, some people with risk factors never get anal cancer. Risk factors for anal cancer are described next. Human papillomavirus infection The risk factor most strongly linked with anal cancer is long-term infection with human papillomavirus (HPV). HPV is a sexually transmitted virus. HPV is extremely common. It affects almost everyone who has ever been sexually active. Most people are unaware that they are–or ever were–infected. In most people, the immune system gets rid of (“clears”) HPV from the body. In some people, however, the virus causes long-term cell changes that develop into cancer

results.question: How is anal cancer staged, and what do the different stages represent?
results.gold_answer: Anal cancer is staged using the AJCC TNM system, with Stage 0 as carcinoma in situ or anal dysplasia, Stage I for tumors ≤2 cm without spread, Stage II for tumors >2 cm without spread, Stage III indicating lymph node involvement or local invasion, and Stage IV representing distant metastasis.

results.question: What are the standard treatment approaches for non-metastatic and metastatic anal cancer?
results.gold_answer: Non-metastatic anal cancers (Stages I-III) are primarily treated with chemoradiation using IMRT or EBRT and regimens such as mitomycin with capecitabine or 5-FU, while metastatic (Stage IV) disease is managed with systemic chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and palliative radiation.
results.answer: Chemoradiation (mitomycin + capecitabine or 5-FU; or 5-FU + cisplatin) with IMRT for non-metastatic; systemic chemotherapy for metastatic.

results.info_summary:
**Surgical Procedures for Anal Cancer Management:**

1. **Local Excision** – An option for some early-stage, low-risk perianal cancers (certain stage I and IIA cases). It involves removing only the tumor and a small margin of surrounding tissue. Eligibility depends on the cancer not having invaded the sphincter muscle and on tumor grade (lower grade = better candidate). Most perianal cancers, however, are treated with chemoradiation rather than surgery.

2. **Abdominoperineal Resection (APR)** – A radical surgery indicated when cancer does not respond to initial chemoradiation or when cancer recurs in the anus after a cancer-free period. It requires incisions in both the abdomen and perineum and typically removes the anus, rectum, the rectosigmoid junction, and fatty tissue surrounding the rectum, necessitating a permanent colostomy. If groin lymph nodes are known to contain cancer, they are removed during a **groin dissection**.

3. **Muscle Flap Reconstruction** – May accompany APR because prior radiation weakens/damages the perineum and can interfere with healing; the flap provides healthy tissue to support reconstruction.

(1) Local excision is indicated for some early-stage, low-risk perianal cancers (certain stage I and IIA cases) where the cancer has not invaded the sphincter muscle and the tumor grade is lower. (2) Abdominoperineal resection (APR) is indicated when cancer does not respond to initial chemoradiation or recurs in the anus after a cancer-free period; it removes the anus, rectum, rectosigmoid junction, and surrounding fatty tissue, requiring a permanent colostomy, and may include groin dissection if groin lymph nodes contain cancer. (3) Muscle flap reconstruction may accompany APR because prior radiation weakens the perineum and impairs healing, providing healthy tissue for reconstruction. Most perianal cancers are treated with chemoradiation rather than surgery.

results.info_summary:
Anal cancer treatment—especially radiation therapy, and in some cases chemotherapy—can cause infertility by damaging the ovaries, sperm, or eggs. Radiation can also cause premature ovarian insufficiency (POI) or radiation-induced premature menopause, and may lead to vaginal stenosis (narrowing/shortening of the vagina, pain during sex and pelvic exams).

Fertility preservation options include:
- Sperm banking (semen cryopreservation)
- Egg freezing (oocyte cryopreservation)
- Ovarian tissue banking (removing part or all of an ovary, freezing egg-containing tissue, and later reimplanting it)
- Ovarian transposition (oophoropexy)—moving the ovaries/fallopian tubes out of the radiation beam

Patients of childbearing age should tell their doctor if they want children after treatment or are unsure, and may be referred for fertility preservation counseling. NCCN Guidelines for Patients recommend that patients play an active role in their care by asking questions and making shared decisions with their care team.

results.info_summary:
Recurrences of anal cancer are managed based on the site of recurrence:

- **If cancer returns to the anus (or is locally progressive/non-metastatic):** Surgery to remove the anus—abdominoperineal resection (APR)—is recommended. APR removes the anus, rectum, the area where the rectum and colon meet, and surrounding fatty tissue, and may include groin lymph node removal (groin dissection) if nodes have cancer. Radiation damage to the perineum can impair healing, sometimes requiring muscle flap reconstruction. Before surgery, doctors may recommend trying immunotherapy with an immune checkpoint inhibitor; in some patients this worked well enough that surgery was not needed, though research on this approach is limited.

- **If cancer returns to lymph nodes in the groin (but not the anal area) and radiation was part of initial treatment:** Groin dissection and/or chemotherapy is recommended.

- **If cancer returns to distant areas (e.g., liver or lungs) — metastatic disease:** Treated with chemotherapy; if it does not respond or worsens, immunotherapy with an immune checkpoint inhibitor is recommended if eligible.

results.info_summary:
**Diagnostic methods for ALL:**
- Blood tests (general health tests)
- Bone marrow tests (bone marrow aspiration/biopsy) — diagnosis generally requires **20% or more lymphoblasts** in the bone marrow (at least 1 of every 5 marrow cells); in certain cases, diagnosis is possible with **less than 20%** lymphoblasts
- Lumbar puncture (to assess central nervous system involvement)
- Imaging tests
- Heart tests
- Fertility testing (all genders)
- Testing for biomarker and genetic changes, including pharmacogenomic testing and B-ALL risk group classification

**Common sites of involvement:**
- Bone marrow
- Blood
- Organs such as the **testicles** and the **central nervous system (CNS)**

**Key context:** ALL is a fast-growing blood cancer starting in lymphocytes (disease-fighting white blood cells); bone marrow produces too many immature lymphocytes called lymphoblasts, which crowd out other blood cells. The 2 main types are **B-cell (B-ALL)** and **T-cell (T-ALL)**.

results.question: How are the subtypes of ALL classified and what are their distinguishing features?
results.gold_answer: ALL is classified into B-cell ALL and T-cell ALL, with B-ALL starting in B-cell lymphocytes and being more common, while T-ALL arises from T-cell lymphocytes and may cause an enlarged thymus; mature B-cell ALL (Burkitt leukemia) and lymphoblastic lymphomas are notable subtypes with specific sites of growth.

The new information provided focuses on general cancer care guidance, clinical trials, and patient advocacy—none of which relates to the classification or distinguishing features of ALL subtypes. Therefore, the existing summary remains accurate and complete, and no changes are warranted.

**Refined summary:**

ALL has 2 main types: B-cell (B-ALL) and T-cell (T-ALL). Within each type are several subtypes, classified mainly by: (1) the type of lymphocyte (B cell or T cell) in the leukemia cells and how mature the cells are (the immunophenotype), and (2) specific gene or chromosome changes. B-ALL starts in B-cell lymphocytes and is more common than T-ALL; a rare subtype is mature B-cell ALL (Burkitt leukemia), which is essentially the same as Burkitt lymphoma but treated differently from B-ALL. When B-cell lymphoblasts grow mostly in lymph nodes instead of bone marrow, it is called B-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma (B-LL or B-LBL). T-ALL starts in T-cell lymphocytes and can cause an enlarged thymus, sometimes leading to breathing problems.

results.info_summary:
**Summary: Standard Treatment Approaches for ALL and Variations by Subtype/Prognostic Group**

General treatment: All patients with ALL are treated with steroids and multiagent chemotherapy; other types of systemic therapy may also be given. Treatment options are categorized as preferred therapies, other recommended therapies, and therapies used in certain cases.

Subtype-specific approaches:
- **BCR::ABL1-negative or BCR::ABL1-like B-ALL** (most common type of B-ALL): A clinical trial is the preferred treatment.
- **BCR::ABL1-positive B-ALL**: Treatment aims to stop the activity of the BCR::ABL protein caused by the BCR::ABL1 gene; usually an intensive combination of systemic therapies.
- **T-ALL** (less common than B-ALL; starts in T-cell lymphocytes): Treatment options include a clinical trial or chemotherapy.
- **Infant ALL** (infants under 12 months of age): Treatment is different than for other age groups.

Additional considerations:
- Clinical trials are voluntary, and patients may seek treatment outside a trial at any time. If standard treatment has already started, eligibility for certain trials may be affected. Placebos are almost never used alone

Additional considerations about clinical trials and placebos are also included. However, the information lacks details on other prognostic groups (e.g., by age, white blood cell count, cytogenetics, minimal residual disease) and specific treatment regimens (e.g., induction, consolidation, maintenance, CNS prophylaxis, stem cell transplant indications). results.info_summary:
**Refined summary:**

Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is a fast-growing blood cancer that starts in lymphocytes (disease-fighting white blood cells of the immune system). It is the most common cancer diagnosed in children. In ALL, the bone marrow makes too many immature lymphocytes called lymphoblasts, which crowd out normal bone marrow and other blood cells, leading to reduced blood production and blood that does not work as it should. ALL is thought to arise from stem cells that produce an increased amount of lymphoid progenitor cells. There are 2 main types: B-cell (B-ALL) and T-cell. Diagnosis generally requires 20% or more lymphoblasts in the bone marrow (at least 1 in 5 marrow cells), though in certain cases diagnosis is possible with less than 20%. ALL can be found in bone marrow, blood, and organs such as the testicles or central nervous system (CNS). Treatment depends on the type of ALL, age at diagnosis, and other factors; everyone with ALL is treated with steroids and multiagent chemotherapy, and a clinical trial is the preferred treatment for BCR::ABL1-negative or BCR::ABL1-like B-ALL.

results.info_summary:
**Follow-Up and Surveillance After Initial Treatment**

**Initial follow-up exam:** 8–12 weeks after completing chemoradiation, with DRE (and possibly imaging) to assess treatment results. Cancer is categorized as complete remission, persistent disease, or progressive disease.

**Surveillance during complete remission:**
- **DRE:** every 3–6 months for 5 years
- **Inguinal lymph node exams:** every 3–6 months for 5 years
- **Anoscopy:** every 6–12 months for 3 years (may be omitted or done less often if radiation causes pain/discomfort)
- **Imaging (stage II and III):** every year for 3 years — CT of chest, abdomen, and pelvis with contrast, OR CT of chest without contrast plus MRI of abdomen and pelvis with contrast

**Persistent disease:** May be safe to monitor up to 6 months after treatment to see if cancer improves; this may avoid surgery to remove the anus. If remission occurs, standard surveillance begins.

**Progressive disease:** Biopsy performed to confirm; then treatment as below.

**Recurrence/treatment failure:** APR surgery (removes anus, creates permanent colostomy).

For patients in complete remission, surveillance includes DRE and inguinal lymph node exams every 3–6 months for 5 years, anoscopy every 6–12 months for 3 years (may be omitted or less frequent if radiation causes pain/discomfort), and for stage II and III, imaging every year for 3 years with either CT of chest, abdomen, and pelvis with contrast, or CT of chest without contrast plus MRI of abdomen and pelvis with contrast. For persistent disease, it may be safe to monitor up to 6 months after treatment to see if cancer improves, possibly avoiding surgery; if remission occurs, standard surveillance begins. For progressive disease, a biopsy is performed to confirm, then treatment as below. For recurrence or treatment failure, APR surgery (removes anus, creates permanent colostomy) is indicated.

Clinical trials play a key role in treating specific ALL subtypes:

Title: . Content: 389: cancer affects cell growth. Pancreatic cancer cells make many new cancer cells and do not die when they should. The overgrowth of pancreatic cancer cells becomes a mass called a tumor. Pancreatic cancer cells also don’t stay in place and may grow into nearby body tissue. They may break away from a tumor, spread to other areas, and form more tumors. There are 2 main types of pancreatic cancer The more common type of pancreatic cancer forms from exocrine cells. Exocrine cells make and move digestive enzymes. Pancreatic adenocarcinomas form from exocrine cells that line the tube-like ducts of the pancreas. They are also called pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) and are the focus of this book. Pancreas Sounds like PAN-kree-us. The pancreas is deep inside the body. It sits just below the liver and behind the stomach. In adults, the pancreas is about 6 inches long. Less often, pancreatic cancer forms from endocrine cells. Endocrine cells make hormones. results.info_summary: PDAC (pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma) forms from exocrine cells lining the pancreas ducts. Early stages have no tell-tale signs; symptoms may overlap with other conditions. Providers may suspect it based on symptoms such as jaundice (yellowed skin or eyes). X-ray signs include wider-than-normal pancreatic ducts or an inflamed pancreas. Diagnosis requires a series of tests: imaging (key for staging and deciding surgery eligibility), endoscopic tests, biopsy, blood tests, genetic tests for inherited mutations, and biomarker tests for profiling. A multidisciplinary consult reviews medical history and prior tests. Testing can also reveal unique cancer features with specific treatments.

results.question: Which risk factors and hereditary syndromes are associated with increased risk of pancreatic cancer?

Many people with cancer wonder how they got it. Experts don’t know exactly what causes pancreatic cells to become cancer cells. But they do know several factors that increase the chance of developing pancreatic cancer. Such risk factors include: Lifestyle factors, such as smoking tobacco, heavy alcohol use, and a less healthy diet Major contact with cancer-causing chemicals, such as pesticides Health conditions, such as diabetes and chronic inflammation of the pancreas Close blood relatives with pancreatic, breast, ovarian, or colorectal cancers or melanoma About 1 in 10 pancreatic cancers are hereditary. This means that a higher risk was passed down to you by your parents through your genes. The genetic cause of hereditary pancreatic cancer is unknown in most families. results.info_summary:
**Risk Factors for Pancreatic Cancer:**
- Lifestyle: smoking tobacco, heavy alcohol use, less healthy diet
- Environmental: major contact with cancer-causing chemicals (e.g., pesticides)
- Health conditions: diabetes, chronic inflammation of the pancreas
- Family history: close blood relatives with pancreatic, breast, ovarian, or colorectal cancers, or melanoma

**Hereditary Factors:**
- About 1 in 10 pancreatic cancers are hereditary (genetic cause unknown in most families)
- Hereditary syndromes that increase risk:
  - Hereditary breast-ovarian cancer syndrome (HBOC)
  - Peutz-Jeghers syndrome
  - Lynch syndrome
  - Li-Fraumeni syndrome
  - Familial malignant melanoma syndrome (melanoma-pancreatic cancer syndrome / familial atypical multiple mole melanoma [FAMMM] syndrome)
  - Hereditary pancreatitis

Genetic tests can detect genes linked to these hereditary conditions.

results.question: How are the stages of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma defined and what is the significance of Stage IV disease?
results.gold_answer: The stages of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma range from Stage 0, confined to the duct wall, to Stage IV, which is characterized by distant metastasis to organs such as the liver, lungs, or abdominal lining and is also known as metastatic pancreatic cancer.
results.answer: Staging runs from 0 to IV based on tumor size and spread. Stage IV is metastatic disease, generally not curable with surgery.

results.info_summary: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) arises from the exocrine cells lining the pancreatic ducts. Staging runs from 0 to IV (0–4 or Roman numerals I–IV) and is based on tumor size and the extent of spread. Stage 0 is confined to the innermost layer of the duct wall. Stage I is a tumor ≤4 cm that has not spread outside the pancreas. Stage II is a tumor >4 cm or spread to 1–3 nearby lymph nodes. Stage III has grown through the pancreas into nearby major arteries (e.g., the celiac axis) or has spread to 4 or more lymph nodes. Stage IV is metastatic disease, with cancer having spread far from the pancreas—commonly to the liver, lungs, or the lining of the abdomen. Stage IV is significant because most pancreatic cancers are already metastatic at diagnosis, and this stage is generally not curable with surgery. Reflecting this, initial treatment for PDAC is usually not planned mainly by the five stages; a different system is used for non-metastatic cancers. Surgery may be an option for some patients with Stage I, II, or III disease, but for most people with pancreatic cancer surgery is not the best treatment

results.info_summary:
Genetic testing and biomarker testing are part of the series of tests used to identify pancreatic cancer and make a treatment plan.

**Genetic testing** looks for inherited mutations (germline mutations). About 1 in 10 pancreatic cancers are hereditary—meaning a higher risk was passed down through genes. Known hereditary conditions that increase pancreatic cancer risk include HBOC, Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, Lynch syndrome, Li-Fraumeni syndrome, and familial malignant melanoma syndrome. A family history—the health history of blood relatives on both sides of the family, including specific cancer types, where the cancer started, and age at diagnosis—helps determine which treatment is best.

**Biomarker testing** (also called molecular testing, tumor profiling, tumor sequencing, gene expression profiling, or genomic testing) is performed on a biopsy sample to look for specific DNA mutations/alterations, protein levels, or other molecular features. Testing is done case-by-case and may lengthen the time for biopsy results. Testing can show whether the cancer has unique features for which there is specific treatment, helping guide the treatment plan.

Biomarker testing (also called molecular testing, tumor profiling, etc.) is performed on a biopsy sample to detect specific DNA mutations, protein levels, or other molecular features. It is done case-by-case and can identify unique cancer features that may have targeted treatments. Together, these tests help diagnose pancreatic cancer, assess individual risk, and inform treatment planning. Patients can also actively participate in shared decision-making with their care team.

**Diagnostic Methods and Biomarkers for Prostate Cancer Across Stages**

**Screening/Initial Detection:**
- **PSA (prostate-specific antigen) test** – elevated PSA in the bloodstream may indicate prostate cancer; a key biomarker.
- **Digital rectal exam (DRE)** – simplest way to assess prostate size and texture.
- Additional inputs: blood or urine tests, plus factors like family history, race, and age.

**Diagnostic Testing (if screening suggests cancer):**
- **Biopsy** – confirms diagnosis by removing cell/tissue samples. Imaging may be used before (to determine necessity), during (to guide removal), or after (to assess size/location for treatment planning).

analysis.current_understanding: Prostate cancer diagnosis and biomarker use vary by stage. For screening/initial detection, the primary methods are the PSA blood test (a key biomarker) and digital rectal exam (DRE), along with additional blood/urine tests and risk factors like family history, race, and age. **Summary: Symptoms of Advanced and Metastatic Prostate Cancer**

Advanced-stage (metastatic) prostate cancer has grown outside the prostate and may spread to lymph nodes, bones, liver, lungs, and other organs. Symptoms are more common in advanced disease (early-stage prostate cancer often shows no symptoms). Symptoms, if they occur, can include:

- Blood in the urine or semen
- Burning or pain while urinating
- Unexplained weight loss
- Bone, hip, or back pain

Note: These symptoms overlap with benign prostatic hyperplasia (enlarged prostate), so they are not exclusive to cancer.

analysis.current_understanding: Molecular biomarker and genetic testing play distinct but complementary roles in prostate cancer management. Germline (hereditary) testing uses blood, urine, or saliva to detect inherited mutations (e.g., BRCA1, BRCA2, ATM, CHEK2) present in every cell. It is recommended for patients with specific family histories, high-risk/very-high-risk/regional/metastatic disease regardless of family history, Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry, or other cancers. A genetic counselor helps decide whether to test and interpret results, which may also have implications for family members. Molecular biomarker testing (also called genomic testing, tumor profiling, or molecular tumor testing) examines the molecular components of a biopsy sample to assess how likely the cancer is to spread. It can be considered for localized, regional, or metastatic prostate cancer, and its main purpose is to determine whether a patient has lower- or higher-risk prostate cancer, helping lower-risk patients avoid or delay treatment and its side effects, while giving higher-risk patients a head start on treatment. These results are combined with other tests such as PSA.

results.question: How does the staging of prostate cancer affect diagnostic and imaging strategies?

Staging of prostate cancer significantly influences diagnostic and imaging strategies:

- **Early-stage/low-risk prostate cancer:** Imaging may not be needed if PSA, digital rectal exam, and biopsy results indicate low risk of metastasis. PSMA/PET imaging may also not be necessary at initial diagnosis for early-stage patients.
- **Advanced-stage prostate cancer:** Imaging becomes essential to detect spread (metastasis). Advanced-stage disease is usually life-long, and imaging helps plan treatment, monitor treatment effectiveness, and detect recurrence.

**Imaging methods** include MRI, CT, PET, ultrasound, bone scan, or combinations:
- **MRI:** Provides detailed view of cancer within the prostate; detects spread to nearby lymph nodes or pelvic bones. May be used before biopsy to target suspicious areas or after diagnosis to assess advancement outside the prostate.
- **PSMA/PET:** Especially useful for detecting spread to nearby lymph nodes or distant metastasis; also monitors recurrence after treatment.
- **Bone scan:** Detects spread to bones; used if bone pain, high risk for bone metastases, or certain test result changes; also monitors treatment.
- **PET/CT:** Combines scans to identify cancer in prostate and spread to pelvic lymph nodes.

analysis.current_understanding: Staging of prostate cancer affects diagnostic and imaging strategies in several ways. For early-stage/low-risk prostate cancer, imaging may not be needed if PSA, digital rectal exam, and biopsy results indicate low risk of metastasis, and PSMA/PET imaging may not be necessary at initial diagnosis. For advanced-stage prostate cancer, imaging becomes essential to detect metastasis, plan treatment, monitor treatment effectiveness, and detect recurrence. Imaging methods include MRI (provides detailed view of cancer within the prostate and detects spread to nearby lymph nodes or pelvic bones, used before biopsy to target suspicious areas or after diagnosis to assess advancement), PSMA/PET (especially useful for detecting spread to nearby lymph nodes or distant metastasis and monitoring recurrence after treatment), bone scan (detects spread to bones, used if bone pain, high risk for bone metastases, or certain test result changes, and monitors treatment), and PET/CT (combines scans to identify cancer in prostate and spread to pelvic lymph nodes). The timing of imaging relative to biopsy is also influenced by staging, though the available information appears to be cut off on this specific point.

results.info_summary: Adrenal tumors are categorized as benign, functional, or malignant. **Adenoma (adrenocortical adenoma)** is the most common type—noncancerous, and can be functioning or nonfunctioning; small/non-hormone-producing adenomas may need no treatment. Functional benign tumors can produce hormones: an **aldosteronoma** produces excess aldosterone, and a cortisol-producing adenoma causes **Cushing syndrome**. **Adrenocortical carcinoma (ACC)** is the most common adrenal gland cancer but very rare (1–2 per 1 million people); it starts in the adrenal cortex and can be functioning (possibly producing more than one hormone) or nonfunctioning. **Neuroblastoma** is a rare cancerous tumor affecting children ages 5 and under (mostly infants) and can spread to bones. **Pheochromocytoma** begins in the adrenal medulla, causes high blood pressure, headache, rapid heartbeat, and sweating; most are benign but can be cancerous. Malignant adrenal tumors are rare (~300–500 diagnoses/year); benign tumors do not metastasize.

results.question: What are the key symptoms and hormone-related syndromes associated with adrenocortical carcinoma and functional adrenal tumors?
results.gold_answer: Adrenocortical carcinoma may cause symptoms such as weight gain, muscle weakness, stretch marks, hormonal changes, and loss of appetite, while functional adrenal tumors can lead to hormone excess syndromes like Cushing syndrome from cortisol-producing adenomas and excess aldosterone from aldosteronoma.

results.info_summary:
**Summary: Symptoms and Hormone-Related Syndromes in Adrenocortical Carcinoma and Functional Adrenal Tumors**

**Adrenocortical Carcinoma (ACC):**
- Rare adrenal cortex cancer (~1–2 per 1 million people); most common adrenal gland cancer but very rare (~300–500 diagnoses/year).
- Can be functioning (hormone-producing) or nonfunctioning; functioning tumors may produce more than one hormone.
- About half of patients have symptoms caused by tumor-produced hormones; others have symptoms from tumor pressing on nearby organs.
- Symptoms include: weight gain, muscle weakness, pink/purple stretch marks on skin, hormonal changes (excess facial hair, hair loss on head, irregular periods, enlarged breast tissue, shrinking testicles), nausea, vomiting, abdominal bloating, back pain, fever, loss of appetite, and unintended weight loss.

**Functional Adrenal Tumors:**
- Usually benign but can produce hormones and cause hormone-related symptoms.
- **Aldosteronoma:** Adenoma producing excess aldosterone.
- **Cortisol-producing adenoma:** Causes **Cushing syndrome** (excess cortisol/stress hormone).

results.question: Which diagnostic methods are commonly used to evaluate adrenal tumors and what is their purpose?
results.gold_answer: Adrenal tumors are commonly evaluated using imaging tests such as CT scan, MRI scan, PET scan, FDG-PET/CT, and SSTR-PET/CT, as well as blood and biochemical tests to detect hormone secretion, with genetic testing and biopsy also used for diagnosis.

Types of PET scans that can be helpful for those with adrenal tumors include FDG-PET and SSTRPET. FDG-PET/CT scan An FDG-PET scan uses a radioactive type of sugar (18-fluorodeoxyglucose) as its tracer. Active cancer cells use sugar faster than normal cells. This will make the cells look brighter in pictures. Many adrenal tumors are not fast-growing and not very bright on FDG-PET scans. FDG-PET scans can help determine if neuroendocrine tumors are becoming more aggressive. SSTR-PET/CT scan A somatostatin receptor (SSTR) antagonist is a protein found on the surface of cells that bind to a hormone called somatostatin. Somatostatin helps to control other hormones in the body. SSTRs are found on many different types of cells. A SSTR-PET uses a tracer that binds to these SSTRs. results.question: How do the symptoms and diagnostic approaches differ between pheochromocytoma and adrenocortical carcinoma?
results.gold_answer: Pheochromocytoma typically presents with high blood pressure, headache, rapid heartbeat, and sweating, and is diagnosed using CT scan, MRI scan, and biochemical tests, whereas adrenocortical carcinoma presents with a broader range of symptoms including hormonal changes and is diagnosed with a wider array of imaging, blood, genetic, and biopsy tests.
results.answer: Pheochromocytoma: medulla; hypertension, headache, palpitations, sweating; diagnosed by metanephrines/catecholamines. ACC: cortex; hormonal or mass effects; diagnosed by imaging, hormone tests, biopsy.

results.info_summary:
Patients with adrenal cancer may experience symptoms from two main origins: hormones produced by the tumor or tumor growth pressing on nearby organs.

**Hormone-related symptoms** (occur in about half of patients):
- Weight gain
- Muscle weakness
- Pink or purple stretch marks on the skin
- Hormonal changes such as excess facial hair, hair loss on the head, irregular periods, enlarged breast tissue, and shrinking testicles

**Symptoms from tumor size/pressure on nearby organs:**
- Nausea
- Vomiting
- Abdominal bloating
- Back pain
- Fever
- Loss of appetite
- Loss of weight without trying

Note: Adrenal tumors often do not cause symptoms and may be found incidentally through imaging tests such as CT or MRI. Functional tumors can produce hormones (e.g., excess cortisol causing Cushing syndrome, or excess aldosterone from an aldosteronoma). Pheochromocytoma, which begins in the adrenal medulla, is characterized by high blood pressure, headache, rapid heartbeat, and sweating.

Breast cancer subtypes are defined by the type of epithelial cells in the terminal duct lobular units (TDLUs) from which the cancer arises. Almost all breast cancers are carcinomas—cancers starting in cells lining inner or outer body surfaces. The most common types are:

- **Ductal carcinoma**: starts in the cells lining the milk ducts; it is the most common type of breast cancer.
- **Lobular carcinoma**: starts in the lobules (milk glands) of the breast.

**Distinguishing clinical/pathological features:**
- Breast cancer arises from epithelial cells in the TDLUs and can spread into surrounding tissue.
- **Invasive breast cancer**: has grown outside the ducts or lobules into surrounding breast tissue or nearby lymph nodes.
- **Metastatic breast cancer (MBC)**: has spread outside the breast and lymph nodes (e.g., axillary lymph nodes); MBC can occur even when axillary lymph nodes do not contain cancer.
- Breast cancer occurs more frequently in persons assigned female at birth, but anyone can develop it, including those assigned male at birth; treatment is very similar across genders.

**Key Biomarkers and Genetic Alterations in Breast Cancer Diagnosis and Targeted Therapy:**

- **Hormone receptor status:** Biopsy samples are tested for estrogen and progesterone receptors to guide endocrine therapy selection.
- **HER2 status:** Human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) is assessed as part of standard biomarker testing to determine eligibility for HER2-targeted therapies.
- **Biomarker testing** (also called molecular testing, tumor profiling, tumor sequencing, gene expression profiling, or genomic testing) analyzes tumor DNA mutations/alterations, protein levels, and other molecular features to guide treatment selection.
- **Tumor mutation testing:** Identifies specific somatic DNA mutations in cancer cells (distinct from inherited germline testing). Certain mutations such as **PIK3CA** can be targeted with specific therapies.
- **Tumor mutational burden-high (TMB-H):** Defined as ≥10 mutations per million base pairs of tumor DNA; predicts response to immune checkpoint inhibitors targeting **PD-1** and **PD-L1**.
- **MSI-H/dMMR:** Microsatellite instability-high/deficient mismatch repair is a relevant biomarker for immunotherapy response.
- **Tumor markers (blood/tissue proteins):** CEA

results.question: How does the stage of breast cancer influence treatment options and management strategies?
results.gold_answer: Breast cancer stage determines treatment approaches: Stage 0 (DCIS) is managed with surgery and radiation; Stages I-III (invasive) involve surgery, radiation, chemotherapy, endocrine, HER2-targeted, and immunotherapy; Stage IV (metastatic) emphasizes systemic therapies, targeted agents, and palliative interventions.

results.info_summary:
Breast cancer staging determines the extent of cancer and is essential for predicting prognosis (the likely course of the disease) and making treatment decisions. The AJCC TNM system stages cancer based on tumor size/extent (T), lymph node status (N), and metastasis (M), and also incorporates hormone receptor (ER/PR) and HER2 status, plus tumor grade. Grade describes how abnormal the tumor cells look under a microscope (histology). Regional lymph nodes are found near the breast.

Stages range from 0 to IV. Stage 0 (DCIS) is noninvasive, confined to ducts (Tis, N0, M0). Stages I–III are invasive; cancer has grown outside ducts/lobules or breast skin and may involve nearby (regional) axillary lymph nodes. Stage III is sometimes called advanced disease. Stage IV is metastatic, meaning cancer has spread to distant sites (most commonly bone and lung); it can develop from earlier stages or be diagnosed de novo.

- Additional considerations apply to special populations: those who are pregnant or lactating, and transgender individuals.

results.info_summary:
**Summary: Clinical Significance and Assessment of Tumor Grade in Breast Cancer**

**Significance:**
- Tumor grade describes how abnormal the tumor cells look under a microscope (histology).
- Higher-grade cancers tend to grow and spread faster than lower-grade cancers.
- A low-grade tumor has a low risk of recurrence; a high-grade tumor has a higher risk of recurrence (cancer returning).
- Grade is included in prognostic staging (along with anatomic TNM and biomarker status such as HER2, ER, and PR) to help predict prognosis and guide treatment decisions.

**Assessment/Grading Scale:**
- GX – Grade cannot be determined
- G1 – Low grade
- G2 – Intermediate grade
- G3 – High grade (highest grade for breast cancers)

**Additional Context:**
- Grade is determined from a biopsy sample of the tumor, tested alongside ER status, PR status, and HER2 status.
- Staging (including grade) is often done twice—before surgery (clinical stage, cTNM) and after surgery (pathologic/surgical stage, pTNM)—with post-surgery staging providing more specific and accurate details.

**Summary: Systemic Therapies for Breast Cancer and Their Indications**

**Definition:** Systemic therapy is drug therapy that works throughout the body. It is broader than "chemotherapy" and includes chemotherapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and endocrine (hormone) therapy, among others.

**Main Types of Systemic Therapy and Indications:**

1. **Chemotherapy** – Kills fast-dividing cells throughout the body. May be a single agent or a multi-agent (combination) regimen, given in cycles of treatment days followed by rest days to allow the body to recover; cycle length, treatment days per cycle, and total cycles vary by drug. Examples of antimetabolites: gemcitabine (Gemzar, Infugem) and methotrexate. Most often used for inflammatory breast cancer (often multi-agent). Patient presents with a suspicious lesion on the left cheek. Key risk factors include significant sun exposure, fair skin, and a personal history of skin cancer. **Consult Summary: Suspected Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC) — Facial Lesion**

**Overview/Epidemiology**
- BCC is the most common skin cancer; ~3 million cases diagnosed annually in the US.
- Rarely metastasizes; highly treatable and curable if caught early. Most common treatment is surgery; radiation or systemic therapy may be used in some cases.

**Risk Factors**
- UV radiation exposure (sun, tanning beds) — damages basal cell DNA, causing uncontrolled growth.
- Fair skin, red/blond hair, light eye color (less melanin protection).
- Increasing age (cumulative sun exposure); however, incidence is rising in younger people.
- Personal or family history of skin cancer.
- Prior radiation therapy, especially at a young age.
- Immune suppression (organ transplant, autoimmune disease).

**Clinical Presentation**
- Typically arises in sun-exposed areas: face, head, neck, arms, legs, trunk (can occur anywhere).
- In lighter skin: flat pale/yellow scar-like areas; red itchy patches; small pink/red shiny bumps possibly with blue/brown/black areas; non-healing open sores that bleed or recur.

**Summary: Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC) – Key Facts for Patient Letter**

**What it is:** BCC is the most common type of skin cancer, with about 3 million cases diagnosed yearly in the United States. It occurs when basal cells in the skin's top layer (epidermis) become abnormal and grow out of control. It usually develops in sun-exposed areas (face, head, neck, arms, legs, trunk) but can occur anywhere. It rarely metastasizes (spreads), so if caught early it is highly treatable and curable in most cases.

**Causes/Risk Factors:**
- Caused by exposure to UV radiation from the sun or indoor tanning (booths, beds), which damages DNA in basal skin cells; frequent tanning and sunburns increase risk
- Fair skin, red or blond hair, or light eye color (less melanin to filter UV rays)
- Age (risk increases as sun exposure builds over time; increasingly common in younger people)
- Personal or family history of skin cancer
- Prior radiation therapy, especially at a young age
- Immune suppression (organ transplants, autoimmune diseases)
- Outdoor workers and people with years of cumulative sun exposure

We are observing a rise in basal cell carcinoma (BCC), the most common type of skin cancer, especially among older adults with fair skin and light-colored eyes or hair. results.question: Imagine you are a neuro-oncology fellow. Write a detailed initial diagnostic workup and staging plan for a 62-year-old patient presenting with progressive leg weakness, memory problems, and blurry vision, suspected of having primary CNS lymphoma. Your plan should outline all relevant assessments and justify their use.
results.gold_answer:
For a 62-year-old patient presenting with progressive leg weakness, memory problems, and blurry vision, the initial diagnostic workup for suspected primary CNS lymphoma should include:

1. Neurological examination to assess the extent of neurological deficits and establish a clinical baseline.
2. MRI of the brain with gadolinium contrast as the most sensitive imaging modality to identify CNS lesions characteristic of lymphoma.
3. Eye examination using slit lamp and potentially vitrectomy if ocular involvement is suspected, given the blurry vision.
4. Stereotactic biopsy of the brain lesion to obtain histopathologic confirmation, as this is the standard diagnostic procedure.
5. Laboratory assessments including complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) levels, and HIV and hepatitis B testing to evaluate for risk factors and baseline organ function.
6. Lumbar puncture to analyze cerebrospinal fluid for malignant cells, especially given the possibility of CSF involvement in primary CNS lymphoma.
7. Performance status evaluation to guide further diagnostic and treatment decisions.
This comprehensive approach ensures accurate diagnosis, detection of disease extent (including possible eye and CSF involvement), and risk factor assessment to inform treatment planning.
results.answer: MRI, stereotactic biopsy.

results.question: As a hematologist, develop a comprehensive induction and consolidation treatment plan for a newly diagnosed immunocompetent adult with primary CNS lymphoma confined to the brain. The plan should detail drug regimens, rationale, and supportive care measures.
results.gold_answer:
For an immunocompetent adult with newly diagnosed primary CNS lymphoma confined to the brain, the treatment plan consists of:

Induction Phase: Initiate high-dose methotrexate-based chemotherapy, as this is the mainstay of induction for primary CNS lymphoma. Combine with rituximab, the primary immunotherapy agent, to enhance response. Consider adding agents such as temozolomide or vincristine as per protocol and patient tolerance. Supportive corticosteroids may be used to reduce cerebral edema and symptoms.

Consolidation Phase: Upon achieving remission or maximal response, proceed to consolidation with whole-brain radiation therapy (WBRT), which is the most commonly used radiation technique in this context. Alternatively, high-dose chemotherapy followed by hematopoietic stem cell rescue may be considered based on patient performance status and institutional protocols.

Throughout treatment, provide supportive care to manage symptoms and treatment side effects, involving a multidisciplinary team as needed. Monitor performance status regularly to adjust therapy and consider clinical trial participation if available.
results.answer: HD-MTX + rituximab–based induction, then consolidation.

**Summary: Induction and Consolidation for Newly Diagnosed Primary CNS Lymphoma (Confined to Brain)**

**General approach:** Treatment is a two-step process—induction (eliminate lymphoma cells) followed by consolidation (destroy residual cells, prevent recurrence). A multidisciplinary team should be involved, and clinical trial enrollment is recommended for everyone. If a trial is unavailable or declined, standard induction is high-dose methotrexate (HD-MTX)–based chemotherapy. - Recommended regimen: **High-dose methotrexate (HD-MTX)**, often combined with **rituximab** (the main immunotherapy drug for PCNSL) and other chemotherapies.
- Rationale: Methotrexate is the most effective drug for PCNSL; it blocks folate use, impairing lymphoma cell proliferation. High doses are required to cross the blood-brain barrier.
- Rituximab works better combined with chemotherapy than alone.

results.gold_answer:
Dear Neuro-Oncology Colleague,

I am referring a 58-year-old patient with recent onset progressive arm weakness, confusion, and double vision. MRI with gadolinium contrast revealed a solitary enhancing lesion in the right frontal lobe. The patient has no known history of immunodeficiency but is an older adult. Given these findings, primary CNS lymphoma is strongly suspected.

To confirm the diagnosis, I recommend proceeding with stereotactic biopsy, as this is the standard diagnostic procedure. Additional workup should include comprehensive laboratory tests (CBC, CMP, LDH, HIV, and hepatitis B), lumbar puncture to assess for cerebrospinal fluid involvement, and detailed eye examination due to reported visual symptoms. Performance status assessment is essential to guide both treatment planning and clinical trial eligibility.

For management, high-dose methotrexate-based chemotherapy, with consideration for rituximab, should be initiated as induction therapy, followed by consolidation with whole-brain radiation therapy or high-dose chemotherapy with stem cell rescue as appropriate. Supportive care should be provided throughout. I recommend considering clinical trial enrollment if available.

Thank you for your expert evaluation and management.
